If \(X-Y,V\in L^2(P;H)\), then the domination makes \(A\) square-integrable. Therefore \(A-V\), and hence \(X'-Y'\), is also square-integrable. All norms in the following estimate are consequently finite:

\[\begin{aligned} \|X'-Y'\|_{2,P}&=\|A-V\|_{2,P}\\ &\le\|A\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}\\ &\le q\|X-Y\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}. \end{aligned}\]

The first inequality is Minkowski, and the second follows by squaring the nonnegative pointwise domination, integrating, and taking square roots. This proves the numerical affine recurrence together with the finite moment needed to interpret it.

UnadjustedLangevin/Integrability.lean.title: Propagation of finite error moments
UnadjustedLangevin/Integrability.lean.summary:
Suppose \(E=A-V\) almost everywhere, \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, and \(\|A\|\le q\|D\|\). Finite \(L^p\) membership of \(D\) transfers to \(A\) by domination, and finite \(L^p\) membership of \(V\) then gives that of \(E\). Applied to successive coupled Euler updates, this proves finite second moments of every error from the finite initial error and finite defects.

The common noise cancels in the difference of the updates. Hence the moment induction uses only the preceding error and the defect. A contraction factor strictly below one is not needed for this finiteness result; that restriction is imposed when summing the convergence recurrence.

steps.title: Finite moments under domination and addition
steps.body:
Let \(p\in[0,+\infty]\), \(q\in\mathbb R\), and \(D,A,V,E:\Omega\to H\). Assume \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, \(E=A-V\) almost everywhere, and \(\|A\|\le q\|D\|\) almost everywhere. If \(D,V\in L^p(P;H)\), then \(E\in L^p(P;H)\).

The domination transfers the finite \(L^p\) moment of \(D\) to \(A\).

The difference \(A-V\) belongs to \(L^p\). Almost everywhere equality then transfers this property to \(E\).

The comparison of norms supplies finite \(p\)-moment size, while almost-everywhere strong measurability supplies the measurability part of membership. Combining both is necessary: a numerical upper bound alone would not define a valid Bochner-integrable random variable. The equality \(E=A-V\) then transfers membership through the algebra of \(L^p\).

steps.title: All coupling errors have finite second moment
steps.body:
Assume \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(q\ge0\), and the initial vector, every noise vector, and every \(Y_k\) are measurable. Suppose

\[Y_{k+1}=T_h(U,h,Y_k,\xi_k)+V_k\quad\text{almost everywhere},\]

and common-noise updates satisfy \(\|T_h(U,h,x,z)-T_h(U,h,y,z)\|\le q\|x-y\|\). If \(X_0-Y_0\in L^2\) and every \(V_k\in L^2\), then \(X_n-Y_n\in L^2\) for all \(n\). This assertion does not require stationarity or \(q<1\).

Let the iterates be \(X_k\), whose measurability follows from the chain lemma. We must prove \(X_n-Y_n\in L^2\).

Induct on \(n\). The initial case is the assumed finite initial error; for the successor, assume \(X_n-Y_n\in L^2\).

Set \(A=T_h(U,h,X_n,\xi_n)-T_h(U,h,Y_n,\xi_n)\), the update difference before adding the reference defect.

The gradient and both update inputs are measurable, so the update difference \(A\) is measurable and hence almost everywhere strongly measurable.

Subtract the recursive updates on the full-measure set where the reference equation holds. This gives \(X_{n+1}-Y_{n+1}=A-V_n\).

The common-noise contraction gives \(\|A\|\le q\|X_n-Y_n\|\) pointwise, hence almost everywhere.

Apply the finite-moment lemma to the induction hypothesis and \(V_n\in L^2\), proving \(X_{n+1}-Y_{n+1}\in L^2\).

At step \(n\), the shared-noise update difference is dominated by \(q\|X_n-Y_n\|\). The assumed defect has a finite second moment, so their difference does as well. Induction repeats this argument for every finite index. The proof establishes moments even in regimes with \(q\ge1\); the strict upper bound on \(q\) is used only later for decay.

UnadjustedLangevin/Recurrence.lean.title: Iteration of the scalar error estimate
UnadjustedLangevin/Recurrence.lean.summary:
Let a real sequence satisfy \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), with \(q\ge0\). Induction gives \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j\). If \(0\le q<1\), the sum equals \((1-q^n)/(1-q)\). When \(b\ge0\), it is bounded by \(1/(1-q)\), giving a uniform additive bound \(b/(1-q)\).

The upper-bound sequence \(q^ne_0+b/(1-q)\) converges to \(b/(1-q)\). Therefore every tolerance strictly above this value eventually bounds the errors. This conclusion does not imply that the error sequence itself converges or has this limit.

steps.title: Iteration gives a geometric sum
steps.body:
If \(q\ge0\) and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\) for every \(k\), then

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j.\]

Induct on \(n\). At zero the sum is empty and both sides equal \(e_0\). Assume the bound at \(n\).

Multiply the induction inequality by \(q\ge0\), preserving its direction.

Write \(S_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j\). The geometric identity gives \(qS_n+1=S_n+q^n\); multiply this equality by \(b\).

Combine the one-step bound with the multiplied induction bound. Since \(S_{n+1}=S_n+q^n\), obtain \(e_{n+1}\le q^{n+1}e_0+bS_{n+1}\).

The empty sum at \(n=0\) is zero, so the initial condition is preserved exactly. The next step multiplies every previous contribution by \(q\) and inserts one new defect of size \(b\). The resulting powers in the geometric sum have indices \(j=0,\ldots,n-1\).

steps.title: The finite geometric-sum bound
steps.body:
If \(0\le q<1\) and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), then

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+\frac{b(1-q^n)}{1-q}.\]

Apply the geometric-sum bound and evaluate the sum as \((q^n-1)/(q-1)\). Its denominator is nonzero because \(q<1\).

Change the signs of numerator and denominator simultaneously and put \(b\) in the numerator to obtain \(b(1-q^n)/(1-q)\).

The numerator \(1-q^n\) retains the finite-horizon effect of the defects: no defect has acted before time zero, and only \(n\) of them have appeared by index \(n\). Dividing by \(1-q>0\) evaluates the finite sum. This is the bound before replacing the finite sum by its infinite-sum upper bound.

steps.title: A uniform additive error bound
steps.body:
If \(0\le q<1\), \(b\ge0\), and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), then

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+\frac b{1-q}.\]

Start from the exact finite-horizon bound. Its denominator \(1-q\) is positive.

Since \(q^n\ge0\) and \(b\ge0\), the numerator satisfies \(b(1-q^n)\le b\).

Divide by the positive denominator, add \(q^ne_0\), and compose with the exact bound.

Since \(0\le q^n\le1\), dropping \(1-q^n\) enlarges only the nonnegative forcing contribution. The initial term remains \(q^ne_0\). The additive term in this upper bound is independent of the iteration count, and the initial-error term decreases geometrically.

steps.title: Limit of the upper-bound sequence
steps.body:
For \(0\le q<1\) and arbitrary real \(b,e_0\),

\[q^ne_0+\frac b{1-q}\longrightarrow\frac b{1-q}\quad(n\to\infty).\]

The geometric powers satisfy \(q^n\to0\).

Multiply this limit by \(e_0\) and add the constant \(b/(1-q)\).

The upper-bound sequence is the sum of a constant and \(q^ne_0\). For \(0\le q<1\), the latter tends to zero for every fixed real initial value. Hence this upper-bound sequence tends to \(b/(1-q)\). A bound by this sequence controls the limiting upper error; it need not imply that the sequence itself converges.

steps.title: Eventual error below any larger tolerance
steps.body:
Assume \(0\le q<1\), \(b\ge0\), and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\). For every \(\varepsilon>b/(1-q)\), the errors satisfy \(e_n<\varepsilon\) for every sufficiently large \(n\).

The upper-bound sequence tends to a value strictly below \(\varepsilon\), so it is eventually below \(\varepsilon\).

At each such index, bound \(e_n\) by that sequence by the recurrence bound and then below \(\varepsilon\).

Given \(\varepsilon>b/(1-q)\), the difference from the limiting upper bound is positive. The homogeneous term eventually lies below this difference. Choose an index after which \(q^ne_0\) lies below that gap. The uniform recurrence bound then places every later error below \(\varepsilon\), which is the precise eventual-accuracy conclusion.

UnadjustedLangevin/InitialCoupling.lean.title: Passing from a chosen initial coupling to an infimum
UnadjustedLangevin/InitialCoupling.lean.summary:
Let the output measures be fixed and assume that every initial coupling gives an affine bound in its cost with the same constants. Taking the infimum over couplings gives the corresponding bound in \(W_2(\mu,\nu)\). This uses the infimum property and does not assume an optimal coupling.

If the initial transport distance is finite, a finite-cost coupling exists. Approximate minimizing couplings then suffice even if the assumed estimate is stated only for finite-cost couplings. When the affine coefficient is zero, one such coupling already proves the constant bound. When it is positive, couplings with cost approaching the infimum give the result by taking a limit.

steps.title: A uniform affine estimate passes to the infimum
steps.body:
Let \(a\ge0\) be finite, \(b\in[0,+\infty]\), and \(\Gamma(\mu, u) e\varnothing\). If the fixed output measures satisfy

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le ac(\gamma)+b\quad ext{for every }\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u),\]

then \(W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b\).

Use the nonempty coupling family and expand transport distances as infima.

Multiplication by finite \(a\ge0\) and addition of \(b\) commute with the nonempty extended-real infimum, including \(a=0\). Thus \(aW_2(\mu, u)+b=\inf_\gamma(ac(\gamma)+b)\).

The output distance lies below every member of this last family, hence below its infimum.

For \(a>0\), choose couplings whose costs approach the infimum and apply the estimate to each one. Multiplication by \(a\) and addition of \(b\) commute with this monotone affine approximation. At \(a=0\), the conclusion is simply the common constant bound \(b\), so no optimizer or limiting transport cost is required.

steps.title: A finite infimum supplies a finite-cost coupling
steps.body:
If \(W_2(\mu,\nu)<+\infty\), then some \(\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)\) has \(c(\gamma)<+\infty\). Attainment of the infimum is not asserted.

The coupling-cost infimum is strictly below \(+\infty\) by the finiteness hypothesis.

An infimum strictly below a threshold has a member strictly below that threshold. Apply this with threshold \(+\infty\).

If every admissible coupling had infinite cost, the infimum of their costs would also be infinite. Thus a finite infimum provides at least one finite-cost plan. More quantitatively, an approximate minimizer with cost below the finite infimum plus one is sufficient to establish the required finiteness.

steps.title: The real uniform-coupling estimate
steps.body:
Let \(a,b\ge0\) be finite and assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<+\infty\). If \(W_2(\mu', u')\le ac(\gamma)+b\) for every initial coupling, then

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b.\]

A finite initial distance supplies a coupling. Apply the extended uniform-coupling lemma to obtain the desired inequality in extended reals.

The product \(aW_2(\mu, u)\) is finite.

Its sum with finite \(b\) is finite, so the extended output inequality permits monotone real conversion.

Distribute real conversion through the finite sum and product to obtain the real inequality.

The extended estimate is first applied while retaining finite transport and coupling values. Their embeddings and real values then agree, so the affine inequality may be read in ordinary real arithmetic. Every quantity used in this real inequality is finite by the preceding bounds.

steps.title: Finite-cost initial couplings suffice
steps.body:
Let \(a,b\ge0\) be finite and assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\) and \(W_2(\mu', u')<\infty\). Suppose every finite-cost initial coupling satisfies

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le a c(\gamma)+b\qquad (\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u),\ c(\gamma)<\infty).\]

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), finiteness of the initial infimum supplies a coupling \(\gamma_\varepsilon\) with

\[c(\gamma_\varepsilon)<W_2(\mu, u)+\varepsilon<\infty.\]

Insert this coupling into the uniform estimate. For \(a>0\), let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) to obtain

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b.\]

If \(a=0\), any one of these finite-cost couplings already gives the conclusion \(W_2(\mu', u')\le b\). Thus no expression involving zero times infinite cost is needed. Infinite-cost couplings cannot improve a finite infimum, and no minimizing coupling is assumed to exist.

UnadjustedLangevin/Convergence.lean.title: The conditional common-noise convergence theorem
UnadjustedLangevin/Convergence.lean.summary:
Let \(X_k\) be the numerical iterates and \(Y_k\) a supplied reference on the same probability space, with \(\mathcal L(Y_k)=\pi\). Assume a common-noise update contraction with factor \(0\le q<1\), a finite initial mean-square difference, and square-integrable reference defects bounded in norm by \(b\). Subtracting the updates gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), where \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_k\|_2\). Moment propagation ensures these norms are finite.

The joint law of \((X_n,Y_n)\) bounds \(W_2(\mathcal L(X_n),\pi)\) by \(e_n\). Iteration gives the stated transport estimate. Its initial term is the cost of the supplied coupling. Replacing that cost by an initial Wasserstein distance requires the same construction and constants for every finite-cost initial coupling.

steps.title: Transport bound from a supplied discrete reference
steps.body:
Let \(\nabla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(0\le q<1\), and \(b\ge0\). Assume the initial vector, all noise vectors, and all reference vectors \(Y_k\) are measurable; \((Y_k)_\#P=\pi\); and

\[Y_{k+1}=T_h(U,h,Y_k,\xi_k)+V_k\quad\text{almost everywhere}.\]

Suppose the common-noise update is \(q\)-contractive, \(X_0-Y_0\in L^2\), every \(V_k\in L^2\), and \(\|V_k\|_2\le b\). Then

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_0\|_2+\frac b{1-q}.\]

The initial term is the cost of the chosen coupled pair.

Let the iterates be \(X_k\) and let \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_k\|_2\).

Finite moments propagate from the initial error and the defects, so each \(e_k\) is a finite \(L^2\) norm. Every numerical iterate is measurable.

To derive the recurrence, fix \(k\) and set \(A=T_h(U,h,X_k,\xi_k)-T_h(U,h,Y_k,\xi_k)\).

Measurability of the gradient and the inputs makes \(A\) measurable, hence almost everywhere strongly measurable.

Subtract the two updates on the full-measure set where the reference identity holds. This yields \(X_{k+1}-Y_{k+1}=A-V_k\).

The common-noise contraction gives \(\|A\|\le q\|X_k-Y_k\|\).

The finite-moment synchronous bound and \(\|V_k\|_2\le b\) give the recurrence \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\).

The joint law of the coupled pair bounds transport by \(e_n\). Its reference marginal is \(\pi\) by the supplied stationary law.

Iterate the derived recurrence to get \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b/(1-q)\), and compose with the transport comparison.

For the chosen reference, let \(e_k=(\mathbb E\|X_k-Y_k\|^2)^{1/2}\). The shared-noise decomposition gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), with all norms finite by the preceding induction. Therefore \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b(1-q^n)/(1-q)\). The coupling inequality and stationarity of \(Y_n\) yield the displayed result after replacing the finite geometric factor by its uniform upper bound.

UnadjustedLangevin/HilbertDalalyan.lean.title: Convergence in a Hilbert space of random variables
UnadjustedLangevin/HilbertDalalyan.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal H=L^2(P;H)\) and let the gradient act by pointwise composition. Supply continuous reference segments \(Y_{k,t}\), joining at grid endpoints, whose grid laws equal \(\pi\). Their endpoint noise is the innovation driving the numerical step. The reference integral equation and the bounds \(\|g(Y_{k,t})\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\) and \(\|B_{k,t}\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) give a defect norm at most \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}\) when \(Lh\le2\).

The common-noise subtraction and the deterministic Euler contraction give an affine recurrence in \(\mathcal H\). Its geometric sum bounds the transport distance of the numerical law from \(\pi\). The two step ranges use factors \(1-mh\) and \(Lh-1\), respectively. The reference and its stationary laws are hypotheses here; the Brownian construction later supplies them.

steps.title: The recursion on square-integrable random variables
steps.body:
For an initial \(X_0\in L^2(P;H)\) and innovations \(\xi_k\in L^2(P;H)\), set \(X_{k+1}=X_k-h\widehat{\nabla U}(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k\).

The initial iterate is the supplied random vector.

Each successor uses the Euler update using the given gradient.

The drift lift evaluates the original gradient almost everywhere, so this recursion represents the ordinary ULA method on random inputs. The reference equation and defect integral are Bochner equations in this same Hilbert space. Each step stays square-integrable by the Lipschitz growth estimate for the gradient.

steps.title: The successor update
steps.body:
The next iterate is exactly one L² ULA update of the current iterate.

Evaluate the successor clause of the definition.

The successor step uses the innovation at the same index as the reference endpoint. Subtracting a reference equation using that same innovation removes the stochastic increment exactly. The resulting error equation therefore contains only the deterministic Euler difference and the local defect.

steps.title: The continuous reference assumptions
steps.body:
For an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, step \(h\), noise vectors \(\xi_k\in\mathcal H\), and a measure \(\pi\), a reference consists of segments \(Y_{k,t}\in\mathcal H\) and increments \(B_{k,t}\in\mathcal H\) satisfying the following conditions.

Supply the two families \((Y_{k,t})\) and \((B_{k,t})\) in the Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).

Require continuity of \(t\mapsto Y_{k,t}\) in the \(L^2\) norm for every \(k\).

Require compatible endpoints, common endpoint noise, and stationary grid laws:

\[Y_{k,h}=Y_{k+1,0},\qquad B_{k,h}=\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k,\qquad(Y_{k,0})_\#P=\pi.\]

For \(0\le t\le h\), require

\[Y_{k,t}-Y_{k,0}=-\int_0^t g(Y_{k,s})\,ds+B_{k,t}.\]

Require the score moment bound \(\|g(Y_{k,t})\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\) throughout each closed step interval.

Require the increment moment bound \(\|B_{k,t}\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) on the same interval.

The segment-joining condition makes the local initial point of segment \(k+1\) equal to the endpoint of segment \(k\). The stationary grid-law condition identifies each comparison marginal with \(\pi\), while the endpoint-noise condition identifies the reference's final increment with the algorithm innovation. The two moment assumptions have different roles: drift controls the deterministic segment increment, and noise controls its square-root growth.

steps.title: Convergence from the supplied integral reference
steps.body:
Suppose a reference with the preceding properties is supplied, \(h\ge0\), and \(Lh\le2\). Let \(0\le q<1\), and assume the lifted Euler map contracts:

\[\|(X-hg(X))-(Y-hg(Y))\|_2\le q\|X-Y\|_2.\]

For any initial vector \(X_0\in\mathcal H\), the \(L^2\) chain driven by the reference endpoint noise satisfies

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-q}.\]

The statement is conditional on the supplied reference, and the initial term is the cost of the chosen coupling.

Set \(g=\widehat{\nabla U}\), write the numerical iterates as \(X_k\), and define

\[b=\frac{33}{20}Lh\sqrt{hd},\qquad D_k=\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_{k,t})-g(Y_{k,0})\bigr)\,dt.\]

The bound \(b\) is nonnegative. Apply the local-defect theorem to the gradient map on square-integrable classes and the supplied equation and moment bounds, deriving \(\|D_k\|_2\le b\).

We claim the reference endpoints obey

\[Y_{k+1,0}=Y_{k,0}-hg(Y_{k,0})+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k-D_k.\]

The lifted gradient is Lipschitz and the reference segment is continuous, so their composition is continuous and Bochner integrable on \([0,h]\).

Apply the Euler-defect identity at \(t=h\), then substitute the segment join and endpoint noise identities. This proves the claimed reference update. Its defect has a minus sign.

Fix \(k\) and compare the numerical update with the reference endpoint equation, both using the same \(\xi_k\).

Cancel their identical noise terms. Because the reference subtracts \(D_k\),

\[X_{k+1}-Y_{k+1,0}=\bigl(X_k-hg(X_k)\bigr)-\bigl(Y_{k,0}-hg(Y_{k,0})\bigr)+D_k.\]

Apply the triangle inequality, Euler contraction, and the defect bound. Setting \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_{k,0}\|_2\) gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\).

The joint law of the pair supplies a finite-cost coupling, so its transport distance is at most \(e_n\). The second marginal is \(\pi\) by the stationary grid-law assumption.

Apply the scalar recurrence bound to the derived inequality and compose it with the transport comparison.

The defect has size \(b=(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}\), and this size is uniform in \(k\) because the supplied moment bounds hold on every segment. The recurrence is consequently homogeneous in its constants. Its initial value remains the norm of the supplied pair, so this bound retains the cost of the supplied initial coupling until the subsequent infimum argument.

steps.title: The small-step bound
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(H\), \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(0<m\le L\). Let \(0<h\le2/(m+L)\), and supply a reference with the preceding properties. For any initial vector \(X_0\in\mathcal H\),

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le(1-mh)^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}.\]

This uses a chosen initial coupling and a supplied stationary reference. Replacing the initial cost by \(W_2(\mathcal L(X_0),\pi)\) needs the additional uniform family of reference couplings explained in the final section.

Since \(m+L>0\), clear the positive denominator in the step hypothesis to obtain \(h(m+L)\le2\).

Use \(m\le L\) to get \(2mh\le h(m+L)\le2\), hence \(mh\le1\).

The same threshold gives \(Lh\le2\). Thus \(q=1-mh\ge0\); since \(mh>0\), also \(q<1\).

The sharp small-step contraction of the lifted Euler map gives the contraction hypothesis with \(q=1-mh\). Apply the integral-reference theorem.

Because \(m,h>0\), simplify the bias term:

\[\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-(1-mh)}=\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{mh}=\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}.\]

Substitute the bias identity into the integral-reference bound.

The factor \(q=1-mh\) lies in \([0,1)\) under the positive-curvature small-step assumptions. Its gap is exactly \(mh\), so dividing the local \(h^{3/2}\) error by that gap produces the global \(\sqrt h\) bias. The remaining factor \(L/m\) is the condition-number dependence of this estimate.

steps.title: The large-step bound
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(H\), \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(0<m\le L\). Let \(h>0\), \(h\ge2/(m+L)\), and \(Lh<2\), and supply a reference with the stated properties. For any initial vector \(X_0\in\mathcal H\),

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le(Lh-1)^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{33}{20}\frac{Lh}{2-Lh}\sqrt{hd}.\]

The denominator is positive by strict stability. The reference remains an input, and the initial term remains the chosen coupling cost.

Since \(m+L>0\), clear the denominator in the lower step threshold to obtain \(2\le h(m+L)\).

Use \(m\le L\) and \(h\ge0\): \(2\le h(m+L)\le2Lh\). Thus \(Lh\ge1\) and \(q=Lh-1\ge0\).

Strict stability \(Lh<2\) gives \(q=Lh-1<1\).

Apply the sharp large-step Euler contraction with \(q=Lh-1\), then invoke the integral-reference theorem.

Use \(1-(Lh-1)=2-Lh\) and factor out \(\sqrt{hd}\):

\[\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-(Lh-1)}=\left(\frac{(33/20)Lh}{2-Lh}\right)\sqrt{hd}.\]

Substitute this identity into the integral-reference bound to obtain the large-step formula.

Here \(q=Lh-1\) and the gap is \(1-q=2-Lh>0\). Dividing the same local-defect estimate by that gap gives the displayed additive large-step bound. As the denominator decreases to zero, this geometric-sum upper bound increases. The strict condition on the step keeps the denominator positive.

UnadjustedLangevin/L2Convergence.lean.title: Convergence for Euclidean random vectors
UnadjustedLangevin/L2Convergence.lean.summary:
Take the pointwise state space to be \(\mathbb R^d\). The norm on the random-variable space is \(\|X\|_2=(\mathbb E\sum_iX_i^2)^{1/2}\). The reference assumptions, integral equation, and endpoint innovation identities are those of the Hilbert-space result. Equality of the Euclidean and Hilbert-space recursions follows by induction from their equal initial values and equal successor maps.

Consequently the same defect and contraction estimates give the Euclidean transport bounds. The constants and the supplied initial coupling are unchanged by this specialization. In particular, these statements do not add existence or stationarity of the reference; those remain the stated hypotheses.

steps.title: The reference assumptions in Euclidean space
steps.body:
For an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, step \(h\), noise vectors \(\xi_k\in\mathcal H\), and a measure \(\pi\), a reference consists of segments \(Y_{k,t}\in\mathcal H\) and increments \(B_{k,t}\in\mathcal H\) satisfying the following conditions.

Use the same segment and increment assumptions with Euclidean pointwise states.

Specializing the ambient state to \(\mathbb R^d\) changes the pointwise norm to the Euclidean norm and leaves the \(L^2\) construction intact. The segment equation, endpoint joining, noise normalization, stationary law, and two moment bounds are all the same assumptions. The definition specifies these reference properties; it does not prove that such a reference exists.

steps.title: Equality of the two recursions
steps.body:
For every \(n\), the Euclidean L² chain equals the common Hilbert-space L² chain.

Induct on the index and unfold the matching recursive clauses.

Both chains start from the same \(L^2\) class and apply the same gradient and innovation at the next index. Induction therefore identifies their states at every finite index. Equality as classes also identifies their pushforward laws and their errors against any common reference class, allowing the general theorem to be expressed in Euclidean notation.

steps.title: Convergence from the integral reference in Euclidean space
steps.body:
Suppose a reference with the preceding properties is supplied, \(h\ge0\), and \(Lh\le2\). Let \(0\le q<1\), and assume the lifted Euler map contracts:

\[\|(X-hg(X))-(Y-hg(Y))\|_2\le q\|X-Y\|_2.\]

For any initial vector \(X_0\in\mathcal H\), the \(L^2\) chain driven by the reference endpoint noise satisfies

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-q}.\]

The statement is conditional on the supplied reference, and the initial term is the cost of the chosen coupling.

Apply the shared theorem, then rewrite the recursion to its Euclidean notation.

The local defect and synchronous contraction estimates already hold in arbitrary Hilbert spaces of random vectors. Applying them with Euclidean pointwise states yields the same geometric initial-error term and additive bound. No additional dimension factor appears at this specialization: the dimension has already entered through the Gaussian noise and Gibbs score moments.

steps.title: The small-step bound in Euclidean space
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^d\), \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(0<m\le L\). Let \(0<h\le2/(m+L)\), and supply a reference with the preceding properties. For any initial vector \(X_0\in\mathcal H\),

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le(1-mh)^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}.\]

This uses a chosen initial coupling and a supplied stationary reference. Replacing the initial cost by \(W_2(\mathcal L(X_0),\pi)\) needs the additional uniform family of reference couplings explained in the final section.

Apply the shared theorem, then rewrite the recursion to its Euclidean notation.

The coefficient \(1-mh\) is nonnegative because \(mh\le1\) in this regime. The local error is divided by its gap \(mh\), giving \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{hd}\). The finite initial cost is the Euclidean \(L^2\) separation of the supplied initial and reference vectors, exactly as in the general Hilbert result.

steps.title: The large-step bound in Euclidean space
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^d\), \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(0<m\le L\). Let \(h>0\), \(h\ge2/(m+L)\), and \(Lh<2\), and supply a reference with the stated properties. For any initial vector \(X_0\in\mathcal H\),

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le(Lh-1)^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{33}{20}\frac{Lh}{2-Lh}\sqrt{hd}.\]

The denominator is positive by strict stability. The reference remains an input, and the initial term remains the chosen coupling cost.

Apply the shared theorem, then rewrite the recursion to its Euclidean notation.

The Euclidean specialization retains the strict stability condition \(Lh<2\), ensuring a positive denominator. As in the Hilbert argument, the stationary reference remains an input at this stage. A later construction uniform over all finite-cost initial couplings replaces the chosen initial error by the initial Wasserstein distance.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Theorem.lean.title: Entropy convergence under interpolation assumptions
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Theorem.lean.summary:
Let \( ho_k\) be the ULA laws, let \( u\) satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha>0\), and let \( abla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. This result assumes a positive differentiable relative density for each interpolation, finite entropy and Fisher information, an entropy derivative estimate, and a bound on the initial gradient moment. Under \(\alpha\le L\) and \(0

For one step put \(H(t)=\operatorname{KL}( ho_{k,t}\mid u)\), \(I(t)=I_ u( ho_{k,t})\), and \(G_k=\int\| abla U\|^2d ho_k\). The assumed inequalities are \(H'\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_k+2tdL^2\), \(I\ge2\alpha H\), and \(G_k\le(4L^2/\alpha)H_k+2dL\). The equalities \( ho_{k,0}= ho_k\) and \( ho_{k,h}= ho_{k+1}\) then give a recurrence for \(H_k\). These analytic interpolation assumptions are retained in this theorem.

steps.title: Iteration of the conditional entropy estimate
steps.body:
Suppose each interpolation satisfies the stated regularity, finiteness and derivative assumptions. The one-step calculation gives

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2.\]

Induction therefore yields \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+6h^2dL^2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{-\alpha hj}\). The assumptions on the constants give \(\alpha h\le\alpha^2/(4L^2)\le1/4\). For \(0\le x\le1/4\), \(1-e^{-x}\ge3x/4\); hence the geometric sum is at most \(4/(3\alpha h)\). Substitution proves

\[H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid\nu)+\frac{8hdL^2}{\alpha}.\]

Here \(\rho_0=\mu\) identifies the initial entropy. The conclusion depends on all the interpolation assumptions stated above.

steps.title: Finiteness of the entropy of each iterate
steps.body:
Assume the interpolating law has finite relative entropy at every elapsed time in \([0,h]\), including zero. At elapsed time zero the equality of laws is \(r_{k,0} u= ho_k\). Therefore

\[\operatorname{KL}( ho_k\mid u)=\operatorname{KL}(r_{k,0} u\mid u)<\infty.\]

This argument applies to every index \(k\). It establishes finiteness before the divergences are treated as real numbers in the recurrence. Finiteness of Fisher information at a positive time has a different use: together with LSI it bounds the entropy at that time.

steps.title: The gradient second moment at the start of a step
steps.body:
Assume \(\|\nabla U\|^2\) is integrable under \(\rho_k\), and define

\[G_k=\int\|\nabla U(x)\|^2\,d\rho_k(x).\]

The index \(k\) is fixed during the interpolation, so \(G_k\) does not depend on its elapsed time. The assumed bound \(G_k\le(4L^2/\alpha)H_k+2dL\) separates the part proportional to the starting entropy from the remaining constant. Multiplying it by \(t^2L^2\) gives the error term in the differential inequality. The integrability assumption is needed because that calculation uses an ordinary finite integral.

steps.title: The one-step entropy inequality
steps.body:
The interpolation identities imply \(H(0)=H_k\) and \(H(h)=H_{k+1}\). Its laws are probability measures, so each positive normalized relative density is admissible for LSI. Finiteness of entropy and Fisher information permits the real inequality \(I(t)\ge2\alpha H(t)\). Combining it with the derivative assumption gives

\[H'(t)\le-\frac{3\alpha}{2}H(t)+t^2L^2G_k+2tdL^2.\]

Insert the assumed bound on \(G_k\). The step restriction bounds the part proportional to \(H_k\) by \(\alpha H_k/4\), and bounds the remaining part by \((5/2)hdL^2\). Integration of this affine differential inequality, followed by the elementary exponential comparison for \(0\le\alpha h\le1/4\), gives

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2.\]

The differentiability, continuity and finiteness hypotheses justify this integration; they are assumptions of the present result.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/FunctionalInequal.title: Relative entropy, Fisher information and the log-Sobolev inequality
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/FunctionalInequal.summary: Let \( u\) be a probability measure and let \(r\) be a positive normalized density relative to \( u\). Write \( ho_r=r u\). Relative entropy and relative Fisher information are denoted by \(H_ u( ho_r)=\operatorname{KL}( ho_r\mid u)\) and \(I_ u(r)=\int\| abla\log r\|^2d ho_r\). Both may initially equal infinity. The log-Sobolev convention used here is \(2\alpha H_ u( ho_r)\le I_ u(r)\), tested on strictly positive \(C^1\) densities of probability measures. Finite-value versions of the inequality are used only after both quantities have been proved finite.

steps.title: The measure defined by a density
steps.body: For a measurable real function \(r\), let \(r_+(x)=\max\{r(x),0\}\) and define \( ho_r(A)=\int_A r_+\,d u\). If \(r\ge0\), this is the usual measure \(r u\). If also \(\int r\,d u=1\), it is a probability measure. Thus the measure can be defined without imposing normalization; normalization is an additional hypothesis when probability identities are used. Strict positivity is required later to differentiate \(\log r\).

steps.title: Relative Fisher information
steps.body:
For a specified positive differentiable density \(r\), define

\[I_ u(r)=\int\| abla\log r(x)\|^2\,d ho_r(x).\]

This is a nonnegative integral, with value in \([0,\infty]\). It does not require choosing a differentiable version of an unspecified almost-everywhere density: the function \(r\) itself is given. If \( u\) has Gibbs density \(J=Z^{-1}e^{-U}\) and \( ho_r\) has Lebesgue density \(p\), then \(r=p/J\) and \( abla\log r= abla\log p+ abla U\). Consequently the Fisher information measures the squared difference between the logarithmic derivatives of the two densities.

steps.title: The log-Sobolev convention
steps.body:
The statement that \( u\) satisfies LSI with constant \(\alpha\) means that \( u\) is a probability measure and

\[2\alpha\operatorname{KL}(r u\mid u)\le I_ u(r)\]

for every strictly positive \(C^1\) function \(r\) such that \(r u\) is a probability measure. The inequality is initially understood for nonnegative extended quantities. The test class is part of the hypothesis: no claim that an arbitrary probability measure has such a density is included. In the ULA proof, the Gaussian convolution is first shown to produce a density in this test class; LSI is then applied to that density.

steps.title: LSI when entropy and Fisher information are finite
steps.body:
Suppose \(\alpha\ge0\), \(r>0\), \(r\in C^1\), and \(r u\) is a probability measure. Assume both \(\operatorname{KL}(r u\mid u)\) and \(I_ u(r)\) are finite. The extended inequality supplied by LSI is then an inequality between finite nonnegative numbers. Its ordinary real form is

\[2\alpha H_ u(r u)\le I_ u(r).\]

The coefficient is unchanged because \(2\alpha\ge0\). Establishing the two finiteness conditions first permits subsequent subtraction and integration of ordinary real functions.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyFlow.lean.title: Entropy decay from a dissipation identity
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyFlow.lean.summary: Let \(r_t\nu\) be a specified path of probability measures. Suppose the densities are strictly positive and \(C^1\), entropy and Fisher information are finite, entropy is continuous in time, and its right derivative equals minus the Fisher information. If \(\nu\) satisfies LSI with constant \(\alpha>0\), then \(H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\). The proof concerns any path satisfying these assumptions. A ULA interpolation has an additional drift-error term and requires a separate estimate.

steps.title: Entropy of a specified relative density
steps.body: For \( ho_r=r u\), write \(H_ u(r)=\operatorname{KL}( ho_r\mid u)\) whenever the divergence is finite. This notation refers to the divergence of the two measures, not to an independent error function. Under the appropriate integrability assumption it equals \(\int r\log r\,d u\). That equality must be established before differentiating the integral. In particular, differentiation of an entropy integral requires both identification with the divergence and control of its integrand.

steps.title: Exponential entropy decay
steps.body:
For each \(t\in[0,T]\), apply the finite LSI to the density \(r_t\). It gives \(2\alpha H(t)\le I(t)\). The assumed right-dissipation identity therefore implies \(H'(t)\le-2\alpha H(t)\) for \(t\[(e^{2\alpha t}H(t))'\le0.\]

The right-derivative comparison, together with continuity of \(H\) on the closed interval, shows that the weighted entropy is nonincreasing. Evaluating at zero yields \(H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\). Positivity, differentiability and normalization of the densities are used at the LSI step; the time regularity is used in the scalar comparison.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ULALaw.lean.title: The Gaussian ULA transition and its interpolation
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ULALaw.lean.summary: Let \(\gamma_d\) denote standard Gaussian measure, and set \(T_t(x,z)=x-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z\) for \(t\ge0\). For an initial law \(\mu\), define \(P_t\mu=(T_t)_*(\mu\otimes\gamma_d)\). The product measure specifies that the Gaussian variable is independent of the initial state. For a fixed step \(h\), put \(\rho_0=\mu\) and \(\rho_{k+1}=P_h\rho_k\). The interpolation during step \(k\) is \(\rho_{k,t}=P_t\rho_k\); it satisfies \(\rho_{k,0}=\rho_k\) and \(\rho_{k,h}=\rho_{k+1}\).

steps.title: Entropy of the ULA iterates
steps.body: Define \(H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\mid\nu)\), where \(\rho_k\) is obtained by applying the Gaussian transition \(k\) times. The divergence is allowed to equal infinity at the definition stage. To use the sequence in a real recurrence, one must prove \(H_k<\infty\) at every index. In the final convergence theorem this is proved by induction from finite initial entropy, using the positive-time Gaussian density and LSI.

steps.title: Entropy at the initial law
steps.body: The zeroth iterate of the transition is the identity, so \(\rho_0=\mu\). Substitution in the definition of entropy gives \(H_0=\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid\nu)\). This equality holds independently of the step size. When the initial divergence is finite, it provides the numerical initial value in the entropy recurrence.

steps.title: Definition of the interpolating law
steps.body:
Let \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Z\sim\gamma_d\) be independent. Define

\[P_t\mu=\operatorname{Law}(X-t\nabla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z)=(T_t)_*(\mu\otimes\gamma_d).\]

Conditional on \(X=x\), the new variable has Gaussian law with mean \(x-t\nabla U(x)\) and covariance \(2tI_d\). The gradient is evaluated at the initial state throughout this interpolation. This conditional law determines the mixture density and the drift discrepancy used in the entropy calculation.

steps.title: Iteration of the transition
steps.body: For a fixed \(h\), define \(\rho_k=P_h^k\mu\). Each transition is applied to the law obtained at the preceding index and integrates a new independent Gaussian variable. A stochastic recursion with innovations independent of its initial state and of its past has these marginal laws: conditioning on the current state gives \(P_h\), and induction identifies its distribution at every index. The definition by measures therefore does not depend on a particular probability space realizing the recursion.

steps.title: The final law of one interpolation step
steps.body:
The interpolation starting from \(\rho_k\) is \(\rho_{k,t}=P_t\rho_k\). At elapsed time \(h\), the defining recursion gives

\[\rho_{k,h}=P_h\rho_k=\rho_{k+1}.\]

Consequently an entropy estimate for the interpolation at \(h\) is an estimate for the next ULA iterate. This equality, rather than an approximation by a continuous diffusion, is used to derive the discrete recurrence.

steps.title: Each iterate is a probability measure
steps.body: Suppose \(\mu\) is a probability measure and \(\nabla U\) is Lipschitz. The gradient is continuous, so the Gaussian update map is measurable. The transition preserves total mass because it is a pushforward of the product of two probability measures. Starting with \(\rho_0=\mu\), induction using \(\rho_{k+1}=P_h\rho_k\) proves that every \(\rho_k\) has mass one. The probability assumptions in the subsequent entropy identities thus hold at every index.

steps.title: The interpolating law at zero
steps.body: At \(t=0\), the map satisfies \(T_0(x,z)=x\): both time-dependent terms vanish. Its pushforward is the first marginal of \(\mu\otimes\gamma_d\). Since the Gaussian measure has mass one, that marginal is \(\mu\). Therefore \(P_0\mu=\mu\). The proof is an equality of measures and uses no limiting argument or regularity of \(U\).

steps.title: The zeroth iterate
steps.body: By definition, the zeroth iterate of any transition map is the identity map on measures. It follows that \(\rho_0=\mu\). No Gaussian transition is performed at this index. In particular, the initialization in the stochastic recursion and in the entropy estimate refers to the same measure.

steps.title: The recursion for successive laws
steps.body:
The elementary identity for iterates of a map gives \(P_h^{k+1}\mu=P_h(P_h^k\mu)\). In the notation for ULA laws this is

\[\rho_{k+1}=P_h(\rho_k).\]

The order of composition agrees with one additional update of the current state using a fresh Gaussian variable. This identity is used when the one-step entropy estimate is iterated.

steps.title: The interpolation preserves total mass
steps.body: Assume \(\nabla U\) is Lipschitz and \(\mu\) is a probability measure. For fixed \(t\), addition, scalar multiplication and continuity of the gradient make \(T_t\) measurable. The product \(\mu\otimes\gamma_d\) has total mass one. A measurable pushforward has the same total mass as its source; hence \(P_t\mu\) is a probability measure. This argument also verifies the normalization of each density used in LSI.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianDrift.lea.title: Gaussian displacement and the gradient error
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianDrift.lea.summary: Let \(Z\) be a standard Gaussian vector in dimension \(d\), independent of \(X\), and let \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). If \(G_0=\mathbb E\| abla U(X)\|^2<\infty\), then \(\mathbb E\|Y_t-X\|^2=t^2G_0+2td\). Centering and independence make the mixed term vanish. If the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). These statements require a moment of the gradient, not a second moment of the absolute position.

steps.title: The Gaussian second moment
steps.body: Let \((e_i)_{i=1}^d\) be an orthonormal basis. Parseval's identity gives \(\|Z\|^2=\sum_i\langle e_i,Z\rangle^2\). Each coordinate is a centered real Gaussian with variance one, so its second moment is one. All coordinates are square-integrable, and the sum is finite; hence integration commutes with this sum and gives \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=d\). When \(d=0\), the sum is empty and both sides are zero.

steps.title: The second moment of an affine Gaussian expression
steps.body:
Let \(g(X)\) be square-integrable and independent of \(Z\). Expanding the squared norm gives

\[\|ag(X)+bZ\|^2=a^2\|g(X)\|^2+2ab\langle g(X),Z\rangle+b^2\|Z\|^2.\]

Cauchy–Schwarz proves integrability of the mixed term. Independence permits its expectation to be written as \(\langle\mathbb E g(X),\mathbb E Z\rangle\), which is zero because \(\mathbb E Z=0\). The two square terms are integrable by the assumed moment and the Gaussian moment formula. Therefore \(\mathbb E\|ag(X)+bZ\|^2=a^2\mathbb E\|g(X)\|^2+b^2d\).

steps.title: The proposal displacement
steps.body:
Subtracting the initial point from the update map gives

\[T_t(x,z)-x=-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z.\]

The equality follows by cancellation of the two occurrences of \(x\). Thus all estimates for the displacement involve only the initial gradient and the Gaussian vector. In particular, square-integrability of the absolute initial position is not needed for the displacement estimate.

steps.title: The displacement second moment
steps.body:
Use the affine Gaussian formula with \(a=-t\), \(b=\sqrt{2t}\), and \(g=\nabla U\). For \(t\ge0\), the squared coefficients are \(t^2\) and \(2t\). It follows that

\[\mathbb E\|T_t(X,Z)-X\|^2=t^2\mathbb E\|\nabla U(X)\|^2+2td.\]

There is no estimate of a mixed term in this formula: its expectation is exactly zero by independence and centering. This accounts for the coefficient \(2\) of the dimensional term.

steps.title: The gradient discrepancy
steps.body:
Assume the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz. Pointwise,

\[\| abla U(T_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2\|T_t-X\|^2.\]

The right-hand side is integrable by the displacement moment formula. The left-hand side is measurable by continuity of the gradient and measurability of the proposal, so this domination also proves its integrability. Integrating the pointwise inequality gives \(\mathbb E\| abla U(T_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The conditional expectation given the final state is introduced separately; the present estimate is on the joint law of the initial state and Gaussian variable.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the displacement
steps.body: On the product probability space, the first-coordinate function \(\nabla U(X)\) is square-integrable by assumption, and the second-coordinate Gaussian \(Z\) is square-integrable by its second moment. Multiplication by the fixed scalars \(-t\) and \(\sqrt{2t}\) preserves square-integrability. Their sum is therefore in \(L^2\). The proposal displacement identity identifies this sum with \(T_t(X,Z)-X\), justifying the squared-norm integrals above.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/KLOfDensity.lean.title: Integral formulas for relative entropy and Fisher information
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/KLOfDensity.lean.summary: Suppose \(r>0\) is a measurable relative density and \( ho_r=r u\) is a probability measure. Its Radon–Nikodym derivative with respect to \( u\) is \(r\), so its logarithmic likelihood ratio is \(\log r\), almost everywhere under \( ho_r\). Weighted log-integrability then gives finite relative entropy and the formula \(\operatorname{KL}( ho_r\mid u)=\int r\log r\,d u\). For a differentiable density, the corresponding finite Fisher integral is \(I_ u(r)=\int r\| abla\log r\|^2d u\).

steps.title: The logarithmic likelihood ratio
steps.body: Since \( ho_r=r u\), the measure \( ho_r\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \( u\), and its Radon–Nikodym derivative equals \(r\) almost everywhere under \( u\). Absolute continuity transfers this equality to a full-measure set for \( ho_r\). Positivity of \(r\) permits taking logarithms there. The logarithmic likelihood ratio of \( ho_r\) relative to \( u\) is consequently \(\log r\), almost everywhere under the measure used in the entropy integral.

steps.title: Finiteness from weighted logarithmic integrability
steps.body: Assume \(r\log r\in L^1( u)\). Changing measure gives \(\int|\log r|\,d ho_r=\int r|\log r|\,d u<\infty\). The logarithmic likelihood ratio is \(\log r\) almost everywhere, so it is integrable under \( ho_r\). Together with absolute continuity, the finite-divergence criterion implies \(\operatorname{KL}( ho_r\mid u)<\infty\). This establishes finiteness for the divergence of the measures, before replacing it by an ordinary signed integral.

steps.title: The entropy integral
steps.body:
Assume \( u\) and \( ho_r\) are probability measures and the logarithmic likelihood ratio is integrable under \( ho_r\). In the finite-divergence formula, the correction for unequal total masses is zero because \( u(E)= ho_r(E)=1\). Substituting the logarithmic likelihood ratio and changing measure gives

\[H_ u(r)=\operatorname{KL}( ho_r\mid u)=\int\log r\,d ho_r=\int r\log r\,d u.\]

The integrability assumption justifies the signed integrals in these equalities.

steps.title: The Fisher integral
steps.body:
Suppose the squared relative score is integrable under \( ho_r\). It is nonnegative, so its extended integral agrees with its finite ordinary integral. Changing from \( ho_r\) to \( u\) yields

\[I_ u(r)=\int\| abla\log r\|^2\,d ho_r=\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u.\]

Both formulas use the same specified differentiable density. This identity is used when integration by parts expresses entropy dissipation as a weighted score integral.

steps.title: Integration against the density measure
steps.body:
Let \(r\ge0\) be measurable. For an integrable scalar- or vector-valued function \(g\), the formula for integration with respect to a weighted measure is

\[\int g\,d\rho_r=\int r(x)g(x)\,d\nu(x).\]

The condition is absolute integrability in the scalar case and Bochner integrability in the vector case. The density is finite at every point, so the multiplication on the right is ordinary scalar multiplication. This formula is also used to compare the integrability conditions in the two measures.

steps.title: Equivalent logarithmic integrability conditions
steps.body:
Apply the weighted-measure integrability criterion to \(g=\log r\). It gives

\[\log r\in L^1(\rho_r)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\log r\in L^1(\nu).\]

Indeed the corresponding absolute integrals are equal: \(\int|\log r|\,d\rho_r=\int r|\log r|\,d\nu\). The criterion therefore controls both the positive and negative parts of the logarithmic likelihood. It supplies the integrability needed in the entropy formula.

steps.title: Finiteness of Fisher information
steps.body: The squared score is a nonnegative measurable function. If it is integrable under \(\rho_r\), its ordinary integral is finite and equals its nonnegative extended integral. The latter is the definition of relative Fisher information. Hence \(I_\nu(r)<\infty\). This is the finiteness condition used when LSI is written as an inequality between real-valued quantities.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDerivative.title: Differentiation of the entropy integral
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDerivative.summary: For a positive differentiable function \(r\), the scalar derivative is \((r\log r)'=r'(\log r+1)\). Applying this identity to a density depending on time gives a derivative of its entropy integral when the differentiated integrands have a common integrable bound on a time neighborhood. This bound and the relevant measurability and integrability assumptions are hypotheses of the result.

steps.title: The derivative of a positive function times its logarithm
steps.body: Assume \(r\) is differentiable at \(t\) and \(r(t)>0\). The product rule and the derivative of the logarithm give \((r\log r)'(t)=r'(t)\log r(t)+r(t)r'(t)/r(t)\). Positivity implies \(r(t)\ne0\), so cancellation yields \(r'(t)(\log r(t)+1)\). The constant term is retained at this stage. Its contribution can be removed from an entropy calculation only after the derivative of total mass has been shown to vanish.

steps.title: Differentiation under the integral sign
steps.body:
Fix \(t\), and assume that almost every spatial function \(u\mapsto r_u(x)\) is positive and differentiable on a common neighborhood of \(t\). Suppose there is an integrable function \(M(x)\) such that \(|\partial_u r_u(x)(\log r_u(x)+1)|\le M(x)\) on that neighborhood. Assume also measurability of the integrands and integrability of \(r_t\log r_t\). The scalar chain rule identifies the pointwise derivative, and the dominated differentiation theorem gives

\[\frac{d}{dt}\int r_t\log r_t\,d\nu=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d\nu.\]

The same bound proves integrability of the derivative integrand. Uniformity on a time neighborhood, rather than a bound at one time alone, is what justifies exchanging differentiation and integration.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Regularity.lean.title: Local assumptions for differentiating relative entropy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Regularity.lean.summary: Let \(r_t\) be a family of positive densities relative to a probability measure \(\nu\). The local assumptions below give pointwise time derivatives and an integrable bound for \(\partial_t r_t(\log r_t+1)\) on a neighborhood of each time. They imply differentiability of the entropy integral. Normalization and logarithmic integrability identify that integral with relative entropy. An admissible weak equation then gives the entropy derivative estimate. The local assumptions, the weak equation and its energy conditions are retained as hypotheses.

steps.title: The local differentiation assumptions
steps.body: At a fixed time \(t\), assume a common time neighborhood on which the densities are positive and pointwise differentiable. Require measurability of the entropy and derivative integrands, integrability of the entropy integrand at \(t\), and an integrable spatial function bounding \(|\partial_u r_u(\log r_u+1)|\) throughout that neighborhood. These are local assumptions: the neighborhood and its bound may depend on \(t\). They contain no assumption about the derivative of the integrated entropy or its sign.

steps.title: The derivative of the entropy integral
steps.body:
Apply the scalar product and logarithm chain rules to \(r_u(x)\log r_u(x)\). The local bound in the hypotheses dominates this derivative uniformly for nearby \(u\). Dominated differentiation therefore proves integrability of \(\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\) and gives

\[\frac d{dt}\int r_t\log r_t\,d\nu=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d\nu.\]

The conclusion follows from the stated density regularity and domination; differentiability of the entropy integral is not separately assumed.

steps.title: An entropy derivative bound from the weak equation
steps.body:
Write \(s_t= abla\log r_t\), \(I(t)=\int r_t\|s_t\|^2d u\), and \(E(t)=\int r_t\|e_t\|^2d u\). Local differentiation gives \(H'(t)=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)d u\). Suppose the weak equation admits this test and both energies are finite. Its right-hand side is \(-I(t)+\int r_t\langle e_t,s_t angle d u\). Young's inequality bounds the last term by \(I(t)/4+E(t)\). Hence

\[H'(t)\le- rac34I(t)+E(t).\]

This result uses the stated error energy but does not assert any numerical bound on that energy.

steps.title: Finite relative entropy
steps.body: At the selected time, the local assumptions give integrability of \(r_t\log r_t\). The positive \(C^1\) density is measurable, and normalization makes \(r_t u\) a probability measure. Changing measure gives integrability of \(\log r_t\) under \(r_t u\). Absolute continuity and the finite-divergence criterion then imply \(\operatorname{KL}(r_t u\mid u)<\infty\). This conclusion precedes the use of the real-valued entropy derivative.

steps.title: Continuity of entropy on the stated interval
steps.body: Suppose the local differentiation assumptions hold at every point of the closed interval. They imply local differentiability, and hence continuity, of \(t\mapsto\int r_t\log r_t\,d u\). At every time in the interval, positivity, normalization and integrability identify this integral with \(\operatorname{KL}(r_t u\mid u)\). Equality of the two functions on the interval transfers continuity to relative entropy, including continuity relative to the interval at its endpoints.

steps.title: The right derivative of relative entropy
steps.body: Fix \(t\in[0,T)\). The local assumptions differentiate the ordinary entropy integral. For all sufficiently close \(u\ge t\), one has \(u\in[0,T]\); normalization and logarithmic integrability there identify the integral with relative entropy. Since these two functions agree at \(t\) and in a right neighborhood, they have the same right derivative at \(t\). This argument does not assume normalization or a probability interpretation outside the stated time interval.

steps.title: The derivative estimate using relative Fisher information
steps.body: The change-of-density formula identifies \(\int\| abla\log r_t\|^2d(r_t u)\) with \(\int r_t\| abla\log r_t\|^2d u\). The corresponding integrability criterion proves that both are finite under the assumed score-energy bound. Thus the weighted energy in the weak-equation calculation is precisely the Fisher information used in LSI. Combining this identification with the right derivative of relative entropy gives \(H'(t)\le-3I(t)/4+E(t)\) for the same probability law.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ScoreCalculus.lea.title: Relative scores and the entropy test
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ScoreCalculus.lea.summary: For a strictly positive differentiable density, \( abla\log r= abla r/r\). Consequently \(\langle abla r, abla(\log r+1) angle=r\| abla\log r\|^2\). Substituting \(\log r+1\) in a weak equation therefore gives the Fisher information term in the entropy derivative. Because this test may be unbounded and noncompact, its admissibility and the integrability of its pairings are explicit hypotheses here.

steps.title: The gradient of the logarithm
steps.body:
At a point where \(r\) is differentiable and positive, the scalar logarithm chain rule gives \(D\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1}Dr(x)\). In a real Hilbert space the gradient represents the derivative by the inner product. This representation is linear, so the scalar coefficient is unchanged:

\[\nabla\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1}\nabla r(x).\]

Positivity is used both to apply the logarithm derivative and to define the reciprocal.

steps.title: The gradient of the entropy test
steps.body: Adding the constant one changes no spatial derivative. Therefore \(\nabla(\log r+1)=\nabla\log r\). The logarithm is differentiable under the positivity and differentiability assumptions on \(r\). Although the term one appears in the time derivative of \(r\log r\), its spatial derivative is zero, which is why only the relative score remains in the weak-equation pairing.

steps.title: The Fisher integrand
steps.body:
Multiply the score identity by \(r>0\) to obtain \( abla r=r abla\log r\). Taking its inner product with the gradient of \(\log r+1\) gives

\[\langle abla r, abla(\log r+1) angle=r\langle abla\log r, abla\log r angle=r\| abla\log r\|^2.\]

This is a pointwise identity. Its integral is justified only when the displayed energy is integrable.

steps.title: Entropy production for the unforced weak equation
steps.body:
Assume the weak equation admits the test \(\psi=\log r+1\), with integrable left-hand side and Dirichlet pairing. Positivity and \(C^1\) regularity of \(r\) make the test \(C^1\). Substituting it and using the pointwise Fisher identity yields

\[\int\dot r(\log r+1)\,d u=-\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u.\]

The hypotheses must allow this particular test. A weak equation known only for compactly supported tests does not by itself justify this substitution.

steps.title: Entropy production with a drift discrepancy
steps.body:
Suppose the forced weak equation admits \(\log r+1\), and assume the derivative term, Fisher term and forcing pairing are integrable. The identities for the two gradients give

\[\int\dot r(\log r+1)\,d u=-I_ u(r)+\int r\langle e, abla\log r angle\,d u.\]

The second term is the contribution of the drift discrepancy. Its absolute integrability is required independently of finite entropy. Under these assumptions all terms are ordinary signed integrals.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDecay.lean.title: Comparison for an affine differential inequality
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDecay.lean.summary: Let \(a>0\), and suppose \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\) with a right derivative satisfying \(H'\le-aH+b\). The comparison solution is \(e^{-at}H(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-at})\). A one-sided Gronwall inequality bounds \(H\) by this solution. Applying the result to \(H'=-I\) and \(I\ge2\alpha H\) gives exponential decay with rate \(2\alpha\).

steps.title: The affine comparison inequality
steps.body:
Let \(G(t)=e^{-at}H(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-at})\). It satisfies \(G(0)=H(0)\) and \(G'=-aG+b\). The difference \(H-G\) is continuous and has right derivative at most \(-a(H-G)\). The one-sided Gronwall comparison, applied with zero initial difference, implies \(H-G\le0\). Therefore

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at}).\]

Only \(a>0\), continuity and the stated right-derivative bound are needed; neither \(H\) nor \(b\) is required to be nonnegative.

steps.title: Decay under dissipation and LSI
steps.body: Suppose \(\alpha>0\), the entropy derivative satisfies \(H'=-I\), and \(2\alpha H\le I\) at each required time. Then \(H'\le-2\alpha H\). Apply the affine comparison with \(a=2\alpha\) and \(b=0\) to obtain \(H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\). The result is a scalar implication from the two stated inequalities. Proving the dissipation identity for a particular evolution is a separate analytic step.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DriftError.lean.title: Young inequalities for the entropy error term
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DriftError.lean.summary: Let \(s=\nabla\log r\) and let \(e\) be a drift discrepancy. Cauchy–Schwarz and \((\|e\|-\|s\|/2)^2\ge0\) imply \(|\langle e,s\rangle|\le\|e\|^2+\|s\|^2/4\). With a nonnegative weight \(r\), finite integrals of the two squares first imply integrability of the pairing. Integration then bounds entropy production by \(-3I/4+\int r\|e\|^2d\nu\).

steps.title: A pointwise Young inequality
steps.body: Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\langle e,s\rangle\le\|e\|\|s\|\). Expanding the nonnegative square \((\|e\|-\|s\|/2)^2\) gives \(\|e\|\|s\|\le\|e\|^2+\|s\|^2/4\). Combining the inequalities proves \(\langle e,s\rangle\le\|s\|^2/4+\|e\|^2\). The particular coefficients are chosen so that adding this upper bound to a term \(-\|s\|^2\) leaves \(-3\|s\|^2/4\).

steps.title: Integrability of the weighted pairing
steps.body:
Suppose \(r\ge0\), the pairing is measurable, and both \(r\|s\|^2\) and \(r\|e\|^2\) are integrable. The absolute Young inequality gives

\[|r\langle e,s\rangle|\le\frac14r\|s\|^2+r\|e\|^2.\]

The right-hand side is integrable by linearity and the two hypotheses. Domination therefore proves that the signed weighted pairing is integrable. This fact is established before applying integral linearity to the entropy identity.

steps.title: The entropy production bound
steps.body:
Assume the entropy test is admissible for the forced weak equation and the two weighted square energies are finite. The absolute Young bound proves integrability of the forcing pairing. The weak identity then reads \(H'=-I+\int r\langle e,s angle d u\). Applying the integrated Young inequality gives

\[H'\le-I+ rac14I+\int r\|e\|^2d u=- rac34I+\int r\|e\|^2d u.\]

Thus the differential inequality follows from the stated weak equation and integrability assumptions.

steps.title: The absolute Young inequality
steps.body: The absolute Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \(|\langle e,s\rangle|\le\|e\|\|s\|\). The same nonnegative-square calculation as above bounds this product by \(\|s\|^2/4+\|e\|^2\). This proves an absolute bound, which is suitable for integral domination and Fubini's theorem. It requires no moments other than the two square energies after weighting and integration.

steps.title: Integration of the weighted Young inequality
steps.body:
Multiply the pointwise Young inequality by \(r\ge0\). Since the pairing and both square terms are integrable, monotonicity and linearity of the integral give

\[\int r\langle e,s angle d u\le rac14\int r\|s\|^2d u+\int r\|e\|^2d u.\]

Nonnegativity of \(r\) is necessary for the multiplication to preserve the inequality. The weight need not have integral one.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/OneStep.lean.title: A one-step entropy bound
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/OneStep.lean.summary: Assume \(0<\alpha\le L\), \(0

steps.title: An exponential comparison for a small argument
steps.body:
Let \(0\le x\le1/4\). The tangent inequality gives \(e^{-3x/2}\ge1-3x/2\ge1/2\), and \(e^{x/2}\ge1+x/2\). Multiplying the latter inequality by the positive factor \(e^{-3x/2}\) yields

\[e^{-x}\ge e^{-3x/2}+\frac x2e^{-3x/2}\ge e^{-3x/2}+\frac x4.\]

Thus the difference between the two exponential factors is at least \(x/4\). The next estimate applies this inequality with \(x=\alpha h\).

steps.title: Integration of the entropy differential inequality
steps.body:
Combining \(2\alpha H\le I\), \(H'\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\), and \(G_0\le(4L^2/\alpha)H(0)+2dL\) gives \(H'\le-(3\alpha/2)H+b\), where \(b=(\alpha/4)H(0)+(5/2)hdL^2\). Here the coefficient estimates follow from \(t\le h\) and the step restriction. The affine comparison bounds the integrated error by \(bh\), because \(1-e^{-ah}\le ah\) for \(a>0\). Therefore

\[H(h)\le e^{-3\alpha h/2}H(0)+\frac{\alpha h}{4}H(0)+\frac52h^2dL^2.\]

Since \(H(0)\ge0\), the preceding exponential comparison bounds the first two terms by \(e^{-\alpha h}H(0)\). Finally \((5/2)h^2dL^2\le6h^2dL^2\). The stated continuity and derivative assumptions justify the affine comparison.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DiscreteEntropy.l.title: Iteration of the entropy recurrence
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DiscreteEntropy.l.summary: For \(\alpha,h>0\), put \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\) and \(c=6h^2dL^2\). The recurrence \(H_{k+1}\le qH_k+c\) gives \(H_k\le q^kH_0+c(1-q^k)/(1-q)\). If \(\alpha h\le1/4\), then \(1-q\ge3\alpha h/4\), and the accumulated error is at most \(8hdL^2/\alpha\).

steps.title: The finite geometric sum
steps.body:
Since \(\alpha h>0\), one has \(0\[H_k\le q^kH_0+c\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j=q^kH_0+c\frac{1-q^k}{1-q}.\]

The identity \(q^k=e^{-\alpha hk}\) expresses the decay in terms of the elapsed time \(hk\). This finite-sum statement does not require \(H_0\ge0\).

steps.title: A bound for the geometric denominator
steps.body: For \(x\ge0\), the tangent inequality \(e^x\ge1+x\) implies \(e^{-x}\le1/(1+x)\). Consequently \(1-e^{-x}\ge x/(1+x)\). If also \(x\le1/4\), the denominator is at most \(5/4\), so this last quantity is at least \(4x/5\), and hence at least \(3x/4\). Thus \(1-e^{-x}\ge3x/4\) throughout the stated interval. This positive lower bound is used before division in the recurrence estimate.

steps.title: The uniform entropy estimate
steps.body:
The constant \(c=6h^2dL^2\) is nonnegative and \(0\[\frac{6h^2dL^2}{1-e^{-\alpha h}}\le\frac{6h^2dL^2}{3\alpha h/4}=\frac{8hdL^2}{\alpha}.\]

Combining this with the homogeneous term proves \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hdL^2/\alpha\). The strict positivity of \(\alpha h\) justifies the cancellation and division.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/RegularizedTheore.title: Entropy convergence from regular density interpolations
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/RegularizedTheore.summary: Suppose a positive regular density path represents each Gaussian ULA interpolation. Assume its weak equation admits the entropy test, its score and error energies are finite, and the stated numerical error and gradient-moment estimates hold. These assumptions imply the entropy derivative estimate, the one-step recurrence, and the iterated KL bound. The construction of the density path and the analytic estimates remain hypotheses of this conditional theorem.

steps.title: Derivation from the regular interpolation assumptions
steps.body:
The equality between the density measure and the ULA interpolation proves normalization. Local domination of the differentiated entropy integrand gives finite KL, continuity, and the right derivative

\[H'_k(t)=\int\dot r_{k,t}(\log r_{k,t}+1)\,d\nu.\]

The finite score energy gives finite Fisher information. The admissible weak equation and Young's inequality imply \(H'_k(t)\le-3I(t)/4+E(t)\). Insert the assumed bound \(E(t)\le t^2L^2G_k+2tdL^2\) and the entropy-dependent bound on \(G_k\). The one-step comparison gives the recurrence with coefficient six, and geometric iteration gives the final coefficient eight. This derives the entropy derivative and recurrence from the listed assumptions; it does not derive those assumptions merely from LSI.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationData.title: Assumptions for a regular ULA interpolation
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationData.summary: The assumptions specify relative densities \(r_{k,t}\) representing the Gaussian ULA interpolation, their time derivatives, and drift discrepancies. They require positivity, spatial regularity, local integrable domination for entropy differentiation, a weak equation valid for the entropy test, finite score and error energies, and the stated moment estimates. Under these assumptions and LSI, the probability, finiteness, one-step and iterated entropy conclusions below follow.

steps.title: The regular interpolation assumptions
steps.body: For every index \(k\) and elapsed time \(t\in[0,h]\), suppose \(r_{k,t}\nu=\rho_{k,t}\). Require positive \(C^1\) densities, local time derivatives and domination of their entropy derivatives, an admissible forced weak equation, integrable score and discrepancy energies, and the numerical bounds on these energies and the starting gradient moment. The equality of measures holds throughout the interpolation, so the density at every time represents the same law used in the algorithm. An entropy derivative, a recurrence, or a convergence bound is not among these assumptions.

steps.title: Normalization of the represented density
steps.body: The Gaussian transition preserves probability, and each ULA iterate is a probability measure. Therefore the interpolation starting from that iterate has total mass one. The equality \(r_{k,t}\nu=\rho_{k,t}\) gives \(\int r_{k,t}\,d\nu=1\). This establishes the normalization required to apply LSI to the relative density.

steps.title: Finite entropy of each iterate
steps.body: Local entropy regularity gives integrability of \(r_{k,t}\log r_{k,t}\), hence finite KL for the represented probability measure. At elapsed time zero the equality of measures becomes \(r_{k,0}\nu=\rho_k\). Thus \(\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\mid\nu)<\infty\) for every \(k\). The target is assumed to be a probability measure; in applications this property is included in LSI.

steps.title: The one-step consequence
steps.body: Define the proposed entropy derivative by integrating \(\dot r_{k,t}(\log r_{k,t}+1)\). The local differentiation assumptions prove that this is the right derivative of relative entropy. The weak equation and finite energies give the Fisher-information derivative bound. LSI and the stated moment estimates then satisfy the hypotheses of the scalar one-step comparison. Identifying the laws at zero and \(h\) yields the recurrence for successive ULA entropies.

steps.title: The iterated consequence
steps.body: Under LSI, gradient Lipschitzness and the positive step restriction, the regular interpolation assumptions imply the one-step bound at every index. Every entropy is finite by the preceding argument. Apply the finite geometric-sum estimate to obtain the stated bound for \(\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\mid\nu)\). All density, weak-equation and moment hypotheses remain in this conditional conclusion.

UnadjustedLangevin/Gibbs.lean.title: Gibbs normalization and second moments
UnadjustedLangevin/Gibbs.lean.summary:
Let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, with \(m>0\). Its quadratic lower bound at zero, followed by the scalar square inequality for the linear term, gives \(U(x)\ge U(0)-\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/m+(m/4)\|x\|^2\). Thus the Gibbs weight and its squared-norm multiple are dominated by integrable Gaussians.

Consequently \(Z_U=\int e^{-U}dx\) is finite. Continuity and pointwise positivity of the weight make it strictly positive. Division by \(Z_U\) gives the probability \(\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\), with finite second moment. Translation by any fixed vector preserves square-integrability.

steps.title: The unnormalized Gibbs weight
steps.body:
The unnormalized density is \(w_U(x)=e^{-U(x)}\), viewed as a nonnegative function whose integral may be infinite. The exponential is finite and positive pointwise.

The exponential is strictly positive for every finite potential value. Thus this weight has no zero set, a fact used later both for positivity of the partition and for equivalence of Gibbs and Lebesgue null sets.

steps.title: The partition function
steps.body:
The partition function is \(Z_U=\int e^{-U(x)}\,dx\), formed as a nonnegative extended integral. At this definition no finiteness assumption is made. Later normalization uses separate proofs of \(0<Z_U\) and \(Z_U<\infty\), which are needed to justify cancellation with its inverse.

The partition records the total unnormalized mass before division. Leaving finiteness open at this definition allows the later normalization theorem to state precisely which potential assumptions make a probability measure available.

steps.title: The normalized Gibbs measure
steps.body:
When \(0<Z_U<\infty\), define \(\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\). The nonnegative density is measurable and integrates to \(Z_U^{-1}Z_U=1\), so it defines a probability. The following strong-convexity estimates establish the required partition bounds before normalization is used.

For a measurable test \(f\), the normalized integral formula is \(\int f\,d\pi_U=Z^{-1}\int fe^{-U}dx\). This formula is used only after positivity and finiteness of \(Z\) have been established.

steps.title: Integrability of a radial Gaussian
steps.body:
For \(a>0\), \(e^{-a\|x\|^2}\) is Lebesgue integrable in finite dimension. The proof specializes the absolutely convergent Gaussian Fourier integral to real positive precision \(a\) and zero linear term, then takes the real part. The complex Gaussian integrand is the real embedding of the desired exponential, so the final simplification identifies the functions exactly. This also includes dimension zero.

The one-dimensional Gaussian integral factors over an orthonormal coordinate system. Positive precision \(a\) makes each scalar integral finite, so the product integral is finite in every finite dimension.

steps.title: A quadratic lower bound on the potential
steps.body:
Apply the strong supporting-plane inequality at zero: \(U(x)\ge U(0)+\langle abla U(0),x angle+ rac m2\|x\|^2\). Cauchy–Schwarz and \(ab\le a^2/m+(m/4)b^2\), valid for \(m>0\), absorb the linear term. The result is \(U(x)\ge U(0)-\| abla U(0)\|^2/m+(m/4)\|x\|^2\). Completing the scalar square justifies the linear-term absorption.

Completing a scalar square bounds \(-\| abla U(0)\|\|x\|+(m/2)\|x\|^2\) below by \(-\| abla U(0)\|^2/m+(m/4)\|x\|^2\). The resulting quadratic coefficient remains positive.

steps.title: Integrability of the Gibbs weight
steps.body:
Exponentiating the quadratic lower bound gives \(e^{-U(x)}\le e^{-U(0)+\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/m}e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\). The right side is an integrable Gaussian multiple. Differentiability supplies continuity and measurability of the left side, so integrable domination transfers integrability from that explicit dominating function.

The prefactor is independent of \(x\); all spatial decay lies in the Gaussian factor. Hence its integrability transfers directly to the Gibbs weight by domination, with no assumption that the origin minimizes the potential.

steps.title: The Gaussian weighted second moment
steps.body:
For \(a>0\), split the Gaussian decay into two equal factors. The scalar function \(s\mapsto s e^{-(a/2)s}\) is bounded on \([0,\infty)\), so \(\|x\|^2e^{-a\|x\|^2}\le C_a e^{-(a/2)\|x\|^2}\). The remaining Gaussian is integrable; the proof checks measurability and nonnegativity before applying domination.

For \(s\ge0\), the maximum of \(s e^{-as/2}\) is finite. Taking \(s=\|x\|^2\) leaves an integrable factor \(e^{-a\|x\|^2/2}\), proving the polynomially weighted Gaussian tail claim.

steps.title: The weighted Gibbs second moment
steps.body:
Multiply the previous Gibbs Gaussian domination by \(\|x\|^2\). Its right side has the form \(C\|x\|^2e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\), whose integrability was proved separately. The pointwise inequality uses \(\|x\|^2\ge0\), so multiplying it preserves order; this is the second-moment input for the normalized measure.

The squared norm is nonnegative, so multiplying the density domination preserves its direction. The resulting majorant is precisely the weighted Gaussian whose integrability has just been proved.

steps.title: Strict positivity of the partition
steps.body:
The continuous function \(e^{-U}\) is strictly positive everywhere. Its extended integral cannot vanish: a zero integral of a nonnegative measurable function would force it to vanish almost everywhere, contradicting positivity on a nonzero-volume open set. This proves \(0<Z_U\) without requiring an upper bound on \(Z_U\).

Continuity and positivity at one point give a neighborhood on which the weight is bounded below by a positive constant. That neighborhood has positive Lebesgue volume, forcing the partition to be strictly positive.

steps.title: Finiteness of the partition
steps.body:
Strong convexity with \(m>0\) has already given ordinary integrability of \(e^{-U}\). For a nonnegative integrable function its extended integral is finite. Unfolding the partition function identifies that integral exactly with \(Z_U\), proving the finiteness needed to divide by the partition.

For a nonnegative measurable function, ordinary integrability is equivalent to finiteness of its nonnegative extended integral. Applying this equivalence to the already dominated weight supplies the finite partition needed for normalization.

steps.title: The ordinary integral formula for the partition
steps.body:
Assume the Gibbs weight \(e^{-U}\) is measurable and integrable, as established from the preceding positive strong-convexity hypotheses. Since the weight is nonnegative, its nonnegative extended integral is finite and equals the ordinary Lebesgue integral. Thus the partition has the conventional formula

\[Z_U=\int_H e^{-U(x)}dx<\infty.\]

The equality is justified by the absolute integrability already proved, rather than by assigning a real value to a divergent integral. This same finite scalar can consequently be used in the normalized density and in ordinary weighted-integral formulas. Strict positivity, needed to divide by \(Z_U\), is supplied by the positive-weight argument.

steps.title: Positivity of the ordinary normalizer
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is continuous and the preceding argument has established integrability of \(e^{-U}\). At any fixed point \(x_0\), the value \(e^{-U(x_0)}\) is strictly positive. Continuity therefore gives a neighborhood on which the weight is bounded below by a positive constant.

Such a neighborhood has positive Lebesgue volume, so its weighted integral is positive. Together with the finite partition formula this proves

\[0<\int_H e^{-U(x)}dx=Z_U<\infty.\]

Both positivity and finiteness are now available before taking the reciprocal. Hence \(Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\) is an ordinary normalized probability density, and every later division by the normalizer is legitimate.

steps.title: Normalization of the Gibbs probability
steps.body:
The mass of a density measure is its extended density integral. Pull the constant \(Z_U^{-1}\) out to get \(\pi_U(H)=Z_U^{-1}Z_U\). The proofs that \(Z_U\ne0\) and \(Z_U\ne\infty\) justify this product being one. This theorem constructs probability normalization rather than assuming normalization.
