Evaluating the weighted measure on the whole space gives \(Z^{-1}Z\). Both factors are finite and \(Z>0\), so this product is one, proving normalization of the Gibbs measure defined by this density.

steps.title: The normalized Gibbs second moment
steps.body:
Changing measure converts integrability under \(\pi_U\) to integrability of \(Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\|x\|^2\) under volume. The weighted second moment is already integrable, and the real normalizing factor is a finite scalar. The weighted-density theorem supplies the almost-everywhere measurability and finiteness hypotheses for this conversion.

The weighted squared-norm integral is finite before dividing by the partition. Multiplication by the finite scalar \(Z^{-1}\) therefore gives a finite Gibbs second moment, establishing square-integrability of the state.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the Gibbs state
steps.body:
For the identity random variable, membership in \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\) is equivalent to integrability of \(\|x\|^2\). The identity is measurable, and the preceding weighted-moment theorem supplies the integral. The construction uses the \(p=2\) characterization of square-integrability, first applied to the measurable identity function.

Membership of the identity map in \(L^2(\pi_U)\) is exactly the finite second-moment statement. The identity is continuous and therefore measurable, supplying the other part of the membership criterion.

steps.title: Square-integrability after translation
steps.body:
Since \(\pi_U\) is a probability, the constant map \(x\mapsto z\) belongs to \(L^2\). Subtract it from the identity, already in \(L^2(\pi_U)\), to obtain \(x\mapsto x-z\in L^2(\pi_U)\). This is a moment assertion for every chosen center, without requiring that the center minimize the potential.

Use \(\|x-a\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|a\|^2\). The first term has finite Gibbs integral and the second is a constant integrated against a probability measure, so every fixed translation is square-integrable.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsConcentration.le.title: Concentration around a minimizer without differentiability
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsConcentration.le.summary:
Let \(F\) be a continuous \(q\)-strongly convex potential on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, with \(q>0\), and let \(z\) be a supplied minimizer. The midpoint strong-convexity inequality and minimality give \(F(x)\ge F(z)+(q/4)\|x-z\|^2\). This proves integrability of the density and its squared-distance multiple without differentiability.

For \(0<r<1\), dilation about \(z\) and strong convexity give \(Z+(q/2)r(1-r)M\le r^{-d}Z\), where \(M=\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}dx\). Subtracting \(Z\), dividing by \(1-r\), and taking \(r\uparrow1\) gives \(M\le(2d/q)Z\). Dividing by the positive finite partition proves \(\int\|x-z\|^2d\pi_F\le2d/q\).

steps.title: The quadratic potential bound at a mode
steps.body:
Use strong convexity at the midpoint of \(z\) and \(x\), then use minimality \(F(z)\le F((z+x)/2)\). Rearranging yields \(F(x)\ge F(z)+(q/4)\|x-z\|^2\). This argument uses values of \(F\), not a derivative or a first-order optimality assertion at the minimizer.

The midpoint argument uses only function values and minimality. Its lower bound has coefficient \(q/4\), which is positive and sufficient for the Gaussian integrability estimates. No gradient at the minimizer is assumed.

steps.title: Integrability around the mode
steps.body:
For \(q>0\), the midpoint bound gives \(e^{-F(x)}\le e^{-F(z)}e^{-(q/4)\|x-z\|^2}\). Translation invariance reduces integrability of the majorant to the centered Gaussian integral. Continuity makes the density measurable, so domination proves integrability without differentiability of \(F\).

Translate coordinates by \(z\). The preceding bound dominates the density by \(e^{-F(z)}e^{-(q/4)\|x-z\|^2}\). Translation preserves Lebesgue measure, and this Gaussian is integrable because \(q>0\).

steps.title: The weighted squared-distance moment
steps.body:
Multiply the translated Gaussian bound by \(\|x-z\|^2\). Translation preserves Lebesgue measure, and a quadratic times a decaying Gaussian is integrable. Translation transports this integrability through \(x\mapsto x-z\) and then applies the nonnegative domination theorem to the desired weighted moment.

Multiplying that centered Gaussian majorant by squared distance keeps it integrable. This proves the numerator of the centered Gibbs second moment finite before the normalization comparison is used.

steps.title: Contracting coordinates toward the mode
steps.body:
For \(0<r<1\), compare \(F(z+r(x-z))\) with \(F(x)\) using strong convexity and \(F(z)\le F(x)\). Exponentiating and using \(e^u\ge1+u\) produces a linear correction in \(\|x-z\|^2\). The dilation \(x\mapsto z+r(x-z)\) multiplies volume by \(r^d\), hence \(Z+(q/2)r(1-r)M\le r^{-d}Z\), with \(M=\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}dx\).

The map \(x\mapsto z+r(x-z)\) has Jacobian determinant \(r^d\). Its change-of-variables factor is therefore \(r^{-d}\) in the displayed integral comparison. Strong convexity supplies the coefficient \((q/2)r(1-r)\) of the weighted squared distance.

steps.title: A partition comparison for squared distance
steps.body:
Subtract \(Z\) from the dilation inequality and divide by \(1-r>0\). As \(r\uparrow1\), \((r^{-d}-1)/(1-r)\to d\), while \((q/2)rM\to(q/2)M\). The order-closed limit theorem yields \(M\le(2d/q)Z\). The proof establishes the one-sided derivative limit of the scalar power before passing the inequality to the limit.

The weighted squared-distance integral is already finite. The scalar limits on the two sides of the dilation inequality therefore preserve the order and give \((q/2)M\le dZ\). Division by \(q/2>0\) gives the stated factor \(2d/q\).

steps.title: Integrability of distance under Gibbs
steps.body:
The density-measure integrability criterion changes the desired \(\pi_F\)-integral into a constant multiple of \(\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}dx\). Its finiteness follows from the continuous, strongly convex mode estimate. No score moment or smoothness assumption is introduced during normalization.

The centered weighted moment is finite and the partition is finite and positive. Their quotient is consequently the ordinary Gibbs second moment, without any extended-value cancellation.

steps.title: The Gibbs concentration bound around the mode
steps.body:
First prove \(Z>0\), \(Z<\infty\), and integrability of the weighted distance. Then write \(\int\|x-z\|^2d\pi_F=M/Z\) and apply \(M\le(2d/q)Z\). Cancellation is justified by positivity of \(Z\); the result is \(\mathbb E_{\pi_F}\|X-z\|^2\le2d/q\), including \(d=0\).

The bound controls distance from the stated mode rather than the mean. It is a second-moment estimate about the supplied minimizer, without any assumption that the minimizer is the mean.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsScore.lean.title: The Gibbs gradient moment from an exponential bound
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsScore.lean.summary:
Suppose \(U\) is differentiable, its gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and its Gibbs partition is positive and finite. The quadratic upper bound on \(U(x+v)\) implies an exponential bound on \(-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\) after multiplication by the Gibbs weight. Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure cancels the partition and gives the directional sub-Gaussian bound with variance coefficient \(L\|v\|^2\).

The small-parameter exponential comparison gives mean zero and second moment at most \(L\) in every unit direction. Summing over an orthonormal basis yields \(\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\pi_U\le Ld\). These statements assume finite normalization. Positive strong convexity is used by the final specialization to prove that normalization, rather than as an assumption in the directional calculation.

steps.title: The exponential score comparison
steps.body:
The descent lemma gives \(U(x+v)\le U(x)+\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle+(L/2)\|v\|^2\). Negate and exponentiate, then rearrange to \(e^{-U(x)}e^{-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}e^{-U(x+v)}\). The inequality is pointwise and nonnegative, so it can then be integrated.

Evaluate the smooth upper model at \(x+v\), move the linear gradient term to the other side, and exponentiate. The factor \(e^{-U(x)}\) then turns the translated potential into a translated Gibbs weight.

steps.title: The directional log moment-generating bound
steps.body:
Integrate the pointwise exponential-score bound. Translation invariance gives \(\int e^{-U(x+v)}dx=Z_U\); normalization cancels this factor, leaving \(\mathbb E_{\pi_U}e^{-\langle\nabla U,v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\). The cancellation uses the assumed positivity and finiteness of the partition.

Translation invariance gives \(\int e^{-U(x+v)}dx=Z_U\). Dividing by the same positive partition cancels the unnormalized mass and leaves the directional exponential bound with variance proxy \(L\).

steps.title: The sub-Gaussian directional score
steps.body:
Apply the preceding bound with the vector \(-tv\), for every real \(t\). The exponent becomes \(t\langle\nabla U,v\rangle\) and the right side is \(e^{t^2L\|v\|^2/2}\). This is exactly the directional sub-Gaussian moment bound with variance proxy \(L\|v\|^2\); the displayed exponential bound is finite for every real parameter.

Applying the exponential bound to positive and negative scalar multiples of a direction forces the first derivative at zero to vanish. The second-order comparison gives directional score variance at most \(L\|v\|^2\).

steps.title: A square bounded by two exponentials
steps.body:
The series \(\cosh a=\sum_{n\ge0}a^{2n}/(2n)!\) has nonnegative terms, so retaining its first two terms gives \(\cosh a\ge1+a^2/2\). Substitute \(2\cosh a=e^a+e^{-a}\) and rearrange to \(a^2\le e^a+e^{-a}-2\). The construction uses the power series for the hyperbolic cosine with the lower bound obtained by discarding nonnegative series terms, explicitly proving nonnegativity of every discarded even-power term.

The even combination \(e^s+e^{-s}-2\) has leading term \(s^2\) and nonnegative higher even powers. This supplies a pointwise domination of the square by exponential terms whose Gibbs integrals are controlled.

steps.title: A second moment from exponential control
steps.body:
Integrate \(t^2X^2\le e^{tX}+e^{-tX}-2\), giving \(t^2\mathbb EX^2\le2(e^{ct^2/2}-1)\). Subgaussianity provides the exponential integrability and hence the square integrability needed here. Divide by \(t^2\) for \(t\ne0\), and let \(t\to0\) to obtain \(\mathbb EX^2\le c\). The limit preserves the inequality because both sides converge.

Apply the scalar inequality to a small multiple of the score, integrate using the two exponential bounds, divide by the squared multiplier, and send it to zero. The limit yields the variance proxy as a true second-moment bound.

steps.title: The full Gibbs gradient-energy bound
steps.body:
Choose an orthonormal basis \((e_i)_{i=1}^d\) and use Parseval: \(\| abla U(x)\|^2=\sum_i\langle abla U(x),e_i angle^2\). Each coordinate is subgaussian with proxy \(L\), hence has second moment at most \(L\). Finite-sum integrability permits integration term by term, yielding \(\mathbb E_{\pi_U}\| abla U\|^2\le Ld\).

For an orthonormal basis, the squared gradient norm is the sum of the squared directional scores. Each integral is at most \(L\), so summing the \(d\) finite terms gives \(Ld\).

steps.title: Square-integrability of the Gibbs gradient
steps.body:
The coordinate subgaussian bounds prove integrability of every squared gradient coordinate. Summing over the finite orthonormal basis proves integrability of \(\|\nabla U\|^2\). Lipschitz continuity provides strong measurability, and the square-integrability criterion gives \(\nabla U\in L^2(\pi_U)\).

Continuity of the gradient supplies measurability and the preceding energy bound supplies the finite square integral. Together they establish the full \(L^2\) membership needed for the lifted reference drift.

steps.title: The gradient-energy bound under strong convexity
steps.body:
Strong convexity with \(m>0\) supplies the finite-partition premise of the score theorem. Substitute that proof into the first-order smoothness result to obtain \(\mathbb E_{\pi_U}\|\nabla U\|^2\le Ld\). The strong convexity constant is used for normalization here; it does not appear in the resulting gradient-moment bound.

Strong convexity is used here to guarantee a normalized Gibbs probability and finite partition. The score-energy calculation itself comes from the smooth upper model and the translation comparison.

UnadjustedLangevin/StationaryMoments.lea.title: Transfer the Gibbs score estimate to an L² reference
UnadjustedLangevin/StationaryMoments.lea.summary:
Let \(Y\in L^2(P;H)\) have law \(\pi_U\). Change of variables gives \(\| abla U(Y)\|_2^2=\int\| abla U\|^2d\pi_U\). The Gibbs gradient estimate bounds this by \(Ld\), and taking the nonnegative square root gives \(\| abla U(Y)\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\). This is an estimate of a random-vector norm, not a pointwise bound on its values.

The Gibbs law of \(Y\) is a hypothesis of this transfer. The positive strong-convexity specialization proves the required finite target normalization and then applies the same calculation.

steps.title: The reference drift norm from its Gibbs law
steps.body:
A representative of the gradient composition class equals \( abla U(Y)\) almost everywhere. Change variables using \(P\circ Y^{-1}=\pi_U\), so its squared \(L^2(P)\) norm is \(\int\| abla U\|^2d\pi_U\le Ld\). Nonnegativity of the norm and of \(Ld\) then gives \(\| abla U(Y)\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\). The calculation uses the equality of laws and does not require independence.

The equality of laws transports the squared gradient integral from the sample space to Gibbs. The lifted drift's norm-square identity then gives \(\|\mathcal G[Y]\|_2^2\le Ld\), and taking square roots yields the reference bound.

steps.title: The drift moment under strong convexity
steps.body:
Use strong convexity to prove \(Z_U<\infty\), and apply the previous law-transfer theorem with that proof. The conclusion is the same \(\sqrt{Ld}\) bound for the lifted drift of any \(L^2\) variable with Gibbs law. The drift-moment bound is a conclusion of this specialization.

Positive strong convexity supplies the normalization and moment properties needed to apply the preceding stationary-law calculation. The resulting bound is independent of the particular representation or coupling of the stationary random vector.

UnadjustedLangevin/Generator.lean.title: The Gibbs integral of the Langevin generator
UnadjustedLangevin/Generator.lean.summary:
For a compactly supported \(C^2\) test \(\varphi\), set \(\mathcal L\varphi=\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\). In a fixed direction \(v\), the product derivative \(D_v(e^{-U}D_v\varphi)\) equals the Gibbs weight times the directional generator. Its integral is zero because the differentiated product has compact support. Summing over an orthonormal basis and dividing by the positive finite partition gives \(\int\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U=0\).

Continuity and compact support justify the integrals and the finite sums. The resulting identity is infinitesimal invariance on the stated test class; it does not by itself identify the time marginals of a stochastic process.

steps.title: The generator in one direction
steps.body:
For a fixed direction \(v\), define \(L_v\varphi(x)=D(D\varphi(\cdot)[v])(x)[v]-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle D\varphi(x)[v]\). The first term is a directional second derivative of the test; the second is the directional gradient drift. No Hessian of \(U\) is part of this definition.

For a direction \(v\), the second derivative contributes \(D^2\varphi[v,v]\), while the drift contributes \(-\langle\nabla U,v\rangle D\varphi[v]\). The weighted product derivative in this direction is the expression integrated below.

steps.title: The Langevin generator
steps.body:
Choose the standard orthonormal basis and set \(L\varphi=\sum_iL_{e_i}\varphi\). The finite sum makes the construction meaningful in dimension zero and permits integration by parts one direction at a time. A subsequent identity proves that this is the usual basis-independent \(\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\).

Summing over an orthonormal basis yields the Euclidean diffusion operator. The basis is finite, so all sums in the definition and subsequent integrations are finite sums.

steps.title: The weighted Gibbs integral formula
steps.body:
Under the positive finite partition hypothesis, changing measure gives, for every integrable test,

\[\int f\,d\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\int e^{-U(x)}f(x)dx.\]

Continuity of the potential makes the density measurable, and the same finite scalar \(Z_U^{-1}\) multiplies each weighted integral.

Changing to Gibbs inserts the same scalar normalization \(Z^{-1}\) into every weighted integral. Positivity and finiteness of \(Z\) make this the usual density-change formula for signed integrable tests.

steps.title: Integrability of a compactly supported test
steps.body:
A continuous compactly supported \(f\) gives a continuous compactly supported product \(e^{-U}f\), hence a Lebesgue-integrable function. The weighted-density integrability criterion and multiplication by the real normalization factor transfer this fact to \(\pi_U\). This explicitly supplies the integrability needed by subsequent linearity arguments.

A continuous function with compact support is bounded on its support. Multiplication by the continuous Gibbs weight preserves compact support, and hence provides a Lebesgue-integrable weighted function.

steps.title: The derivative of the Gibbs weight
steps.body:
Apply the chain rule to \(x\mapsto e^{-U(x)}\): \(D(e^{-U})(x)[v]=-e^{-U(x)}DU(x)[v]\). The real Hilbert gradient identity rewrites \(DU(x)[v]\) as \(\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\). Only differentiability of \(U\) is used.

The minus sign arises from differentiating \(-U\), and the exponential factor remains unchanged. Identifying the directional derivative of \(U\) with its gradient pairing fixes the sign of the generator drift term.

steps.title: The weighted directional generator integral
steps.body:
Differentiate \(e^{-U(x)}D\varphi(x)[v]\) in direction \(v\). The product rule gives exactly \(e^{-U(x)}L_v\varphi(x)\). Since derivatives of a compactly supported \(C^2\) test remain compactly supported, this weighted first derivative is integrable and has zero integral by integration by parts. The proof establishes continuity and compact support before invoking that theorem.

The product derivative is \(D_v(e^{-U}D_v\varphi)=e^{-U}(D_v^2\varphi-D_vU\,D_v\varphi)\). Its integral vanishes because the product has compact support, giving the weighted directional invariance identity.

steps.title: The directional Gibbs generator integral
steps.body:
Apply the weighted-to-Gibbs integral formula to \(L_v\varphi\). Its weighted Lebesgue integral is zero, so multiplication by the normalization factor still gives zero. This is infinitesimal invariance for a single direction and does not yet identify the law of a time-evolving process.

Dividing the zero weighted integral by the positive partition leaves zero. This is the normalized directional invariance statement, retaining the same compactly supported test and requiring no new derivative calculation.

steps.title: Continuity of the directional generator
steps.body:
The \(C^2\) hypothesis makes the first and second derivatives of \(\varphi\) continuous. The gradient of \(U\) is continuous by its Lipschitz hypothesis. Evaluating continuous linear maps in the fixed direction \(v\), multiplying the scalar factors, and subtracting therefore gives continuity of \(L_v\varphi\).

The second derivative of the test and the gradient of the potential are continuous. Evaluation in a fixed direction, multiplication, and subtraction therefore preserve continuity of the directional generator.

steps.title: Compact support of the directional generator
steps.body:
Outside the compact support of \(\varphi\), the test is locally zero, so its first and second derivatives vanish there. Both terms of \(L_v\varphi\) therefore vanish. The support inclusion puts the support of the generator inside the same compact set; no support property of \(U\) is required.

Outside the support of a smooth compactly supported test, the test vanishes on a neighborhood, so all its derivatives vanish there. Both generator terms therefore have support inside that same compact set.

steps.title: Integrability of the directional generator
steps.body:
Combine continuity of \(L_v\varphi\) with preservation of compact support. The established compact-support Gibbs integrability theorem then gives absolute integrability. This permits ordinary integral algebra, even though the ambient generator is not bounded uniformly for arbitrary tests.

Continuity alone would not ensure integrability on an unbounded space. Here compact support supplies the needed localization, and the Gibbs density is continuous and bounded on that compact set.

steps.title: Integrability of the full generator
steps.body:
The full generator is the finite sum of its directional pieces. Each piece is integrable under \(\pi_U\), so the finite-sum integrability theorem applies. Finiteness of the basis is the reason no exchange of an infinite series and integral is required.

Each directional summand has an absolutely integrable generator value. The finite orthonormal-basis sum is therefore integrable, allowing the full generator integral to be distributed term by term.

steps.title: The weighted full generator integral
steps.body:
Expand the finite basis sum defining \(L\varphi\) and distribute the Gibbs weight over it. Compact support supplies integrability of every summand, allowing \(\int\sum_i e^{-U}L_{e_i}\varphi=\sum_i\int e^{-U}L_{e_i}\varphi\). Every directional integral vanishes, hence so does their sum.

Distribute the Gibbs weight through the finite basis sum and integrate. Every directional integral has already been shown to be zero, so their sum vanishes without an infinite-series interchange.

steps.title: Infinitesimal Gibbs invariance
steps.body:
Normalization changes \(\int L\varphi\,d\pi_U\) into the real inverse partition times its weighted Lebesgue integral. The latter was proved to be zero. This establishes the full Gibbs infinitesimal invariance identity for compactly supported \(C^2\) tests.

The normalization formula identifies the Gibbs generator integral with \(Z^{-1}\) times its weighted Lebesgue counterpart. The latter is zero, proving infinitesimal invariance for the full generator.

steps.title: The Laplacian-minus-drift formula
steps.body:
The sum of the directional second derivatives over an orthonormal basis is the Laplacian. For the drift sum, \(D\varphi(x)[e_i]=\langle abla\varphi(x),e_i angle\); Parseval turns the sum of products with \(\langle abla U(x),e_i angle\) into \(\langle abla U(x), abla\varphi(x) angle\). The proof rewrites the basis definition into this conventional formula pointwise.

Parseval's identity gives \(\sum_i\langle abla U,e_i angle\langle abla\varphi,e_i angle=\langle abla U, abla\varphi angle\). The analogous sum of second directional derivatives is the Laplacian.

steps.title: The stationary identity in conventional notation
steps.body:
Replace the conventional expression \(\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\) by the equal basis-defined generator inside the integral. The established zero-generator integral then gives zero. The rewrite makes the displayed mathematical identity refer to the same function that the preceding calculation integrated.

Substitution of the pointwise generator formula yields the conventional stationary identity. It applies on the stated compactly supported test class; stationarity of the stochastic evolution is established later by identifying its laws.

UnadjustedLangevin/GeneratorDirichlet.le.title: Gibbs Dirichlet form, symmetry and dissipation
UnadjustedLangevin/GeneratorDirichlet.le.summary:
For the stated differentiability and compact-support hypotheses, integration by parts gives \(\int\varphi\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle d\pi_U\). Differentiate the product of the Gibbs weight and \(\varphi\), multiply by the directional derivative of \(\psi\), and sum the resulting directional identities over an orthonormal basis. Compact support and continuity give absolute integrability.

Symmetry of the gradient inner product gives symmetry of the generator integral. Taking \(\psi=\varphi\) identifies it with \(-\int\| abla\varphi\|^2d\pi_U\), which is nonpositive. The individual integrability statements below retain their precise one-test or two-test compact-support hypotheses.

steps.title: Differentiating the Gibbs-weighted test
steps.body:
Differentiate the product \(e^{-U}\varphi\): \(D(e^{-U}\varphi)(x)[v]=e^{-U(x)}(D\varphi(x)[v]-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\varphi(x))\). Combine the product rule with the already proved derivative of the Gibbs weight, then collect the common exponential factor.

Factoring out \(e^{-U}\) from the product rule leaves the test derivative minus its multiplication by the potential's directional derivative. Its two terms give the derivative and drift terms in the generator pairing.

steps.title: Weighted directional integration by parts
steps.body:
Integrate by parts the derivative of \(e^{-U}\varphi\) against \(D\psi[v]\). The weighted product rule separates a \(D\varphi[v]D\psi[v]\) term from the drift term, giving \(\int e^{-U}\varphi L_v\psi=-\int e^{-U}D\varphi[v]D\psi[v]\). Compact support and \(C^2\) regularity justify every derivative and integral involved.

Integrating \(D_v(e^{-U}\varphi D_v\psi)\) gives zero. Expanding this derivative and moving the term involving \(D_v\varphi\) to the other side yields the negative directional energy.

steps.title: The directional Gibbs Dirichlet identity
steps.body:
Convert both sides of the weighted directional identity to Gibbs integrals. The same real normalization factor multiplies both integrals, producing \(\int\varphi L_v\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int D\varphi[v]D\psi[v]d\pi_U\). This is a change of measure, with no new integration-by-parts step.

Both weighted integrals carry the same inverse-partition factor. Applying the Gibbs change of density to each side therefore preserves the equality and its negative sign.

steps.title: Integrability of the gradient pairing
steps.body:
The gradients are continuous; the gradient of the compactly supported test \(\varphi\) vanishes outside its compact support. Thus \(x\mapsto\langle\nabla\varphi(x),\nabla\psi(x)\rangle\) is continuous with compact support. The general compact-test Gibbs integrability theorem applies even though \(\psi\) itself need not have compact support in this statement.

Even if the second test is not compactly supported, the first gradient vanishes outside its compact support. The product of the two gradients is thus localized to a compact set where both are bounded.

steps.title: Integrability of the test-generator product
steps.body:
The generator of the \(C^2\) test \(\psi\) is continuous under the Lipschitz-gradient assumption on \(U\). Multiplication by the continuous compactly supported \(\varphi\) makes the product compactly supported, hence Gibbs integrable. This is the exact product needed on the left side of the Dirichlet identity.

The compactly supported multiplier localizes the continuous generator value. This makes the left side of the Dirichlet identity absolutely integrable before any integration-by-parts algebra is used.

steps.title: The full Dirichlet identity
steps.body:
Sum the directional Dirichlet identities over the orthonormal basis. Finite-sum integrability allows the integral to pass through the sum, and Parseval identifies \(\sum_iD\varphi[e_i]D\psi[e_i]=\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\). Therefore \(\int\varphi L\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle d\pi_U\).

Summing the directional energies reconstructs the gradient inner product through orthonormal expansion. The finite sum and absolute integrability justify carrying this reconstruction through the integral.

steps.title: Symmetry of the generator
steps.body:
Apply the Dirichlet identity in both orders \((\varphi,\psi)\) and \((\psi,\varphi)\). Symmetry of the real inner product makes the resulting energy integrands equal pointwise. Hence \(\int\varphi L\psi\,d\pi_U=\int\psi L\varphi\,d\pi_U\).

Exchanging the two tests exchanges the two gradients in the energy pairing. Symmetry of the real inner product makes these energies identical, proving symmetry of the generator on the stated domain.

steps.title: The generator self-pairing
steps.body:
Specialize the bilinear identity to \(\psi=\varphi\), then rewrite \(\langle abla\varphi, abla\varphi angle=\| abla\varphi\|^2\). This identifies the quadratic generator form exactly: \(\int\varphi L\varphi\,d\pi_U=-\int\| abla\varphi\|^2d\pi_U\).

With the two tests equal, their gradient pairing is the squared gradient norm. This identifies the generator quadratic form as the stated negative energy integral.

steps.title: Dissipativity of the generator
steps.body: For a compactly supported \(C^2\) test function \(\varphi\), the Dirichlet identity gives \(\int\varphi L\varphi\,d\pi=-\int\|\nabla\varphi\|^2d\pi\). The energy integrand is nonnegative and integrable by the preceding estimates. Its integral is therefore nonnegative, and hence \(\int\varphi L\varphi\,d\pi\le0\). This is dissipativity on the stated test class.

UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinIntegral.lean.title: Existence for the Langevin integral equation
UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinIntegral.lean.summary:
Let the state space be a complete real normed space, let \(g\) be globally \(L\)-Lipschitz, and let \(B\) be continuous with \(B(0)=0\). For a fixed initial state \(x\), consider \(Y(t)-x=-\int_0^tg(Y(s))ds+B(t)\). Setting \(Y=Z+B\) gives an integral equation with time-dependent drift \(f(t,z)=-g(z+B(t))\), continuous in time and \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(z\).

A contraction argument gives a continuous solution on a sufficiently short interval. Restarting with the preceding endpoint and shifted additive input, and concatenating finitely many such solutions, gives existence on every finite nonnegative horizon. Taking the state space to be \(L^2(P;K)\) gives continuity and the integral equation in mean square. This does not assert differentiability or sample-path regularity of the noise.

steps.title: Solving the integral equation on a short interval
steps.body:
Remove the additive input by writing \(Y(t)=Z(t)+B(t)\). The new unknown satisfies \(Z(t)=x+\int_0^t f(s,Z(s))ds\), with \(f(s,z)=-g(z+B(s))\). This time-dependent drift is \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(z\) and continuous in time even though \(B\) need not be differentiable.

Bound \(\|B(t)\|\le C'\) on the compact interval and set \(G=\|g(x)\|+LC'\), radius \(a=2hG\), and drift bound \(M=G+La\). The condition \(Lh\le1/2\) proves \(Mh\le a\), giving the ball-invariance condition in the local contraction theorem for the integral equation. The proof checks these bounds and invokes the contraction fixed-point theorem.

The chosen fixed point gives a continuous \(Z\) with its integral identity. Add back \(B\), use \(B(0)=0\), and rewrite the negative drift integral to obtain \(Y(t)-x=-\int_0^tg(Y(s))ds+B(t)\). The integral identity holds for the resulting continuous real-time function on \([0,h]\).

The shifted unknown has an ordinary time integral even if the additive input has no derivative. The short-time radius and drift bounds ensure that the Picard map preserves its closed ball, while the Lipschitz estimate controls contraction there.

steps.title: Splicing two integral-equation segments
steps.body:
Use \(Y(t)\) up to time \(a\), and \(Z(t-a)\) afterward. The equality \(Z(0)=Y(a)\) makes the pasted path continuous at the join. Split \(\int_0^t=\int_0^a+\int_a^t\), translate the second integral, and add the two supplied equations; the terms \(B(a)\) cancel, giving the same equation on \([0,a+b]\).

At the join, the two path values coincide by the restart condition. For later times split the drift integral at the joining time and translate the second part; the two input increments then add to the original input difference.

steps.title: Existence on every finite horizon
steps.body:
Choose a positive segment length small enough that \(L\delta\le1/2\). Construct the first Picard segment, then repeatedly solve with initial state at the previous endpoint and shifted input \(B(a+s)-B(a)\). The splicing lemma combines finitely many segments covering the prescribed horizon. The local contraction restriction determines the construction mesh and imposes no restriction on the final horizon.

A finite horizon can be covered by finitely many equal short intervals. At each restart the shifted input is continuous and starts at zero, so the same local theorem applies repeatedly with a new initial point.

steps.title: A short-interval solution in square mean
steps.body:
Apply the Banach-space Picard theorem to \(H=L^2(P;K)\), \(g(X)=\mathcal G(\nabla U)(X)\). The lifted drift has the same Lipschitz constant as \(\nabla U\). Completeness of \(L^2\) and continuity of the supplied \(L^2\)-noise path are the exact fixed-point hypotheses.

The lifted gradient's global Lipschitz constant is unchanged, and the space of square-integrable vectors is complete. These facts verify the short-interval fixed-point assumptions in the random-vector Hilbert space.

steps.title: A finite-horizon solution in square mean
steps.body:
Use the finite-horizon Banach-space existence theorem with the lifted gradient drift. The conclusion is continuity in the \(L^2\) norm and an equality of \(L^2\) classes at every time in the horizon. The Bochner time integral therefore takes values in the same Hilbert space; no pathwise differentiability of the random noise is asserted.

The finite-horizon construction produces one continuous \(L^2\)-valued curve. Its Bochner drift integral is well defined by continuity, and the integral identity is asserted at each time in the prescribed horizon.

UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinUniqueness.le.title: Stability and uniqueness for additive-noise solutions
UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinUniqueness.le.summary:
Let \(Y,Z\) solve the integral equation with the same continuous additive input, initial states \(x,y\), and an \(L\)-Lipschitz drift. Subtraction cancels the input and yields \(u(t)\le\|x-y\|+L\int_0^tu(s)ds\) for the continuous function \(u(t)=\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|\). Grönwall gives \(u(t)\le e^{Lt}\|x-y\|\). Equal initial states therefore give equal solutions on the interval.

The same argument in \(L^2(P;K)\) gives square-mean stability and uniqueness. Equality of classes is almost-everywhere equality of representatives at each fixed time; the conclusion alone does not supply a single null set valid for all real times.

steps.title: Stability for a common additive input
steps.body:
Subtract the two integral equations so that their common additive input cancels. The integral norm inequality and Lipschitz drift give \(u(t)\le\|x-y\|+L\int_0^t u(s)ds\), where \(u(t)=\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|\) is continuous. Grönwall's inequality yields \(u(t)\le\|x-y\|e^{Lt}\). All time integrals are justified by continuity on the compact horizon.

After cancellation of the common input, the norm difference is bounded by initial separation plus \(L\) times its time integral. The exponential factor comes from this scalar Grönwall comparison, without differentiating the input.

steps.title: Uniqueness with equal initialization
steps.body:
Set the two initial states equal in the stability estimate. The right side becomes \(0e^{Lt}=0\), forcing \(\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|=0\) for each \(t\in[0,h]\). Norm-zero equivalence gives equality of the vectors, so the two functions agree on the interval.

Equal initialization sets the multiplicative initial distance to zero. Nonnegativity of the norm then forces equality of the solutions at every time on the interval, giving uniqueness among the stated continuous integral solutions.

steps.title: Stability of square-integrable solutions
steps.body:
Specialize Banach-space stability to the gradient-composition map on \(L^2(P;K)\). Its Lipschitz theorem supplies the required constant, so \(\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|_2\le e^{Lt}\|Y(0)-Z(0)\|_2\). This compares solutions with a common \(L^2\)-noise input and possibly different initial random variables.

All operations now take place in \(L^2\), so the resulting distance is a root mean square difference. A different coupling of the initial random vectors changes that initial norm but not the stability constant.

steps.title: Uniqueness of square-integrable solutions
steps.body: Apply the same-input uniqueness theorem in \(L^2(P;K)\). Equality here is equality of \(L^2\) classes for each time, hence almost-everywhere equality of representatives at each fixed time. The conclusion does not by itself select one exceptional null set valid simultaneously at every real time.

UnadjustedLangevin/EulerLimit.lean.title: Euler approximations converge to the integral solution
UnadjustedLangevin/EulerLimit.lean.summary:
Let \(Y\) solve the additive integral equation with continuous input \(B\) on \([0,T]\), and use the same input increments in the Euler approximation. Subtracting exact and numerical increments cancels \(B\). If the drift changes by at most \(\varepsilon\) within each mesh interval, the one-step remainder is at most \(h\varepsilon\), and the Euler map has Lipschitz factor \(1+Lh\).

The finite recurrence and \((1+Lh)^n\le e^{Lnh}\) give endpoint error at most \(T\varepsilon e^{LT}\) when \(nh=T\). Uniform continuity of the drift along the solution makes \(\varepsilon\) tend to zero as the mesh tends to zero. The argument applies in a Banach space, including the space of square-integrable random variables; the latter conclusion is convergence in mean square.

steps.title: The Euler chain for a fixed additive input
steps.body:
Define \(X_0=x\) and \(X_{k+1}=X_k-hg(X_k)+B((k+1)h)-B(kh)\). The additive input is one fixed function evaluated at mesh endpoints; consequently the numerical chain and the integral solution can be compared with exactly matching noise increments.

Using increments of one fixed input makes the discrete and continuous equations directly comparable. The numerical error is caused by drift freezing, rather than by approximating the noise itself.

steps.title: Its initial value
steps.body:
Evaluating the recursive definition at index zero gives \(X_0=x\). The proof establishes this by the defining identity; no continuity of the input or positivity of the mesh is required for this initialization identity.

The zero index uses no input increment, so the chain starts exactly at its prescribed point. This supplies the zero initial error when the exact solution is initialized at the same point.

steps.title: Its successor update
steps.body:
The successor definition gives \(X_{k+1}=X_k-hg(X_k)+\Delta B_k\). This defining identity is the equation used when subtracting the exact solution's increment and deriving the error recurrence.

Writing \(\Delta B_k=B((k+1)h)-B(kh)\) isolates the common additive increment. It cancels when this equation is subtracted from the exact integral increment over the same mesh interval.

steps.title: The exact integral increment
steps.body:
Subtract the integral equations at \(b\) and \(a\). Continuity of \(g\circ Y\) makes it interval integrable, so interval-integral additivity gives \(\int_0^b-\int_0^a=\int_a^b\). Thus \(Y(b)-Y(a)=-\int_a^b g(Y(s))ds+B(b)-B(a)\), including oriented intervals when \(b<a\).

The drift integral over \([a,b]\) is the difference of the two integrals starting at zero. This is the exact increment equation on each numerical mesh interval.

steps.title: A finite-horizon recurrence estimate
steps.body:
From \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), \(e_0=0\), \(q\ge1\), and \(b\ge0\), induction proves \(e_n\le nbq^n\). In the successor step bound \(q\cdot kbq^k+b\) by \((k+1)bq^{k+1}\), using \(q^{k+1}\ge1\). This coarse bound avoids dividing by \(q-1\), so it also covers \(q=1\).

The bound \(nbq^n\) remains valid at \(q=1\). It avoids a division by \(q-1\), making the Euler convergence estimate uniform as the mesh tends to zero.

steps.title: Stability of the explicit Euler map
steps.body:
Write the difference as \((x-y)-h(g(x)-g(y))\). The triangle inequality and Lipschitzness give \(\|\cdot\|\le\|x-y\|+hL\|x-y\|=(1+Lh)\|x-y\|\). The hypothesis \(h\ge0\) removes the absolute value in the scalar norm.

This estimate uses only Lipschitzness and a triangle inequality, so its factor is \(1+Lh\). It controls finite-time stability of the approximation without requiring strong convexity or a contractive Euler step.

steps.title: The error from a drift continuity modulus
steps.body:
At one step the common noise cancels. The Euler map contributes \((1+Lh)e_k\), and the exact integral remainder contributes at most \(h\varepsilon\), because the drift changes by at most \(\varepsilon\) within one mesh interval. Apply the finite recurrence bound and \((1+Lh)^n\le e^{Lnh}\), then use \(nh=T\) to obtain \(e_n\le T\varepsilon e^{LT}\).

Within each mesh cell, a drift variation at most \(\varepsilon\) contributes at most \(h\varepsilon\) to the local remainder. Multiplying by the finite-time stability factor and using \(nh=T\) gives the stated uniform horizon bound.

steps.title: Euler convergence with the same additive input
steps.body:
The continuous drift path \(g\circ Y\) is uniformly continuous on \([0,T]\). Given any positive error tolerance, choose a drift modulus \(\varepsilon\) making \(T\varepsilon e^{LT}\) small, then take the mesh \(T/(n+1)\) below its continuity radius. The previous error bound gives endpoint convergence. The case \(T=0\) is separated so no division by the horizon is needed.

Uniform continuity of the exact drift curve supplies a single mesh size that controls every cell of the horizon. Sending that mesh size to zero makes the remainder tolerance arbitrarily small, and hence the endpoint error tends to zero.

steps.title: Euler convergence in square mean
steps.body:
Apply the deterministic matching-input Euler convergence theorem in \(L^2(P;H)\), using the Lipschitz lifted gradient. The numerical endpoint converges in the \(L^2\) norm to the constructed solution at \(T\). Expectations of bounded Lipschitz tests then converge by Cauchy–Schwarz.

Convergence is in the norm of the random-vector Hilbert space. It therefore controls expectations of bounded Lipschitz tests by Cauchy–Schwarz, which is the form later used to identify the limiting marginal law.

UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardTaylor.lea.title: A uniform cubic remainder for smooth test functions
UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardTaylor.lea.summary:
For a smooth test \(\varphi\), expand \(\varphi(x+v)\) through degree two using \(D\varphi(x)[v]\) and \(D^2\varphi(x)[v,v]/2\). The third derivative of \(t\mapsto\varphi(x+tv)\) is \(D^3\varphi(x+tv)[v,v,v]\). A uniform bound on the third-derivative operator norm therefore bounds the remainder by a constant times \(\|v\|^3\), with the Taylor factor \(1/6\).

For a smooth compactly supported test, continuity and compact support of its derivatives give this uniform bound. The resulting expansion can be integrated against Gaussian increments: the centered linear term has zero mean, and the quadratic covariance term gives the Laplacian.

steps.title: The second-order expansion of a test
steps.body:
Define \(T_2\varphi(x;v)=\varphi(x)+D\varphi(x)[v]+\frac12D^2\varphi(x)[v,v]\). The iterated Fréchet derivative is a continuous bilinear map, evaluated twice at the same displacement. This defines the polynomial whose Gaussian expectation is computed in the generator calculation.

The bilinear second derivative is evaluated twice on the same displacement. This retains all mixed coordinate contributions and makes the subsequent Gaussian expectation basis-independent.

steps.title: A cubic Taylor remainder bound
steps.body:
Restrict \(\varphi\) to the segment \(t\mapsto x+tv\). Its third scalar derivative is \(D^3\varphi(x+tv)[v,v,v]\), bounded by \(C\|v\|^3\). Taylor's theorem with the factorial remainder gives \(|\varphi(x+v)-T_2\varphi(x;v)|\le(C/6)\|v\|^3\). Identify the first three coefficients with the iterated Fréchet derivatives.

The scalar segment derivative of order three has three copies of the displacement, hence the factor \(\|v\|^3\). The factorial \(3!=6\) in Taylor's formula determines the precise remainder coefficient.

steps.title: The uniform remainder for a smooth compactly supported test
steps.body:
Smoothness makes \(D^3\varphi\) continuous, and compact support of \(\varphi\) implies compact support of its derivatives. Hence its operator norm is globally bounded by some nonnegative constant. Apply the previous Taylor theorem and absorb the factor \(1/6\) into that constant to obtain a uniform cubic remainder bound.

Compact support extends to derivatives because a smooth function vanishes with all derivatives off its support. Continuity then gives one global third-derivative bound, uniform in both the expansion point and displacement.

UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardAdapted.le.title: Solutions depend measurably on their initial state and past noise
UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardAdapted.le.summary:
The continuous integral solution remains in a complete closed subspace if the initial point and additive input belong to that subspace and the drift maps it into itself. Solve within the subspace, include that solution in the ambient space, and apply uniqueness there. Continuous linear inclusion commutes with the Bochner integral.

The square-integrable variables measurable for a specified sub-sigma-algebra form a closed subspace. Composition with the Lipschitz drift preserves it. Taking the sub-sigma-algebra generated by initialization and the noise up to \(T\) therefore proves measurability of the solution from those data. This is derived from the integral equation and does not assume adaptedness in advance.

steps.title: Preservation of an invariant closed subspace
steps.body:
Solve the same integral equation inside the complete submodule \(S\), using drift invariance, \(x\in S\), and \(B(t)\in S\). Include this solution back into the ambient space; continuous linearity of the inclusion commutes with the Bochner integral. Ambient uniqueness identifies it with \(Y\), so every \(Y(t)\) lies in \(S\).

The closed subspace is complete and invariant under the drift. Solving inside it and using uniqueness of the ambient integral equation proves that the solution belongs to that subspace at every stated time.

steps.title: Measurability of the lifted drift
steps.body:
A Lipschitz map is continuous, so composing it with an almost-everywhere strongly measurable \(X\) preserves that measurability for the specified sub-sigma-algebra. The representative of the lifted drift agrees almost everywhere with this composition. Transport across that equality proves the result independently of the representative selected for the \(L^2\) class.

Composition preserves measurability for the chosen smaller sigma-algebra because the drift is continuous. Almost-everywhere representative equality transfers this property to the lifted class independently of the representative chosen for it.

steps.title: Past measurability of the integral solution
steps.body:
The \(L^2\) variables measurable for a sub-sigma-algebra form a complete closed submodule. The preceding composition theorem makes that submodule invariant under the lifted drift. Apply submodule preservation using measurability of the initialization and every noise value up to \(T\); the integral solution then belongs to the same submodule at each time.

The past-measurable classes form a closed subspace of \(L^2\). Initialization and the relevant noise values belong to it, so the invariant-subspace principle applies to the integral solution up to the chosen horizon.

steps.title: The sigma-algebra generated by past observations
steps.body:
Define the past sigma-algebra as the smallest sigma-algebra making the initialization and every noise observation \(B(t)\), \(0\le t\le T\), measurable. It is the join of their generated sigma-algebras, so it contains exactly the information needed for the stated past-measurability conclusion.

The join is the smallest sigma-algebra making the initialization and all noise observations up to time \(T\) measurable. Thus it expresses exactly the information allowed in the adaptedness conclusion.

steps.title: Inclusion in the ambient sigma-algebra
steps.body:
Every generator of the past is measurable in the ambient sigma-algebra. The universal property of a supremum of sigma-algebras therefore gives \(\mathcal F_T\le\mathcal F\). This inclusion is required to use the closed \(L^2\) subspace of variables measurable from the past.

Each generating sigma-algebra is contained in the ambient one because the original observations are measurable. Taking their join preserves that inclusion, so the corresponding closed subspace of \(L^2\) is defined.

steps.title: Measurability of the initial state from the past
steps.body:
The sigma-algebra generated by the initial variable is one summand of the defining join for \(\mathcal F_T\). Its inclusion makes the initial variable measurable for \(\mathcal F_T\), and the measurable representative of an \(L^2\) variable supplies the almost-everywhere strong-measurability formulation used by the submodule theorem.

Initialization is included as an explicit generator of the past. This retains any dependence present in the initial random state while excluding information from future innovations.

steps.title: Measurability of every previous noise value
steps.body:
For \(t\in[0,T]\), the sigma-algebra generated by \(B(t)\) is included in the indexed join defining the past. Measurability of the representative with respect to its generated sigma-algebra then extends along this inclusion, giving \(B(t)\)'s measurability from \(\mathcal F_T\).

For \(t\le T\), the observation \(B(t)\) is one of the generators. Its measurability follows by the inclusion of that generated sigma-algebra in the joined past.

steps.title: Adaptedness to the natural past
steps.body:
Apply the sub-sigma-algebra solution theorem to the explicitly generated \(\mathcal F_T\). The three preceding lemmas verify the ambient inclusion, initialization, and noise-measurability hypotheses. Thus every solution value up to \(T\) is measurable from initialization and past noise, with no adaptedness assumption added to the solution.

Applying preservation with the constructed past shows that the solution uses only initialization and previous noise values. This is derived from the integral equation and uniqueness, rather than assumed as a separate solution property.

UnadjustedLangevin/FokkerPlanck.lean.title: The weak Fokker–Planck equation and conditional stationarity
UnadjustedLangevin/FokkerPlanck.lean.summary:
A weak Fokker–Planck solution is a probability-valued curve satisfying the stated moment and integrability conditions and the identity \(\int\varphi\,d\rho_t-\int\varphi\,d\rho_0=\int_0^t\int\mathcal L\varphi\,d\rho_sds\) for compactly supported \(C^2\) tests. The constant Gibbs curve satisfies this equation because its test integrals are constant and its generator integrals are zero.

The uniqueness condition in this section is an explicit hypothesis for the same weak-solution class. Under that condition, a solution beginning at Gibbs equals the constant Gibbs curve. The independent approximation proof of Langevin stationarity does not require assuming this weak-solution uniqueness condition.

steps.title: The integrated weak Fokker–Planck equation
steps.body:
A curve \(\rho_t\) is in this weak solution class when it is probability valued, has the stated moment and integrability properties, and satisfies the integrated generator equation against every compactly supported \(C^2\) test. The moment and integrability hypotheses justify the generator expectation and its time integral.

The integrated test identity avoids assuming a density or a pointwise time derivative of the law. Its moment and integrability conditions ensure that the generator expectation and its time integral are meaningful.

steps.title: The constant Gibbs weak solution
steps.body:
Use the proved Gibbs normalization and second moment for the probability and moment hypotheses. Compact-support generator integrability proves integrability of the test-generator terms. Finally \(\int L\varphi\,d\pi_U=0\) makes the time integral vanish, while the constant curve has zero change in \(\int\varphi\,d\rho_t\). These verify the weak equation for the constant curve.

For a constant law curve, every test expectation has zero increment. The Gibbs generator identity makes its integrated right side zero as well, verifying the weak equation for that candidate.

steps.title: The displayed weak-solution uniqueness principle
steps.body:
The uniqueness assumption states that two probability-valued weak solutions in the displayed moment and test class, with the same initial law, agree throughout \([0,T]\). It is an explicit analytic premise of the comparison below. Its validity must be established for that solution class before the conditional stationarity argument is applied.

The uniqueness condition refers to exactly this test class and its accompanying moment assumptions. Stating it records the analytic premise required by the following comparison; it does not establish uniqueness independently.

steps.title: Stationarity under that uniqueness principle
steps.body:
Compare the supplied weak solution \(\rho\) with the constant Gibbs weak solution constructed above. Their time-zero measures agree by hypothesis. The explicit uniqueness hypothesis identifies them at every time. Application to a stochastic process also requires proving that its law curve belongs to this weak-solution class.

Both curves belong to the same weak-solution class and agree initially. The supplied uniqueness principle therefore identifies them throughout the interval. This conclusion remains conditional on that uniqueness premise.

UnadjustedLangevin/TestMeasure.lean.title: Compactly supported smooth tests determine a finite measure
UnadjustedLangevin/TestMeasure.lean.summary:
On the stated finite-dimensional real normed space, two finite Borel measures are equal if their integrals agree for every smooth compactly supported test. One proof uses the common dominating measure \(\mu+\nu\) and the two Radon–Nikodym densities. Equality of the test integrals implies equality of those densities almost everywhere, and integration gives equality of the measures.

Agreement on compactly supported \(C^2\) tests is sufficient, since every smooth compactly supported test is in that class. This criterion requires neither measure to have a Lebesgue density.

steps.title: Measure identification by smooth compact tests
steps.body:
Let \(\xi=\mu+\nu\), so both finite measures are absolutely continuous with respect to \(\xi\). Write their Radon–Nikodym densities as \(f=d\mu/d\xi\) and \(g=d\nu/d\xi\). Equality of the given smooth compact test integrals becomes \(\int\varphi f\,d\xi=\int\varphi g\,d\xi\).

The two densities are locally integrable because they are Radon–Nikodym derivatives of finite measures. Equality against all smooth compactly supported tests therefore gives equality of the densities almost everywhere. Integrating these equal densities against the common dominating measure recovers equality of the original Borel measures.

Smooth compactly supported tests may be approximated and localized without losing finite-measure domination. Equality on this determining class extends to continuous compactly supported tests and then to the Borel measures themselves.

steps.title: Measure identification by twice-differentiable compact tests
steps.body:
Every smooth test is \(C^2\), so the assumed equality on compactly supported \(C^2\) functions applies to the smooth test class used by the preceding measure-determination theorem. Supply that restricted equality and obtain equality of the finite Borel measures. No density or absolute continuity is needed.

The twice-differentiable compact tests form a measure-determining class. They therefore determine the measure while also admitting the generator calculations used in the weak equation.

UnadjustedLangevin/LpCharacteristic.lean.title: Characteristic functions are continuous in L²
UnadjustedLangevin/LpCharacteristic.lean.summary:
For a fixed real frequency \(t\), the function \(x\mapsto e^{itx}-1\) vanishes at zero and is \(|t|\)-Lipschitz. Composition therefore defines a continuous map on \(L^2\). Adding the constant one and integrating gives the characteristic function of the law. On a probability space, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its difference for two variables by their mean-square difference times \(|t|\).

Consequently characteristic functions converge under \(L^2\) convergence. The Gaussian characteristic expression is continuous in its mean and variance. Equality of the approximating characteristic functions and uniqueness of limits therefore preserve the stated Gaussian laws, with the nontrivial-filter qualification in the general convergence statement.

steps.title: The centered characteristic test
steps.body:
Set \(c_t(x)=e^{itx}-1\), with values in the complex plane. Subtracting one makes \(c_t(0)=0\), which is the condition needed by the Lipschitz composition construction on \(L^2\).

Subtracting the constant value at zero makes the test vanish at zero. This permits a norm estimate directly from the size of the random input without altering differences of characteristic expectations.

steps.title: The Lipschitz bound for the centered character
steps.body:
Multiplication by \(t\) is \(|t|\)-Lipschitz, and the unit circle parametrization is \(1\)-Lipschitz. Composing gives \(|c_t(x)-c_t(y)|\le|t||x-y|\). The proof identifies the nonnegative Lipschitz constants before applying the composition theorem.

The scalar inequality \(|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|\) integrates to an \(L^1\) bound. On a probability space, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds that first moment by the \(L^2\) norm.

steps.title: The centered character at zero
steps.body:
At zero the exponential is one, hence \(c_t(0)=e^0-1=0\). This scalar identity is the zero-value hypothesis used for Lipschitz composition on square-integrable classes; no nonzero constant has to be integrated for the centered function.

At a zero input the exponential is one, so the centered test is identically zero. Its expectation therefore vanishes exactly, agreeing with the Lipschitz normalization at the origin.

steps.title: The characteristic random variable in the square-integrable space
steps.body:
Lift \(c_t\) to \(L^2\) by Lipschitz composition, then add the constant class one. The resulting class has representative \(e^{itX}\) almost everywhere. The probability assumption makes the constant function square integrable.

The expectation is well defined because the complex exponential has modulus one. Thus characteristic expectations remain meaningful even without moments; the \(L^2\) structure is used to quantify their continuity.

steps.title: Its representative is the ordinary exponential
steps.body:
Combine the almost-everywhere representative identities for lifted composition, \(L^2\) addition, and the constant class. Their intersection has full measure; there the representative is \((e^{itX}-1)+1=e^{itX}\). This connects quotient-space operations with the random function used in the characteristic integral.

Evaluating the expectation on a representative gives the usual characteristic integral. A change on a null set leaves the integral unchanged, so this expression depends only on the square-integrable class.

steps.title: Recovering the characteristic function of a law
steps.body:
The pushforward integral theorem gives \(\widehat{P_X}(t)=\int e^{itX}dP\). In complex \(L^2\), inner product with the constant one has exactly this integral because its conjugate is one. The representative identity above therefore yields \(\widehat{P_X}(t)=\langle1,e^{itX}\rangle\).

For a vector frequency \(v\), the scalar input is \(\langle v,X\rangle\). Pushing the law of \(X\) through this linear functional converts the vector characteristic function into the scalar characteristic expectation.

steps.title: Continuity of characteristic functions under square-mean convergence
steps.body:
Lipschitz composition is continuous on \(L^2\); adding the constant one preserves continuity. Pairing with one is a continuous linear functional. The preceding integral identity rewrites their composition as \(X\mapsto\widehat{P_X}(t)\), proving continuity of the characteristic function of the probability law at every fixed frequency.

The characteristic difference is at most \(\|v\|\|X-Y\|_2\). Hence \(L^2\) convergence of random vectors yields convergence of their characteristic functions at every fixed frequency.

steps.title: Continuity of Gaussian characteristic parameters
steps.body:
The centered Gaussian characteristic function is \(e^{-t^2\|X\|_2^2/2}\). The norm, its square, and the scalar exponential are continuous, so this characteristic expression varies continuously with the square-integrable class \(X\). Its variance parameter is the squared norm, which is nonnegative.

The Gaussian characteristic function is \(e^{it m-vt^2/2}\). Ordinary continuity of the exponential transfers convergence of the mean and variance parameters into convergence of this expression.

steps.title: Preservation of an eventual Gaussian law in the limit
steps.body:
At each frequency, \(L^2\) convergence makes the characteristic functions converge. It also makes the centered Gaussian characteristic functions with variances \(\|X_i\|_2^2\) converge to variance \(\|Y\|_2^2\). Eventual Gaussianity identifies the two nets eventually, so uniqueness of limits identifies their limits. Uniqueness of a probability measure from its characteristic function then gives the claimed Gaussian law of \(Y\); a nontrivial filter is required for uniqueness.

Along the tail on which the variables have the stated Gaussian laws, characteristic functions converge both by \(L^2\) continuity and by the Gaussian parameter formula. Uniqueness identifies the limiting law.

steps.title: Preservation of a Gaussian law under square-mean convergence
steps.body:
If every approximant has the stated Gaussian law, then the law identity holds eventually for any filter. Apply the preceding limit result using this eventual equality. This version is suited to finite orthogonal sums converging to an infinite Gaussian series.

If every approximating variable has the specified Gaussian law, the preceding eventual argument applies immediately. The conclusion concerns the limiting distribution, without requiring pointwise convergence of sample values.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianHilbert.lean.title: Construct an isonormal Gaussian family from product coordinates
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianHilbert.lean.summary:
Let \((Z_i)\) be independent standard Gaussian coordinates on their product probability space. Their classes are orthonormal in \(L^2\): the diagonal inner products are one, and the off-diagonal inner products vanish by independence and centering. For square-summable coefficients \(a_i\), the finite sums \(\sum_i a_iZ_i\) converge in \(L^2\), with squared norm \(\sum_i a_i^2\).

Composing this linear isometry with the coordinate isometry of a Hilbert basis defines an isonormal map \(I:H\to L^2\). Every evaluation has law \(\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\), because the finite Gaussian sums converge in mean square and their variances converge. Its mean is zero and \(\mathbb E[I(x)I(y)]=\langle x,y\rangle\). Linearity then gives joint Gaussianity of every finite family of evaluations.

steps.title: The independent Gaussian source
steps.body:
Use the product probability \(Q=\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)\) on real coordinate families. The construction uses the countable product measure; the coordinate marginals are standard Gaussian and every finite family of coordinates is independent by the product-measure properties.

The source is a countable product of standard Gaussian probabilities. Its coordinate projections provide independent Gaussian variables from which all later finite sums and \(L^2\) limits are synthesized.

steps.title: The law of each scalar source coordinate
steps.body:
The coordinate projection \(\omega\mapsto\omega_i\) pushes the product measure to its \(i\)-th factor \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). The product marginal theorem proves both almost-everywhere measurability and the pushforward identity, so the stated law follows.

A coordinate projection of a product measure has its designated marginal. Thus each scalar source variable has mean zero and variance one before any Hilbert coefficient is introduced.

steps.title: The square-integrable coordinate class
steps.body:
A scalar source coordinate has second moment one, so it represents an element \(Z_i\in L^2(Q)\). The associated equivalence class identifies variables agreeing almost everywhere. Its norm and law can therefore be computed from the original measurable coordinate projection.

Each scalar coordinate has finite second moment one, so it determines an \(L^2\) class. This places all source coordinates in a common Hilbert space where series convergence can be expressed by norm limits.

steps.title: Its representative identity
steps.body:
The selected representative of \(Z_i\) agrees with the original source coordinate \(\omega_i\) almost everywhere. This equality preserves every integrable expectation and its pushforward law. Consequently the Gaussian marginal, centering, and independence calculations apply to the same square-integrable classes used for synthesis.

The class representative agrees almost everywhere with the original coordinate projection. Consequently law and moment calculations made for the coordinate projection transfer unchanged to the class.

steps.title: Independence of the source coordinates
steps.body:
The coordinate projections of an infinite product measure are jointly independent. Invoke that product theorem for the scalar Gaussian factors. This is independence of every finite set of coordinates, which is precisely what finite Gaussian linear combinations require.

Independence follows from the product law on cylinder events. In particular, distinct coordinate products have expectation equal to the product of their centered means, which is zero.

steps.title: The mean of a scalar coordinate
steps.body:
Change variables through the coordinate law and use the centered Gaussian mean: \(\int\omega_i\,dQ=\int x\,d\mathcal N(0,1)=0\). Gaussian integrability makes this an ordinary expectation identity.

The scalar standard Gaussian is centered. Integrating a coordinate against the product probability therefore gives zero, with all other coordinates integrating to total mass one.

steps.title: Inner products of coordinate classes
steps.body:
For \(i=j\), the \(L^2\) inner product is \(\mathbb EZ_i^2=1\). For \(i\ne j\), independence factors \(\mathbb EZ_iZ_j=(\mathbb EZ_i)(\mathbb EZ_j)=0\). Almost-everywhere representative identities move between \(Z_i\) and the product coordinates. Thus \(\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle=\mathbf1_{i=j}\).

Equal indices give the scalar second moment one. Distinct indices give a product of two zero means by independence, yielding the Kronecker-delta inner product.

steps.title: Orthonormality of the Gaussian coordinates
steps.body:
The preceding inner-product formula is the orthonormality criterion for a family in a real Hilbert space. The identity converts the diagonal value one and off-diagonal value zero into orthonormality of the scalar coordinate classes, the input for the orthogonal-series extension.

The coordinate classes have unit norm and pairwise zero inner products. These are exactly the orthonormality conditions that turn coefficient-square summability into convergence of the synthesis series.

steps.title: Normalization of the source probability
steps.body:
Each scalar Gaussian factor is a probability measure. The product-probability hypothesis therefore gives \(Q(\Omega)=1\). This normalization permits constant functions and integrable functions to be treated in the usual probability-space \(L^2\) theory below.

A countable product of probability measures has total mass one. This permits the expectation and \(L^2\) inequalities used throughout the synthesis construction without additional finite-mass factors.

steps.title: Synthesis from square-summable coefficients
steps.body:
Extend the orthonormal family \(Z_i\) to a linear isometry \(S:\ell^2(\iota)\to L^2(Q)\). The orthogonal-family extension theorem constructs the limit of finite sums and preserves squared norm, \(\|S(a)\|_2^2=\sum_i a_i^2\). It constructs an \(L^2\) limit without asserting pointwise convergence of the random series.

The coefficient sequence of a Hilbert vector is square summable by Parseval. Orthogonality of the Gaussian coordinates then makes the corresponding random series Cauchy in \(L^2\), defining its synthesis limit.

steps.title: Convergence of the synthesis series
steps.body:
The synthesis series \(\sum_i a_iZ_i\) converges in \(L^2\). Its convergence may be expressed by finite-subset partial sums: the squared norm of a tail is the sum of its squared coefficients, which tends to zero by square summability. No enumeration of the index set is required for this orthogonal-series limit.

The squared norm of a partial-sum difference is the sum of squared tail coefficients. Those tails tend to zero, proving that the prescribed series converges to the synthesized class.

steps.title: The isonormal linear map
steps.body:
For a Hilbert basis \(b\), compose its coordinate isometry \(\mathcal C_b:H\to\ell^2(\iota)\) with the Gaussian coefficient-sum isometry. The resulting linear isometry \(I_b\) sends \(x\) to the Gaussian series with coefficients \(\langle b_i,x\rangle\), and preserves all inner products.

This composition defines a linear map on the original Hilbert space. Its norm preservation is the same coefficient-square identity used to prove convergence.

steps.title: The series representation of the isonormal map
steps.body:
Apply the norm convergence of the Gaussian coordinate series to the coefficient family \(\mathcal C_b(x)\). Unfolding the composition gives \(I_b(x)=\sum_i\langle b_i,x\rangle Z_i\) in \(L^2\). This is the exact series represented by the isonormal linear isometry.

The series formula identifies the abstract linear map with the Gaussian-coordinate series. This permits finite-sum moment calculations to pass to arbitrary Hilbert inputs by continuity.

steps.title: Expectation as an inner product with one
steps.body:
On a probability space, the constant one is in \(L^2\). The definition of the real \(L^2\) inner product gives \(\mathbb EX=\langle1,X\rangle\), after replacing the selected constant representative by one almost everywhere. This exhibits expectation as a continuous functional.

On a probability space the constant-one class has norm one. Pairing a scalar class with it is integration, so expectation is a continuous linear functional on \(L^2\).

steps.title: Centering of each coordinate class
steps.body:
Use \(Z_i=\omega_i\) almost everywhere to replace the \(L^2\) representative inside the integral. The already established centered coordinate expectation then gives \(\mathbb EZ_i=0\).

The representative identity transfers the source coordinate's zero mean to its \(L^2\) class. Thus these square-integrable coordinate classes have zero expectation.

steps.title: Centering of the synthesized series
steps.body:
Each finite partial sum \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\) has mean zero by linearity and the coordinate means. Pair the \(L^2\)-convergent series with the constant one; continuity of the inner product passes the zero expectations to the limit, giving \(\mathbb ES(a)=0\).

Every finite synthesis sum has mean zero. Continuity of the expectation functional carries that equality to the \(L^2\) limit, proving the synthesized variable is centered.

steps.title: Centering of every isonormal value
steps.body:
The isonormal variable is the Gaussian coefficient-sum isometry applied to the Hilbert-basis coefficients of \(x\). Specialize the synthesis mean theorem to these coefficients to get \(\mathbb EI_b(x)=0\), using the zero mean of that coefficient-sum limit.

The isonormal value is the synthesized class, so its zero mean follows from the same limit calculation. Linearity ensures that this centering holds for every index vector.

steps.title: Variance from the Hilbert norm
steps.body:
For an \(L^2\) random variable with mean zero, the variance formula reduces to \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\int X^2dQ\). The \(L^2\) norm identity identifies this with \(\|X\|_2^2\). The explicit mean premise is used to remove the centering term.

For a centered scalar class, variance equals its squared \(L^2\) norm. Norm preservation of synthesis therefore identifies the variance with the squared norm of the Hilbert index vector.

steps.title: The representative of a finite partial sum
steps.body:
Induct over the finite set. The zero sum has zero representative almost everywhere; addition and scalar multiplication of \(L^2\) classes agree almost everywhere with the corresponding pointwise operations. Intersect the finitely many full-measure sets to obtain \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i\omega_i\) almost everywhere.

The class of a finite linear combination agrees almost everywhere with the corresponding pointwise coordinate sum. Thus elementary finite-dimensional Gaussian formulas can be applied to that sum.

steps.title: Gaussianity of finite partial sums
steps.body:
Independent scalar standard Gaussians remain Gaussian after a finite linear combination. Apply that finite-sum Gaussian theorem to \(a_i\omega_i\), and transfer the law across the representative equality for the finite Gaussian sum. Thus this square-integrable partial sum has the same Gaussian law as its coordinate representation.

A finite linear combination of independent Gaussian coordinates is Gaussian. Its variance is the sum of squared coefficients because all cross covariances vanish.

steps.title: The mean of each finite partial sum
steps.body:
The integral of a finite \(L^2\) sum is the sum of its integrals, because every summand is integrable. Each coordinate mean is zero, hence \(\mathbb E\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i=0\). This supplies the centering parameter needed to identify its Gaussian law.

Each finite coefficient sum remains centered, since expectation is linear and every scalar coordinate is centered. This identifies its mean parameter before its exact scalar law is recorded.

steps.title: The exact Gaussian law of a partial sum
steps.body:
A scalar Gaussian law is determined by its mean and variance. The finite sum is Gaussian and centered; its variance is its squared \(L^2\) norm. Therefore its law is \(\mathcal N(0,\|\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\|_2^2)\), with the variance converted to a nonnegative real.

For the independent standard Gaussian family \(Z_i\), orthogonality in \(L^2\) gives \(\|\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\|_2^2=\sum_{i\in F}a_i^2\). Thus this Gaussian law has mean zero and variance equal to that finite sum of squared coefficients. The conclusion applies to every finite index set \(F\).

steps.title: The Gaussian law of the synthesis limit
steps.body:
Finite partial sums converge in \(L^2\) to \(S(a)\), and each has the centered Gaussian law with its own squared norm as variance. Apply preservation of a Gaussian law under square-mean convergence; the isometry then rewrites the limiting variance as \(\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2\). This proves Gaussianity of the completed infinite series.

As the finite index sets increase, the partial variances \(\sum_{i\in F}a_i^2\) converge to \(\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2\). Convergence in \(L^2\) implies convergence in \(L^1\), so each characteristic function converges to the characteristic function of the limit. The limiting Gaussian characteristic function identifies the law of \(S(a)\) as \(\mathcal N(0,\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2)\).

steps.title: The Gaussian law of an isonormal value
steps.body:
Apply the synthesis law theorem to \(\mathcal C_b(x)\). The Hilbert-basis coordinate map preserves norm, so the variance becomes \(\|x\|^2\). Hence \(I_b(x)\sim\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\), including the degenerate law for \(x=0\).

Replacing synthesis by the equal isonormal map yields the same centered Gaussian law. This identifies each individual isonormal evaluation without selecting a particular expansion after the limit.

steps.title: Joint Gaussianity of the isonormal family
steps.body:
Each isonormal evaluation has the exact law \(\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\). By linearity, every finite linear combination of these evaluations is another evaluation, at the corresponding linear combination of indices. It is therefore Gaussian, which establishes joint Gaussianity of the finite-dimensional family.

Any finite linear combination of isonormal evaluations is one isonormal evaluation at the corresponding linear combination of indices. Its scalar Gaussian law verifies joint Gaussianity of the family.

steps.title: The isonormal covariance identity
steps.body:
Both variables are centered, so their covariance is \(\mathbb E[I_b(x)I_b(y)]\), the \(L^2\) inner product. The linear isometry preserves that inner product, giving \(\operatorname{Cov}(I_b(x),I_b(y))=\langle x,y\rangle_H\). The moment bound verifies integrability through their \(L^2\) membership.

The inner-product identity follows by polarization of the norm-preserving map \(I_b\). Since both means are zero, no centering term remains when expressing the covariance as this expected product.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianLinearProcess.title: Scalar Gaussian linear maps give jointly Gaussian processes
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianLinearProcess.summary:
Let \(T:H\to L^2(P;\mathbb R)\) be linear and suppose every \(T(x)\) has a scalar Gaussian law. For any finite vectors \(x_i\) and coefficients \(a_i\), linearity gives \(\sum_i a_iT(x_i)=T(\sum_i a_ix_i)\). The right side is Gaussian by assumption, proving joint Gaussianity of the finite family.

Applying this argument to the vectors indexed by finitely many process times gives a Gaussian process. The time index set may be uncountable. This conclusion specifies finite-dimensional laws and does not assert sample-path continuity or independence without the corresponding covariance conditions.

steps.title: Finite-dimensional Gaussianity of a linear family
steps.body:
Use the finite-dimensional Gaussian criterion: every scalar linear functional of \((T(f_i))_i\) must be Gaussian. A finite linear combination equals \(T(\sum_i a_if_i)\) as an \(L^2\) class by linearity, hence agrees almost everywhere as a random variable. The assumed Gaussianity of every \(T(x)\) proves the criterion.

For coefficients \(a_i\), linearity gives \(\sum_i a_iT(v_i)=T(\sum_i a_iv_i)\). The scalar Gaussian hypothesis applied to that one index verifies the Gaussian law of every finite linear combination.

steps.title: A Gaussian process from a Gaussian linear map
steps.body:
For each finite set of times, apply the preceding joint-Gaussian theorem to the corresponding finite family of vectors \(f(t)\). This verifies the finite-dimensional-law definition of joint Gaussianity of every finite collection. The index set may be uncountable; this statement alone asserts no sample-path continuity.

The finite-dimensional criterion just established applies to every finite choice of process times. Thus the family is a Gaussian process, with its joint distributions determined by its mean and covariance data.
