Apply the change-of-variables formula for the weighted pushforward to accepted and rejected branches of the coupled measure. Their cost is the integral of the acceptance-weighted proposal distance plus rejection-weighted stay distance over \(\rho\otimes\gamma\). The integrand is the expression bounded by the pointwise common-noise discrepancy inequality.

Expand the two weighted pushforwards against the distance test. The accepted distance is between the two proposals; the rejected distance is between the ULA proposal and the old MALA state. Both use the same Gaussian variable, so the common-noise estimate applies inside the integral.

steps.title: A one-step cost bound
steps.body:
Integrate the pointwise coupling bound. The old distance integrates to \(\mathcal C(\rho)\); the error depends only on the second state and innovation. Its second marginal is Gibbs by hypothesis, so that integral is bounded by \(C_{U,L}h\sqrt h\). Thus \(\mathcal C(\rho')\le\mathcal C(\rho)+C_{U,L}h\sqrt h\), valid initially as an extended inequality.

After integration, the proposal-contraction term contributes at most the old expected distance. The rejection term depends only on the second marginal and fresh Gaussian noise; if that marginal is Gibbs, the uniform local bound contributes at most \(C_{U,L}h^{3/2}\).

steps.title: The accumulated coupled-chain cost
steps.body:
Induct from zero diagonal cost. The second marginal remains Gibbs by the supplied one-step MALA invariance, so the one-step cost bound applies at every iteration. Summing the same local error gives \(\mathcal C(\rho_n)\le nC_{U,L}h\sqrt h\).

Starting from a diagonal pair, the initial cost is zero. Repeatedly applying \(c_{k+1}\le c_k+b_h\) gives \(c_n\le n b_h\), with \(b_h=C_{U,L}h^{3/2}\). On a fixed horizon this vanishes as the mesh tends to zero.

steps.title: Integrability of the coupled-chain distance
steps.body:
The quantitative extended cost estimate bounds \(\int\|x-y\|d\rho_n\) by a finite embedded real number. The distance is measurable and nonnegative, so finite extended integral is equivalent to ordinary integrability. This proves the required first-moment condition.

The nonnegative cost has a finite extended integral by the preceding explicit bound. Since the distance is measurable, this is precisely finiteness of its ordinary first moment. The signed characteristic-function calculation can therefore use subtraction of finite integrals.

steps.title: The ordinary integral cost estimate
steps.body:
The coupled distance is nonnegative and integrable by the preceding finite-cost argument. Its nonnegative cost integral therefore equals its ordinary expectation. The accumulated bound becomes \(\mathbb E_{\rho_n}\|X-Y\|\le nC_{U,L}h\sqrt h\), with every quantity finite.

Identifying the ordinary expected distance with the finite nonnegative cost transfers the same bound to real expectations. The characteristic-function comparison with the continuous solution uses this finite first-moment estimate.

UnadjustedLangevin/MALAInvariance.lean.title: Exact Gibbs invariance under the Metropolis-adjusted step
UnadjustedLangevin/MALAInvariance.lean.summary:
The joint law of a Gibbs state and its Langevin proposal has density \(Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}q_h(x,y)\). Its reverse-to-forward density ratio is \(e^{R_h(x,y)}\), since both state-independent normalizers cancel. The Metropolis acceptance \(\min(1,e^{R_h})\) therefore gives accepted density \(\min\{Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}q_h(x,y),Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}q_h(y,x)\}\).

This accepted density is symmetric in the two states. Its first and second marginals agree, and rejected mass remains at the current state. Acceptance and rejection sum to the original input measure, so one adjusted step preserves Gibbs. No invariant-law hypothesis for the transition is used in this proof.

steps.title: The joint starting-proposal law
steps.body:
Push \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) through \((x,\xi)\mapsto(x,T_h(x,\xi))\). Its first coordinate retains the current state, and its second records the Gaussian proposal. This joint measure is the input to the accepted-flow detailed-balance theorem.

The first marginal is the starting law because the Gaussian conditional proposal has mass one. Its second marginal is the unadjusted proposal law. Keeping both coordinates makes forward and reverse density comparisons available on the same product space.

steps.title: The Gibbs-weighted proposal density
steps.body:
Set \(w_h(x,y)=\exp(-U(x)-\|y-x+h\nabla U(x)\|^2/(4h))\). The Gibbs and Gaussian normalization constants are kept in a separate symmetric base measure, so \(w_h\) is strictly positive and the ratio involves only its two exponentials.

With respect to Lebesgue product measure, the pair density is the Gibbs density at \(x\) multiplied by the proposal density from \(x\) to \(y\). Both factors are positive, so reverse/forward ratios can be formed pointwise and canceled without exceptional zero-density cases.

steps.title: The forward-reverse density ratio
steps.body:
Divide the two positive exponentials and use \(e^a/e^b=e^{a-b}\). Expanding the definition of \(w_h\) shows the exponent difference is exactly the logarithmic Metropolis ratio. Thus \(w_h(y,x)/w_h(x,y)=e^{R_h(x,y)}\).

Taking logarithms turns multiplication of target and proposal factors into the potential and quadratic terms defining the log ratio. Exponentiating recovers the exact reverse/forward joint-density ratio, so the acceptance used in the coupling is precisely the detailed-balance acceptance.

steps.title: Equality of the innovation and pair-density transitions
steps.body:
Transport acceptance and rejection weights through the measurable pair map using composition of a measurable map with a weighted pushforward. Projecting the accepted pair to its second coordinate gives the proposal; projecting rejected pairs to the first gives the unchanged state. These are precisely the two branches defining one Metropolis-adjusted transition.

Changing variables from Gaussian innovations to proposed positions commutes with multiplication by the corresponding acceptance weight. Consequently the innovation-based transition and the pair-density Metropolis transition have identical accepted and rejected components, not merely the same total mass.

steps.title: The joint proposal density at Gibbs
steps.body:
Apply the Gaussian joint-density theorem with center \(x-h\nabla U(x)\), then multiply its density by the Gibbs density. Combine the exponential factors into \(w_h(x,y)\). Pull the two state-independent normalizers into the base measure \(Z_U^{-1}C_h(dx\,dy)\), which is invariant under coordinate swap.

Disintegrating the state/proposal law gives the displayed density against Lebesgue product measure. Tonelli is available for nonnegative tests; the Gaussian density normalization verifies the conditional mass and the target normalization verifies the total mass.

steps.title: Gibbs invariance of the adjusted transition
steps.body:
The joint proposal measure has a positive density \(w_h\) against a symmetric base. Its acceptance rule is \(\min(1,w_h(y,x)/w_h(x,y))\) by the ratio between the reverse and forward target-weighted proposal densities. Hence its accepted density is the symmetric minimum \(\min(w_h(x,y),w_h(y,x))\).

Apply preservation of the target marginal by the symmetric accepted density and the exact step/output identity. The initial marginal of the proposal pair is Gibbs, since projecting \(\pi_U\otimes\gamma\) to its state returns \(\pi_U\). Thus \(M_h\pi_U=\pi_U\) is proved with no stationarity input.

The accepted density is \(\min(\pi(x)q_h(x,y),\pi(y)q_h(y,x))\), symmetric in \((x,y)\). Its two marginals coincide. Rejected mass stays at \(x\), and accepted plus rejected input mass is Gibbs, proving exact invariance for each positive admissible step.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianLangevin.lean.title: Construct the L² Langevin equation from Brownian-coordinate laws
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianLangevin.lean.summary:
The vector of Brownian coordinates defines an additive input \(N_a(t)=\sqrt2([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])\) in \(L^2\). It is continuous in mean square, vanishes at local time zero, and has norm \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) for nonnegative starting and elapsed times. These properties follow from the coordinate Gaussian increment moments.

Apply the deterministic existence theorem in the Banach space of square-integrable random variables with the Lipschitz gradient-composition map. It gives a continuous solution of the Langevin integral equation on a short interval and, by concatenation, on every finite horizon. The equation and noise moment are proved for the constructed solution; no sample-path differentiability is required.

steps.title: The Langevin-scaled Brownian input
steps.body:
Define \(N_a(t)=\sqrt2([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])\) in \(L^2\), using the real-time Brownian extension. The subtraction fixes the input at zero at local time zero, and the \(\sqrt2\) factor gives the overdamped Langevin diffusion normalization.

The initial absolute time \(a\) fixes which Brownian increment is used during this segment. For \(a,t\ge0\), the input is \(\sqrt2(B_{a+t}-B_a)\), and every scalar coordinate is centered Gaussian with variance \(2t\). Subtracting the value at the starting time ensures that a local integral equation starts with zero additive input even when the driving Brownian path has already evolved before the segment begins.

steps.title: Continuity of the Brownian input in square mean
steps.body:
The real-time Brownian map is continuous in \(L^2\) from its Gaussian increment moments. Composition with \(t\mapsto a+t\), subtraction of the fixed class \([B_a]\), and scalar multiplication preserve continuity. Thus the additive input satisfies the deterministic Picard theorem's continuity requirement.

Mean-square continuity is the relevant regularity for an integral equation in \(L^2\). The increment identity \(\mathbb E\|B_t-B_s\|^2=d|t-s|\) makes the norm difference tend to zero. Translating time, subtracting one fixed vector and multiplying by \(\sqrt2\) preserve this property. Thus continuity is derived from the coordinate increment law.

steps.title: The Brownian input at zero
steps.body:
At local time zero both Brownian terms are \([B_a]\), so they cancel and their scalar multiple is zero. The defining formula gives zero by vector subtraction; no exceptional-set statement is needed because this is equality in \(L^2\).

A local solution is prescribed to have initial state \(Y_0\). Evaluating its integral equation at zero gives \(Y(0)-Y_0=N_a(0)\), since the zero-length integral vanishes. The equality \(N_a(0)=0\) therefore enforces the intended initial condition exactly. This cancellation holds for the square-integrable random vectors themselves, regardless of which pointwise versions are used.

steps.title: The exact input norm
steps.body:
For \(a,t\ge0\), apply the exact real-time Brownian increment moment formula. It gives \(\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\), with \(d=|\iota|\). The scalar Gaussian increment laws prove this value; it is not an additional noise-bound hypothesis.

There are \(d\) scalar increment coordinates, each with variance \(t\) and zero mean. Therefore \(\mathbb E\|N_a(t)\|^2=2\sum_{j=1}^d t=2dt\). Taking the nonnegative square root gives the exact norm. The identity for the squared Euclidean norm is a sum of coordinate squares and contains no mixed terms. Thus the norm formula uses the scalar increment laws alone and requires no spatial independence assumption.

steps.title: A short-interval square-mean Langevin solution
steps.body:
Supply the continuous, zero-starting \(N_a\) to the short-interval fixed-point theorem in the square-integrable Hilbert space. It constructs \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(\nabla U)(Y_s)ds+N_a(t)\) for \(Lh\le1/2\). The same constructed input also satisfies the proved noise norm identity. Neither the integral equation nor its noise estimate is assumed.

On a short interval, the map taking a trial path to \(Y_0-\int_0^t\nabla U(Y_s)ds+N_a(t)\) has contraction constant at most \(Lh\) in the supremum of \(L^2\) norms. The stated restriction makes this map a contraction. The noise is only added, so its continuity is sufficient; it need not have an ordinary time derivative.

steps.title: A solution on every finite horizon
steps.body:
Use the unrestricted finite-horizon \(L^2\) existence theorem with the same constructed Brownian input. The resulting solution is continuous in \(L^2\), starts at the prescribed random variable, and satisfies the gradient integral equation. The exact \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) noise formula is included as a proved property.

The global finite-horizon construction joins sufficiently short fixed-point intervals, using each endpoint as the next initial state. Lipschitzness of the score preserves square integrability and gives uniqueness by Grönwall. The resulting equation is therefore a solution of the gradient integral equation on the required horizon. The Brownian norm formula remains unchanged because it concerns the supplied additive input, not the unknown solution.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianReference.lea.title: Assemble continuous Brownian reference segments
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianReference.lea.summary:
At absolute time \(nh\), solve the square-mean integral equation on the next interval using input \(\sqrt2(B_{nh+t}-B_{nh})\). The endpoint at local time \(h\) is used as the initial class of the next segment. Thus consecutive segments agree at the endpoints as \(L^2\) classes.

Normalize the endpoint input to define the Euler innovation. Multiplication by \(\sqrt{2h}\) recovers the same reference increment. Continuity, the integral equation, joining, and the noise moments follow from the construction. If every segment time has Gibbs law, the Gibbs gradient moment gives the remaining reference drift bound. That stationary-law property is still a hypothesis here and is proved separately.

steps.title: A Brownian-driven segment from a given initial class
steps.body:
Choose the integral solution supplied by finite-horizon existence for the integral equation driven by the continuous Brownian class for the segment starting at absolute time \(nh\), with the supplied initial \(L^2\) variable. Select one of the solutions whose existence was proved. It has the stated integral equation and continuity properties.

Fix a segment length \(h>0\), an index \(n\), and an initial random vector \(K\). The local reference is a solution of \(Y_t-K=-\int_0^t\nabla U(Y_s)ds+\sqrt2(B_{nh+t}-B_{nh})\). Existence has already been proved for this input. Selecting such a solution introduces no extra equation or numerical estimate; all its analytic properties are inherited from that existence result.

steps.title: The defining properties of the segment
steps.body:
The selected solution has continuity, the time-zero initial value, the gradient integral equation on \([0,h]\), and the exact noise norm. These four properties describe the selected segment independently of which solution is selected.

The four properties have distinct later uses. Continuity makes the drift time integral meaningful. The initial-value identity permits adjoining intervals. The integral equation gives the local Euler drift defect after subtraction. Finally the exact Brownian norm controls reference increments quantitatively. These four properties are used in the subsequent coupling estimate.

steps.title: The successive reference knots
steps.body:
Set the zeroth knot to the prescribed initial variable. Define the next knot to be the endpoint at local time \(h\) of the segment started at the current knot. This recursion ensures consecutive segments meet exactly as \(L^2\) classes.

Write \(K_0=Y^{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(K_{n+1}=Y^{(n)}_h\), where the \(n\)-th local solution starts at \(K_n\). This is an ordinary recursion in the space of square-integrable states. Each endpoint belongs to that space by the solution construction. It fixes all future segment initial values from the same original state and Brownian source.

steps.title: The reference segments
steps.body:
At index \(n\), select a restarted Brownian-driven segment with the recursively constructed \(n\)-th knot as initial state. The absolute noise start is \(nh\), so all segments are driven by increments of the same Brownian process.

The segment index changes both its initial state and its absolute noise interval. Its equation uses increments beginning at \(nh\), rather than restarting an unrelated Brownian process at each iteration. Consequently the endpoint increment used for the Euler innovation is the same increment appearing in this reference segment. The two equal endpoint increments therefore cancel in the synchronous comparison.

steps.title: The starting value of each segment
steps.body:
The chosen-segment specification states its value at zero equals its supplied initial state. Here that state is the \(n\)-th knot, so \(Y^{(n)}_0=K_n\) follows directly by specialization.

At local time zero the drift integral and Brownian increment both vanish. The segment equation thus gives \(Y^{(n)}_0=K_n\). Together with \(K_n=Y^{(n-1)}_h\) for \(n>0\), this proves exact joining. The error from joining segments is therefore zero at every boundary.

steps.title: The initial reference knot
steps.body:
Apply the segment-start identity at \(n=0\), then unfold the zeroth knot. The constructed reference therefore begins at exactly the prescribed random variable, preserving its chosen joint realization with the numerical initialization.

The first knot is the prescribed random vector, not merely a new variable with the same law. Hence the first reference segment retains the exact initial coupling with the numerical chain. For each arbitrary initial coupling, their root mean-square separation must remain the initial error used by the synchronous argument.

steps.title: The endpoint Euler innovations
steps.body:
Normalize the segment endpoint noise by \(1/\sqrt{2h}\). This defines the \(L^2\) innovation used by the Euler chain, so it shares the exact Brownian increment driving the reference segment.

The endpoint input is \(N_{nh}(h)=\sqrt2(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})\). Dividing it by \(\sqrt{2h}\) gives \((B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})/\sqrt h\), the standard Brownian increment normalization. Defining the innovation from the same input ensures that multiplication by the Euler amplitude recovers the reference noise exactly; its Gaussian law is verified separately.

steps.title: Identification of endpoint noise
steps.body:
For \(h>0\), \(\sqrt{2h}\ne0\). Multiply the normalized noise class by \(\sqrt{2h}\) and cancel the inverse scalar. The resulting equality identifies the Euler noise contribution with the same Brownian endpoint input in the integral equation.

Positivity of \(h\) makes \(\sqrt{2h}\) strictly positive, so scalar division and multiplication cancel. Thus \(\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n=N_{nh}(h)\) as square-integrable random vectors. This equality is stronger than agreement in distribution: it allows the two noise terms to disappear when subtracting the Euler update and the reference endpoint equation on their common space.

steps.title: The stationary Brownian reference
steps.body:
Use the constructed segments as the reference family. Their specification proves continuity and the integral equation; recursive knots prove endpoint compatibility; normalized noise proves endpoint matching; Gibbs-score moment transfer proves the drift bound. The supplied all-time Gibbs-law premise remains visible and is later proved by the stationarity construction.

Assuming every reference time has Gibbs law, the score moment gives \(\|\nabla U(Y_t^{(n)})\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\). The Brownian construction supplies \(\|N_{nh}(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). Along with segment joining and endpoint noise matching, these bounds meet the analytic coupling hypotheses. Stationarity remains an explicit input at this intermediate stage, rather than a consequence of the integral equation alone.

steps.title: The reference under strong convexity
steps.body:
Positive strong convexity gives a finite positive Gibbs partition and finite target moments. Apply the reference construction using these target properties and the Brownian endpoint-noise identities. Its all-time stationary-law premise remains explicit at this stage and is supplied later by the invariant-approximation argument.

Positive strong convexity implies a finite positive Gibbs partition and a finite second moment. These normalization and integrability facts verify the target normalization and integrability requirements before the reference is assembled. The remaining law premise says that the constructed solution has this target distribution at every segment time. A later stationarity proof supplies that premise using invariant approximations and a continuous-limit argument.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianSegmentsGloba.title: Identify chosen reference segments with one global solution
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianSegmentsGloba.summary:
Restrict a global square-mean integral solution to \([a,a+h]\) and shift its time variable to \([0,h]\). Subtracting its equation at \(a\) gives the local integral equation with initial state \(Y_a\) and input \(\sqrt2(B_{a+t}-B_a)\). It is the same equation as the restarted segment.

Uniqueness identifies these two solutions on their common interval. Induction identifies the recursive knots with \(Y_{nh}\), and then every local segment with \(t\mapsto Y_{nh+t}\), subject to the horizon hypotheses. Any fixed-time law statement for the global solution therefore applies to the segment. This identification itself requires no stationary-law hypothesis.

steps.title: The increment of the Langevin Brownian input
steps.body:
Expand the two increments from zero and subtract them. Their common \([B_0]\) term cancels, leaving \(\sqrt2([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])=N_a(t)\). This is an algebraic cocycle identity in \(L^2\), valid for the real-time extension as defined.

Both sides equal the same linear combination of three Brownian values. Expanding \(N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)\) cancels the two copies of \(B_0\), leaving \(\sqrt2(B_{a+t}-B_a)\). This cocycle property is the noise counterpart of additivity of time integrals and gives the additive input in the equation restarted at any nonnegative absolute time.

steps.title: Shifting the Langevin integral equation
steps.body:
Subtract the global integral equations at \(a+t\) and \(a\). Integral additivity gives the drift integral over \([a,a+t]\), and time translation turns it into \(\int_0^t\nabla U(Y_{a+s})ds\). The noise cocycle gives \(N_a(t)\), yielding the local segment equation with initial state \(Y_a\).

Subtracting the equations removes the original initial state. Additivity gives \(\int_0^{a+t}-\int_0^a=\int_a^{a+t}\), and the substitution \(s=a+r\) puts the latter integral on \([0,t]\). Continuity of the composed score ensures these time integrals exist. The cocycle then produces exactly the local input used in the selected segment construction.

steps.title: A restarted segment equals the global solution
steps.body:
The shifted global path and the selected local segment are continuous solutions of the same \(L^2\) integral equation with the same initial value and noise input. Apply \(L^2\) uniqueness to identify them on \([0,h]\). The horizon premise ensures the shifted interval lies inside the global solution interval.

Let \(D_t\) be the difference between the selected local segment and the shifted global path. Their identical inputs cancel, giving \(\|D_t\|_2\le L\int_0^t\|D_s\|_2ds\) with \(D_0=0\). Grönwall forces \(D_t=0\). Thus any selected local solution has the same values as the shifted global solution on that interval.

steps.title: The knots lie on the global solution
steps.body:
Induct on the knot index. At zero, the global equation and zero-starting noise give the prescribed initial state. If the current knot equals \(Y_{nh}\), segment/global uniqueness makes its endpoint equal \(Y_{(n+1)h}\), establishing the next knot identity.

The induction fixes the relationship between recursive endpoints and absolute time. If \(K_n=Y_{nh}\), local uniqueness identifies the whole next segment with \(t\mapsto Y_{nh+t}\). Its endpoint is therefore \(Y_{nh+h}=Y_{(n+1)h}\). Starting from the original initial equality proves the knot formula for every index whose time lies inside the chosen horizon.

steps.title: Every reference segment lies on the global solution
steps.body:
The knot/global theorem supplies the matching initial value for the \(n\)-th segment. Apply uniqueness of restarted and globally restricted integral solutions to conclude \(Y^{(n)}_t=Y_{nh+t}\) on \([0,h]\). This is a deterministic identification of the constructions, with no stationarity premise.

Once the initial knot has been identified, the segment equation and shifted global equation have the same data. Their equality therefore holds at every local time, including the endpoints. In particular any fixed-time law theorem for the global process transfers to every segment time \(nh+t\). Stationarity can thus be established once for the global solution instead of reproved separately for each recursively selected segment.

UnadjustedLangevin/ChainLaw.lean.title: A noise-driven recursion has a law independent of its realization
UnadjustedLangevin/ChainLaw.lean.summary:
Let \(F\) be a measurable update and define \(X_0=x\), \(X_{n+1}=F(X_n,w_n)\). The output at a fixed finite index is a measurable function of initialization and the finite innovation prefix. If initialization and the whole innovation sequence are independent with laws \(\mu,Q\), the output law is the pushforward of \(\mu\otimes Q\) by this recursion map.

For independent identically distributed innovations with common law \(\eta\), their sequence law is \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Consequently different probability-space constructions with these same input laws have identical output laws. Specializing the update to Gaussian Euler identifies both the pointwise ULA recursion and its square-integrable representative with these distributions.

steps.title: The recursion driven by a noise sequence
steps.body:
Define \(X_0=x\), \(X_{n+1}=F(X_n,w_n)\) for any update and noise path. No distribution assumptions are part of the recursion; they enter only when a law is assigned to its inputs.

For a fixed input \((x,w)\), the finite-time state uses only the first finitely many coordinates of the innovation path. No probability measure is needed to evaluate it. This separates the deterministic algorithm from its probabilistic realization and permits the same recursion to be applied on product probability spaces and on any probability space with the stated input laws.

steps.title: The noise-driven chain at zero
steps.body:
The zero clause of the recursion evaluates to the supplied initial state. This defining identity is the base case for all law and measurability inductions.

Before any update, the output is exactly \(x\), independently of the innovation path. Consequently its law under an independent input product must be the initial marginal. The same identity also starts the induction proving that two deterministic recursions with the same update and inputs agree at every finite step.

steps.title: The successor recursion
steps.body:
The successor clause unfolds to \(X_{n+1}=F(X_n,w_n)\). Substitution of the Euler update identifies this recursion with ULA by induction.

The successor equation identifies which innovation is used next: state \(n\) uses only indices below \(n\), and its successor consumes \(w_n\). The state therefore depends on the preceding innovation prefix. A fresh-noise theorem later separates the prefix \((w_0,\ldots,w_{n-1})\) from this next coordinate.

steps.title: Measurability of the noise-driven chain
steps.body:
Induct on \(n\). The base map is the initial-state projection. At the successor, pair the measurable current state with the measurable coordinate evaluation \(w\mapsto w_n\), then compose with the measurable uncurried update. Thus each iterate is a measurable function of initialization and the full noise path.

This induction requires only measurability of the update in both of its inputs. In particular, it also applies when the update is discontinuous. Measurability of each iterate ensures that its distribution is defined and permits the subsequent integration over the initial state and noise sequence.

steps.title: The marginal law of the recursion
steps.body:
Push \(\mu\otimes Q\) through the measurable recursion output at index \(n\). The product gives independent initialization and noise path. This output law depends only on the initial law, noise-path law, and update, not on a particular sample-space construction.

If \(F_n\) denotes the finite recursion map, define its distribution by \((F_n)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\). The product specifies independence of initialization and the entire innovation path while allowing arbitrary dependence within \(Q\). Thus this definition applies before specializing to iid noise and makes the exact inputs determining the output distribution explicit.

steps.title: Its initial law
steps.body:
At index zero the output map is first-coordinate projection. Since \(Q\) has mass one, the first marginal of \(\mu\otimes Q\) is exactly \(\mu\). This proves that the output law starts from the supplied initial law.

For a measurable initial-state set \(A\), the probability of the zero-step output lying in \(A\) is \((\mu\otimes Q)(A\times\Omega_Q)=\mu(A)Q(\Omega_Q)=\mu(A)\). The noise source's unit mass is the only normalization needed here. This direct marginal computation proves that the product construction preserves the specified initialization.

steps.title: Law identification under independence
steps.body:
Independence gives the joint input law \(P_{(X,W)}=P_X\otimes P_W\). Push that identity through the measurable recursion output and use pushforward composition. The output law is therefore the pushforward of this product input law under the recursion map at the specified index.

Independence means that the joint law of initialization and complete noise path factors into their two marginals. Applying the same measurable recursion to this equality yields equality of output laws. In particular the result does not require the input variables to have a product-space representation; their factorized joint distribution is sufficient.

steps.title: Law identification for independent identical innovations
steps.body:
Joint independence of the innovations and their common law \(\eta\) identify the entire noise-path law with \(\bigotimes_n\eta\). Substitute this identity into the independent-initialization law theorem. Countability of the time index supplies path-valued measurability.

For iid innovations with common law \(\eta\), every finite cylinder event factors as a product of \(\eta\)-probabilities. These cylinder probabilities identify the complete path law as \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Substituting this law in the independent-input result shows that the algorithm's distribution is determined by \(F\), \(\mu\) and \(\eta\), independently of the probability-space representation of those inputs.

steps.title: Uniqueness of the resulting marginal laws
steps.body:
Apply the independent-input pushforward formula on both probability spaces. Equality of their initial laws and the shared innovation law makes the right sides identical, so their iterate laws agree. The theorem compares distributions without coupling the two constructions.

Both realizations are measurable images of the same abstract input probability \(\mu\otimes\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Hence each measurable output set receives the same probability in both. The conclusion is equality of their distributions at a fixed finite iteration, even though their random variables live on different spaces and no joint coupling between them was specified.

steps.title: Equality with the ULA recursion
steps.body:
Induct on the index with \(F(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\). At zero both recursions return the same state. If they agree at index \(n\), their successor equations apply the same function to the same state and innovation, so they agree at index \(n+1\). This identifies the generic noise-driven recursion with ULA pointwise.

With the Euler update \(F(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\), both pointwise constructions have the same initial clause and the same successor clause. Applying the induction hypothesis inside this common function proves equality at the next step. The argument is purely deterministic, so it can be reused with every supplied innovation sequence before assigning Gaussian laws.

steps.title: Measurability of the ULA update
steps.body:
Lipschitzness makes \(\nabla U\) continuous. The joint ULA update is obtained from coordinate projections and that gradient by scalar multiplication and addition, hence is measurable. This discharges the generic recursion's update-measurability premise.

The map \((x,z)\mapsto x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\) is jointly continuous because the gradient is Lipschitz and hence continuous. Coordinate projections, addition and scalar multiplication preserve continuity. Thus its measurability does not require a step restriction, strong convexity, or Gaussianity; those hypotheses enter only the later moment and convergence estimates.

steps.title: The ULA law under independent identical innovations
steps.body:
Use measurability of the Gaussian Euler update in the generic iid law theorem, then rewrite the generic recursion using equality of the two Gaussian Euler recursions. The result identifies the ULA recursion with the product-noise pushforward law.

Apply the general iid realization formula to the measurable Euler update. The deterministic recursion equality identifies its output with the Euler chain. Its time-\(n\) law is therefore the pushforward of the independent initialization and iid innovation path. This equality compares numerical chains on different probability-space extensions by their distributions.

steps.title: The square-integrable chain has the same law
steps.body:
The \(L^2\) chain representative agrees almost everywhere with the pointwise ULA recursion of the input representatives. Apply the pointwise law theorem and transfer pushforwards across that almost-everywhere equality. Quotient representative choices therefore do not change the algorithm law.

At every fixed finite index, the square-integrable recursion and its ordinary pointwise update agree almost surely. Almost-surely equal measurable random variables have the same pushforward law. The pointwise iid theorem therefore transfers to the square-integrable realization. This transfer ensures that analytic \(L^2\) estimates apply to the algorithm law, without depending on choices of representative random functions.

UnadjustedLangevin/MarkovLaw.lean.title: Identify recursive sampling laws with iterated Markov transitions
UnadjustedLangevin/MarkovLaw.lean.summary:
For a measurable update \(F\) and innovation law \(\eta\), define the transition \(M_\eta(\mu)=F_\#(\mu\otimes\eta)\). On the independent innovation product space, the current state is a measurable function of initialization and the preceding finite prefix. Independence of the next coordinate from that prefix and initialization gives joint law \(\mu_n\otimes\eta\) for the current state and next innovation.

Pushing this product law through \(F\) proves the successor marginal identity \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\). Equality at zero and induction identify the noise-driven laws with the iterated transition. Probability normalization is preserved at every step. Equality of input laws then gives this same conclusion on every probability-space realization satisfying the stated independence assumptions.

steps.title: The state as a function of a finite noise prefix
steps.body:
Evaluate the same recursion using only a finite prefix \((w_0,\ldots,w_{n-1})\). At the successor, recurse on the first \(n\) coordinates and use the final coordinate as the next innovation. This makes finite dependence explicit for the fresh-noise independence proof.

A time-\(n\) state can be evaluated from an input in \(E\times E^{\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}\). Restricting the prefix for the recursive call and reserving its final coordinate for the next update makes this finite dependence explicit. It provides the measurable factorization through past coordinates needed to prove independence from the next innovation.

steps.title: Agreement with the full recursion
steps.body:
Induct on prefix length. Restricting an infinite path to its first \(n\) entries gives the same previous state, and the final finite coordinate is \(w_n\). The successor updates thus agree, identifying finite-prefix and infinite-path constructions pointwise.

At length zero both maps return the initial state. At length \(n+1\), their previous states agree by induction after restricting to the first \(n\) coordinates, and both next innovations are \(w_n\). Applying the common update proves equality. Thus replacing the infinite path by its finite prefix does not alter the algorithm output.

steps.title: Measurability of the finite-prefix state
steps.body:
The zero map is the initial projection. At the successor, restriction to the earlier finite coordinates and evaluation of the last coordinate are measurable; combine them with the measurable update and the induction hypothesis. This proves the state depends measurably on a finite prefix.

Restriction of a finite coordinate family and evaluation of its last coordinate are measurable product maps. The induction hypothesis gives measurability of the previous state from the shorter prefix. Pair these two measurable outputs and compose with the update. This proves finite-prefix measurability without any probabilistic assumption and allows independence to be passed through the finite recursion.

steps.title: Independence of the prefix and the fresh innovation
steps.body:
The index sets \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and \(\{n\}\) are disjoint. Independence of the coordinate family on the iid product source therefore gives independence of the whole prefix vector and the next coordinate. This is stronger than pairwise independence of individual past entries.

On the iid path space, disjoint groups of coordinate evaluations generate independent sigma-algebras. The first group contains all indices less than \(n\), and the second contains only \(n\). Therefore the entire past prefix vector is independent of the fresh innovation. This joint statement is what permits an arbitrary measurable function of the prefix, including the current state, to inherit independence.

steps.title: The transition acting on a law
steps.body:
Define \(M_\eta(\mu)=F_*(\mu\otimes\eta)\). Its product measure means the innovation is fresh and independent of the current state. The subsequent theorem derives that independence for the recursion on the independent product space, rather than assuming it at each step.

The transition sends \(\mu\) to the law of \(F(X,Z)\) when \(X\sim\mu\), \(Z\sim\eta\), and \(X\perp Z\). Writing it as a product pushforward records these requirements exactly. Knowing only the two marginals would not determine the output if state and innovation were dependent, so the independence verification for the recursion establishes the required product input law.

steps.title: The iterated Markov laws
steps.body:
Set \(\mu_0=\mu\), \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\). These are iterated independent-noise transition laws. The recursion alone does not yet assert that a previously defined sample-path algorithm realizes them.

The law recursion begins with \(\mu\) and repeatedly applies the same independent-noise transition. It defines a candidate sequence of algorithm distributions without constructing sample paths. The next results show that the measurable iid path recursion realizes precisely this sequence. This separates a transition-level definition from the theorem identifying it with a noise-driven realization.

steps.title: The joint law of a state and fresh innovation
steps.body:
The current state is a measurable function of initialization and the first \(n\) noises. Product-source independence and prefix/fresh independence make it independent of \(w_n\). Its marginal is the output law of a noise-driven chain, and the innovation marginal is \(\eta\); their joint law is therefore the product of these two marginals.

The current state factors through initialization and its finite innovation prefix. Initialization is independent of the entire path, and prefix/fresh independence separates the next coordinate from that past. Regrouping these facts shows independence of the current state and next innovation. Their joint law is consequently the product of the already defined current output law and \(\eta\).

steps.title: The successor marginal transition
steps.body:
The pointwise successor is \(F(X_n,w_n)\). Push the proved product joint law of \((X_n,w_n)\) through \(F\); this yields \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\) for the recursion laws on the product space. No later-time state/noise independence is assumed.

The successor state is the measurable image of \((X_n,w_n)\) under \(F\). The preceding product-law identity therefore gives its distribution as \(F_\#(\mu_n\otimes\eta)\). This proves the Markov successor relation from the supplied iid source. It does not assume conditional independence as a new property of the recursively constructed state.

steps.title: Agreement of path-space and Markov laws
steps.body:
The product-path law and the iterated Markov law have the same initial value and the same successor equation. Induction on \(n\) identifies them at every index. This proves equality of the path-based and transition-based definitions.

Equality at time zero follows from the initial marginal computation. If the two law sequences agree at time \(n\), their common successor transition gives agreement at \(n+1\). This induction identifies the path-space and transition-space formulations for every finite iteration. All later kernel estimates can therefore be transferred to the original finite recursion.

steps.title: Probability preservation by one transition
steps.body:
The independent product of two probability measures has mass one. A measurable pushforward preserves that total mass, so a transition acting on probability measures is again a probability measure.

The product of current-state and innovation probabilities has total mass one. The preimage of the entire output space under a measurable update is the entire product input space. Hence the pushforward transition also has mass one. This conclusion concerns normalization alone and does not assume that the transition preserves second moments or has an invariant distribution.

steps.title: Probability preservation at every iterate
steps.body:
Induct from the initial probability and apply probability preservation by a measurable Gaussian transition at each successor. This proves normalization of every transition iterate and provides the probability hypotheses used in later law comparisons.

Assume the initial law is a probability. The one-step normalization theorem shows that each successor law is a probability whenever its predecessor is. Induction proves the property at every finite index. Keeping this fact available is necessary for later expectation inequalities, where the norm of a constant and the comparison between first and second moments use unit total mass.

steps.title: The noise-driven chain has the iterated transition law
steps.body:
First identify the independent iid realization with the product-path output law. Then apply the equality of the independent-noise marginal recursion and iterated transition laws. Every realization satisfying the original initialization/noise assumptions consequently has the same proved Markov iterate law.

An arbitrary admissible realization first has the same law as the independent path recursion, by equality of its joint input distribution. The product-path recursion then has the same law as the iterated transition. Combining these two identities yields the claimed Markov-law representation for the supplied process, including all initialization and innovation assumptions used to derive it.

UnadjustedLangevin/InitialExtension.lean.title: Realize every initial coupling independently of the noise
UnadjustedLangevin/InitialExtension.lean.summary:
Let \(c\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), and let \(Q\) be the fixed noise probability. On \((H\times H)\times S\), use \(c\otimes Q\). Projection preserves the joint initial law and its two marginals, and the noise projection has law \(Q\). The full initial pair and the full noise source are independent by the product-measure property.

The first initial coordinate together with noise has law \(\mu\otimes Q\), independent of the selected coupling. Every measurable numerical output depending only on these inputs therefore has the same law for all couplings. The squared initial difference integrates to its original coupling integral because \(Q(S)=1\). Finite coupling cost and the target second moment give square-integrable initial classes on this same space, with the prescribed laws and initial separation.

steps.title: Normalization of an initial coupling
steps.body:
The coupling's first marginal is the initial probability. Pushforward preserves total mass, so \(c(H\times H)=\mu(H)=1\). This constructs normalization of the joint measure using the defining marginal identity of the coupling.

For any joint coupling measure, total mass equals the total mass of either marginal. Its first marginal is the initial probability, so the joint measure has mass one. This observation establishes normalization of the coupling before forming a product with noise. It uses only the defining marginal equality and does not require any finite-cost premise.

steps.title: Adjoining independent noise
steps.body:
Extend an initial coupling \(c(dx,dy)\) by an independent noise sample \(s\sim Q\), using \(c\otimes Q\) on \((H\times H)\times S\). Both algorithms retain the prescribed initial joint law while sharing fresh noise independent of the pair.

The extended variable is \(((x,y),s)\), where \((x,y)\) retains the chosen initial coupling and \(s\) is sampled independently from the fixed source. Sharing this one source later synchronizes the numerical and reference noises. The construction changes neither initial marginal nor initial dependence, while making noise independence explicit at the level of a product probability.

steps.title: Normalization of the product extension
steps.body:
The coupling is a probability by its first marginal, and \(Q\) is a probability by hypothesis. Their product therefore has total mass one. This normalization supports all subsequent \(L^2\) constructions on the extension.

The product's total mass is \(c(E\times E)Q(S)=1\). Thus every extended source is a probability space, independently of which initial coupling was chosen. This normalization is used when transferring second moments, integrating constants and applying probability-space \(L^2\) estimates. Finite coupling cost is a separate condition introduced only for the moment constructions.

steps.title: The retained joint initial law
steps.body:
Projecting \(c\otimes Q\) to the first factor integrates out the probability noise coordinate. Since \(Q(S)=1\), the resulting measure is exactly \(c\), preserving the entire initial dependence structure.

For a measurable set \(A\) of initial pairs, its extended preimage is \(A\times S\), with measure \(c(A)Q(S)=c(A)\). Therefore the joint initial law remains exactly \(c\), including its dependence structure. In particular an initial cost depending on both coordinates is preserved, not just the separate marginal distributions.

steps.title: The retained numerical initial marginal
steps.body:
Compose the joint projection with its first state projection. The extension's joint marginal is \(c\), whose first state marginal is \(\mu\). Pushforward composition therefore yields the specified algorithm initialization law.

Project first to the initial pair and then to its first coordinate. Pushforward composition and the first marginal condition give law \(\mu\). The auxiliary reference coordinate and fresh noise are both integrated out. This ensures the algorithm begins with the same prescribed law on every coupling extension, even when the couplings encode different initial dependence.

steps.title: The retained reference initial marginal
steps.body:
Compose projection to the initial pair with its second state projection. The coupling's second marginal is \(\pi\), so the reference initialization on the extension has exactly law \(\pi\).

The second coordinate has law \(\pi\) by the coupling's second marginal identity. Extending by independent noise leaves this distribution unchanged. Thus a reference initialized from the second coordinate starts at the target law while remaining jointly realized with the algorithm initialization. No separate reference variable with only a matching marginal needs to be selected.

steps.title: The retained noise marginal
steps.body:
The coupling measure has mass one. Projecting its product with \(Q\) to the noise factor therefore returns \(Q\). The stated sigma-finiteness condition permits application of the product marginal formula.

For a measurable source set \(A\), its product preimage has mass \(c(E\times E)Q(A)=Q(A)\). Hence the noise projection preserves the source probability exactly. Every noise-defined random object, including a complete path, retains its original law after pullback. This distributional preservation is independent of the input coupling and its quadratic cost.

steps.title: Independence of initial pair and noise
steps.body:
The two coordinate projections of a product probability measure are independent. Here those coordinates are the full coupled initial pair and the fresh noise sample. Independence of either individual initial state from any noise-derived random object follows by composition.

Product factorization says that the full initial pair and the full noise source are independent. Composing with either state projection preserves independence, as does composing the source with a measurable path or innovation map. The conclusion therefore covers the whole innovation sequence at once, which is stronger than separately checking independence from each scalar innovation.

steps.title: The joint initial-noise law
steps.body:
Map \(((x,y),s)\) to \((x,s)\). Product pushforward and the first marginal identity of \(c\) give \(\mu\otimes Q\). Thus removing the reference coordinate leaves the same algorithm input law for every initial coupling.

For measurable sets \(A\) in the initial state and \(B\) in the source, the extended probability of \(x\in A,s\in B\) is \(c(A\times E)Q(B)=\mu(A)Q(B)\). This identifies the joint law as \(\mu\otimes Q\). The reference coordinate disappears from that law, so every coupling gives the same law for any measurable output of these inputs.

steps.title: Pushforward under the product observation
steps.body:
Factor the map through \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,s)\), whose law is \(\mu\otimes Q\). Pushforward composition proves that every measurable output depending only on algorithm initialization and noise has the coupling-independent law \(f_*(\mu\otimes Q)\).

Any measurable output using only \((x,s)\) factors through the projection whose law was just identified. Its pushforward is therefore obtained by applying the same output map to \(\mu\otimes Q\). This proves coupling independence of the output distribution before any numerical recursion is specified. The reference may still depend on \(y\), while the numerical output law remains unchanged.

steps.title: The numerical output law
steps.body:
Apply the pushforward law under the independent product extension to the measurable recursion output. Its product-input pushforward is exactly the output law of a noise-driven chain, so the same output law is realized on every initial-coupling extension. This equality follows from the two marginal identities and independence of the added noise.

Take the output map to be the finite noise-driven recursion. Its measurability was proved independently of all coupling choices. Applying the preceding input-law identity gives exactly the algorithm law defined by the independent input product. Thus an analytic estimate established on one initial-coupling extension always concerns the same numerical marginal, as required when taking an infimum over initial coupling costs.

steps.title: The innovation law after extension
steps.body:
First project the extension to its product-path noise law, then evaluate coordinate \(n\). The marginal of \(\bigotimes_k\eta\) at that coordinate is \(\eta\), giving the requested noise law on the extension.

If the source is an iid path product, evaluation at time \(n\) has law \(\eta\). The extension's source projection preserves that complete product law, so the pulled-back evaluation has the same marginal. This proves the innovation law for the specified random functions used on the extended space, on the same space as the chosen initial pair.

steps.title: Independence of the extended innovations
steps.body:
The iid path has independent coordinate evaluations. Pull this independence back along the extension's measure-preserving noise projection. The resulting innovation sequence remains jointly independent on the coupled initialization space.

Independence is a statement about the joint law of the innovation family. The noise projection preserves that entire law, not merely the individual coordinate distributions. Pulling back an independent path family therefore preserves all finite product factorizations. The innovations remain jointly independent on the same space that carries the initial coupling.

steps.title: Independence of initialization and innovations
steps.body:
The algorithm's initial state is a projection of the initial pair. Compose the pair/noise independence theorem with this state projection. This proves independence from the entire noise sample, not just from each individual noise vector.

Initialization depends only on the first coordinate of the coupling factor. The complete noise path depends only on the independent source factor. Composing the product-coordinate independence with these maps proves independence of initialization and whole path. This is the exact hypothesis needed for the independent-input recursion law theorem and its fresh-noise consequences.

steps.title: The initial displacement cost
steps.body:
The difference \(x-y\) depends only on the initial pair. Its \(L^2\) extended norm under \(c\otimes Q\) equals the same norm under \(c\), because the noise factor has mass one. The latter is exactly the quadratic cost of the initial coupling.

The initial difference \(x-y\) is constant in the added source variable. Integrating its squared norm over \(c\otimes Q\) multiplies the original coupling integral by \(Q(S)=1\). Taking square roots therefore preserves the initial quadratic cost exactly. Extending the probability space introduces no loss in the initial-error coefficient.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the initial difference
steps.body:
The state-difference function is measurable. Its extended \(L^2\) norm equals the finite initial coupling cost by the previous theorem. These two facts prove square-integrability for the difference on the extension.

Measurability of coordinate subtraction gives measurability of the initial difference. The preserved cost identity gives a finite second moment when the coupling cost is finite. Together these facts place that difference in \(L^2\) on the extended space. Finiteness is therefore derived from the chosen transport coupling rather than imposed as a separate random-variable assumption.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the reference initial state
steps.body:
The reference coordinate has law \(\pi\). Pull its supplied \(L^2(\pi)\) identity moment back through this law to get square integrability on the extension. This establishes the reference initialization without choosing a separate realization.

The reference-coordinate law is \(\pi\), so changing variables gives \(\mathbb E\|Y_0\|^2=\int\|y\|^2\pi(dy)\). The assumed target second moment is finite. This provides a square-integrable reference variable on the coupling extension, preserving both its target law and its prescribed dependence with the first coordinate.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the numerical initial state
steps.body:
Write \(x=(x-y)+y\). The difference is in \(L^2\) by finite coupling cost and the reference coordinate is in \(L^2\) by its law. Closure of \(L^2\) under addition gives square integrability of the initial algorithm state; no independent moment premise on \(\mu\) is introduced.

The identity \(X_0=(X_0-Y_0)+Y_0\) expresses initialization as a sum of two square-integrable variables. The triangle inequality gives \(\|X_0\|_2\le\|X_0-Y_0\|_2+\|Y_0\|_2\). Thus finite transport to a finite-second-moment target supplies the initial moment automatically. No extra initial second-moment hypothesis is needed in this coupling construction.

steps.title: The numerical initial class
steps.body:
Use square-integrability of the initial projection on the product space to convert the first state coordinate into an \(L^2\) class. The class is represented almost everywhere by \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\), preserving its relation to the coupling coordinates.

Once the first coordinate is proved square integrable, it determines an \(L^2\) state. Its random-function representative agrees almost surely with the coordinate \(x\). This construction fixes its joint realization with the reference coordinate and noise; it is not merely an abstract variable having law \(\mu\). The ensuing analytic recursion can therefore use the preserved coupling cost.

steps.title: The reference initial class
steps.body:
Convert the square-integrable second state coordinate into an \(L^2\) class. Its representative equals \(((x,y),s)\mapsto y\) almost everywhere, with law \(\pi\), and it shares the same product probability space as the algorithm initialization.

The second-coordinate \(L^2\) state is formed on exactly the same extended source as the first. Almost surely its representative equals \(y\), whose law is \(\pi\). It can be inserted as the initial condition of the reference integral equation, while the first coordinate initializes the Euler chain and both use the independent source.

steps.title: The law of the numerical initial class
steps.body:
The representative of the numerical initial class agrees almost everywhere with the first coordinate of the initial coupling. Its law is therefore the retained first marginal \(\mu\), because almost-everywhere changes leave measurable pushforwards unchanged.

Almost-sure equality implies equal probabilities of membership in every measurable state set. Therefore replacing the chosen square-integrable representative by the raw first coordinate leaves its law unchanged. The previously computed first marginal is \(\mu\), so the analytic initial state has precisely the prescribed algorithm initialization distribution.

steps.title: The law of the reference initial class
steps.body:
Replace the selected \(L^2\) representative by the second state projection almost everywhere. Its already proved marginal is \(\pi\), hence the class used as reference initialization has exactly that law.

The same representative argument applies to the second coordinate. Its target law was established before constructing its \(L^2\) state, so that construction cannot alter the reference marginal. Consequently stationarity results requiring target-distributed initialization apply to the state used in the coupling argument, with no further distributional identification left to assume.

steps.title: The class distance equals the coupling cost
steps.body:
The representative of the class difference equals \(x-y\) almost everywhere. Its squared norm is the integral of the squared displacement under the chosen initial coupling. The finite-cost hypothesis makes this an ordinary finite integral; taking its nonnegative square root gives the quadratic cost.

The difference of the two constructed states represents \(x-y\) almost surely. Its squared \(L^2\) norm is therefore the original finite quadratic coupling integral, and its norm is the coupling's root mean-square cost. This exact equality identifies the initial analytic error with the quantity over which Wasserstein distance takes an infimum.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsStationarity.lea.title: Prove Gibbs stationarity by refining invariant Metropolis chains
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsStationarity.lea.summary:
Let the square-mean Langevin integral solution begin with Gibbs law and use the stated Brownian innovation and initialization independence assumptions. For a fixed horizon \(T\), the Euler approximations using the same Brownian increments converge to the solution at \(T\) in \(L^2\). Their marginal laws are the iterated Gaussian transitions.

For meshes \(h\) with an integer number of steps reaching \(T\), couple each Euler approximation to the Metropolis-adjusted chain started at Gibbs. The second marginal remains Gibbs, and their expected distance is at most \(TC\sqrt h\), tending to zero. Bounded characteristic tests converge under both this first-moment coupling bound and the Euler \(L^2\) convergence. Uniqueness of characteristic functions therefore gives Gibbs law for the solution at every fixed time. This proof does not assume uniqueness of a weak Fokker–Planck equation.

steps.title: The representative of the Hilbert-space chain
steps.body:
Induct over the chain recursion. The representative of the lifted gradient equals the pointwise gradient almost everywhere, and the representative formulas for addition and scalar multiplication give the same Euler successor. Intersect the finite set of null-set complements needed at each index to identify the \(L^2\) chain with the ordinary recursion.

At time zero both descriptions use the same initialization. For the successor, the composed score represents the pointwise gradient almost surely, and addition and scalar multiplication represent the displayed Euler arithmetic. Intersecting these full-measure identities with the induction event proves agreement at the next finite index. The equality permits the class-valued chain and pointwise recursion to be assigned the same law.

steps.title: Its law follows the Gaussian transition
steps.body:
Use the almost-everywhere pointwise-chain identification, the independent-iid realization law theorem, and the equality of product-path and Markov transition laws. With innovation law \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), the generic independent-noise step is exactly the transition \(\mu\mapsto T_{h\#}(\mu\otimes\gamma)\). Thus the \(L^2\) construction has law \(P_h^n(P_{X_0})\).

The innovation assumptions identify the pointwise recursion law with the independent product input law, and the path-to-transition theorem identifies the latter with iterated Gaussian Euler transitions. Almost-sure equality transfers this law to the square-integrable chain. Its distribution is therefore \(P_h^n\mu_0\), which allows transition-level invariant-chain comparisons to be applied to the constructed approximation.

steps.title: Identification of the additive Euler chain
steps.body:
Induct on the mesh index. Both chains start at the same \(L^2\) variable. Their successor equations agree because the supplied additive increment equals \(\sqrt{2h}W_k\), making the noise terms identical as classes.

The additive Euler approximation uses increments of an input path, while the normalized-noise chain multiplies innovations by \(\sqrt{2h}\). When these two increments agree, their successor states agree whenever the preceding states agree. Induction thus identifies the two approximations exactly. This permits convergence results proved for additive-input Euler approximation to be combined with Gaussian transition-law theorems.

steps.title: The grid increment of the Brownian input
steps.body:
Apply the Brownian input cocycle at \(a=kh\), \(t=h\). The elementary identity \((k+1)h=kh+h\) matches its endpoints to the grid notation. This supplies the exact additive increment used by the normalized Euler noise.

The input increment between grid points is \(N_0((k+1)h)-N_0(kh)=\sqrt2(B_{(k+1)h}-B_{kh})\). The cocycle identity rewrites it as \(N_{kh}(h)\). This is precisely the segment endpoint input that defined the normalized Euler noise. The algebra aligns the mesh convention and absolute Brownian times without introducing a discretization error.

steps.title: The Brownian Euler chain equals the square-integrable chain
steps.body:
The Brownian grid-increment identity and the equality between the scaled innovation and Brownian mesh increment verify the increment premise of the generic chain equality. Therefore the deterministic matching-noise Euler approximation is exactly the already defined Brownian-normalized \(L^2\) Euler chain.

The normalized innovation satisfies \(\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k=N_{kh}(h)\). Combining this endpoint identity with the grid-increment formula verifies the matching-increments condition of the chain comparison. Hence the Brownian additive Euler approximation is exactly the same square-integrable chain whose law has been identified as Gaussian Euler. Its convergence and its distributional interpretation now concern one common sequence.

steps.title: The endpoint innovation has the Gaussian vector law
steps.body:
Each normalized coordinate is standard Gaussian. The supplied joint scalar-coordinate independence lets the standard Gaussian joint law of the independent scalar coordinates and independence after grouping scalar innovations into vectors assemble those coordinates into iid standard multivariate Gaussian vectors. These are the exact law hypotheses needed by the Markov-recursion theorem.

A Brownian increment over length \(h\) has variance \(h\), so division by \(\sqrt h\) gives a standard scalar Gaussian. Independence across Brownian coordinates and disjoint grid intervals gives joint independence over coordinate and step. Grouping each finite coordinate block therefore yields independent standard vector Gaussians. The statement verifies the complete input law required by the Markov transition recursion.

steps.title: Passing the invariant Gibbs marginal to the continuous limit
steps.body:
Fix \(T>0\) and choose meshes \(h_n=T/N_n\to0\) small enough for the nonexpansive MALA coupling. Matching-noise Euler approximations converge in \(L^2\) to \(Y_T\). Their laws are exactly \(P_{h_n}^{N_n}\pi_U\), by the proved iid Brownian innovation laws and initialization independence.

Couple each Euler law to \(N_n\) MALA steps started from Gibbs. Exact MALA invariance makes the second marginal \(\pi_U\). The rejection bound gives expected coupling distance at most \(N_nC h_n\sqrt{h_n}=TC\sqrt{h_n}\to0\); integrability of this distance is proved from the finite extended-cost estimate.

Apply identification of limiting laws by characteristic tests and vanishing coupling cost: characteristic functions of the Euler endpoints converge to those of \(Y_T\) by \(L^2\) convergence, and to those of \(\pi_U\) by the vanishing coupling cost. Equality of characteristic functions proves \(P_{Y_T}=\pi_U\). The zero-horizon case follows directly from the integral equation.

UnadjustedLangevin/CouplingLimit.lean.title: A vanishing coupling distance determines the limiting law
UnadjustedLangevin/CouplingLimit.lean.summary:
Suppose \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^2\), and the law of each \(X_n\) has a coupling with a fixed probability \(\pi\) whose expected distance tends to zero. At frequency \(t\), the character \(x\mapsto e^{i\langle t,x\rangle}\) is bounded and \(\|t\|\)-Lipschitz. Integrating its difference under the coupling bounds the difference of characteristic functions by \(\|t\|\) times the expected distance.

The coupling estimate makes the characteristic functions converge to that of \(\pi\), while \(L^2\) continuity makes them converge to that of \(X\). Uniqueness of limits, with the stated nontrivial-filter qualification, identifies these functions at every frequency. Uniqueness of characteristic functions then gives \(\mathcal L(X)=\pi\).

steps.title: A Lipschitz bound for characteristic tests
steps.body:
The unit-circle map is \(1\)-Lipschitz, so the difference of the two characters is at most \(|\langle x-y,t\rangle|\). Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds this by \(\|t\|\|x-y\|\). Thus characteristic tests have an explicit Lipschitz constant at each fixed frequency.

For real numbers, \(|e^{iu}-e^{iv}|\le|u-v|\), obtained by integrating the derivative of the unit-circle map along the interval. Substitute \(u=\langle x,t\rangle\), \(v=\langle y,t\rangle\), then use Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus every fixed-frequency characteristic test is bounded and \(\|t\|\)-Lipschitz, so the integral of the distance bounds the difference of characteristic functions.

steps.title: Characteristic differences controlled by coupling cost
steps.body:
Pull both marginal characteristic integrals back to the coupling space and subtract. Each character is bounded by one, hence integrable under the probability coupling. The integral norm inequality and the pointwise Lipschitz estimate give \(|\widehat\mu(t)-\widehat\pi(t)|\le\|t\|\mathbb E\|X-Y\|\), with the distance's integrability explicitly supplied.

The coupling's marginal identities let both characteristic integrals be evaluated on the same product-state space. Subtract under the integral, use its norm inequality, and apply the pointwise Lipschitz bound. The assumed integrability of distance makes the resulting right side finite. This gives a quantitative estimate for each frequency without requiring a second-moment transport bound on the coupling itself.

steps.title: Continuity of the characteristic law in square mean
steps.body:
Apply the continuous linear functional \(x\mapsto\langle t,x\rangle\) to an \(H\)-valued \(L^2\) variable. Its lifted map is continuous on \(L^2\). The Hilbert-valued characteristic function at \(t\) is the scalar projected characteristic function at frequency one, so the scalar continuity theorem proves the claim.

The scalar projection \(X\mapsto\langle t,X\rangle\) is continuous in \(L^2\) with norm at most \(\|t\|\). Also \(\mathbb E|\langle t,X-Y\rangle|\le\|t\|\|X-Y\|_2\). Applying the exponential Lipschitz inequality shows continuity of its characteristic expectation. Thus \(L^2\) convergence of the approximating endpoints determines convergence of their characteristic functions.

steps.title: Equality of limiting laws from vanishing coupling cost
steps.body:
For each \(t\), the coupling inequality forces the approximating characteristic functions toward \(\widehat\pi(t)\), since the expected distance tends to zero. Independently, \(L^2\) convergence forces them toward \(\widehat{P_X}(t)\). Uniqueness of limits along a nontrivial filter identifies these values, and uniqueness of a probability measure from its characteristic function yields \(P_X=\pi\).

There are two limits of the same scalar characteristic sequence. The \(L^2\) convergence identifies its limit with the characteristic function of the continuous endpoint, while the coupling estimate identifies it with that of \(\pi\). Uniqueness of scalar limits makes them equal at every frequency. The characteristic-function uniqueness theorem for finite-dimensional probability measures then gives equality of the entire endpoint law and \(\pi\).

UnadjustedLangevin/ProductReference.lean.title: A reference for every initial coupling with one output law
UnadjustedLangevin/ProductReference.lean.summary:
For each finite-cost initial coupling \(c\), form its product with a fixed independent noise source. The numerical input law is \(\mu\otimes Q\) on every such extension, so the numerical output law is independent of \(c\). The initial class distance equals the cost of \(c\). Supply a reference on each extension with the stated integral equation, stationary law, and common innovations.

Apply the mean-square convergence estimate on every extension. Since its output law and constants are independent of \(c\), take the infimum of the initial costs to obtain \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\). One finite-cost initial coupling first proves that the output transport distance is finite. The two stable step ranges then give the stated initial-error factors and additive bounds.

steps.title: The pointwise numerical update
steps.body:
Define the ordinary Euler update \(F_h(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\) in an arbitrary Hilbert-space presentation. It is the pointwise function whose lifted composition gives the \(L^2\) numerical chain.

The update uses one current state and one innovation vector. Its additive Gaussian coefficient is \(\sqrt{2h}\), corresponding to covariance \(2hI\) when the innovation is standard. Defining this ordinary map before lifting it to \(L^2\) specifies the update whose law is computed by measurable pushforwards.

steps.title: Measurability of the update
steps.body:
The Lipschitz gradient is continuous. Compose it with the first coordinate projection and combine the remaining continuous scalar and vector operations. The uncurried map \((x,z)\mapsto F_h(x,z)\) is therefore measurable.

Lipschitzness of the gradient gives continuity of \(x\mapsto\nabla U(x)\). Both coordinate projections on the state–innovation product are continuous, and fixed scalar combinations preserve continuity. Thus the entire update is measurable for any fixed step. No coupling or reference hypothesis enters this elementary regularity fact.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the product noise
steps.body:
The noise projection from \(c\otimes Q\) to \(Q\) is measure preserving because the coupling is a probability. Pull back the supplied \(L^2(Q)\) noise function along this projection. Its square integrability is unchanged.

For a source innovation \(W_n\), the extended variable is \(W_n(s)\). Its squared norm integral under \(c\otimes Q\) equals \(c(E\times E)\int\|W_n\|^2dQ\), hence the original finite second moment. The added initial coordinates therefore do not alter innovation integrability, just as they do not alter its distribution.

steps.title: The product-space noise class
steps.body:
Use the preceding square-integrability proof to form the class of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto W_n(s)\) on the product extension. Both the numerical chain and reference use this same \(L^2\) innovation.

The lifted innovation is the square-integrable variable represented by the pulled-back source function. It is fixed before selecting any reference trajectory, so both numerical and reference constructions can be required to use precisely this innovation. This choice is what later makes the algorithm's output law independent of the second initial marginal and coupling dependence.

steps.title: Its representative identity
steps.body:
The selected noise representative equals the pulled-back source innovation \(W_n(s)\) almost everywhere. Thus its arithmetic inside the square-integrable update agrees with the ordinary pointwise Gaussian update, and its coordinate laws are those of the original innovation.

Almost surely, evaluating the constructed innovation gives exactly the original source innovation evaluated at \(s\). Consequently its scalar arithmetic in the square-integrable Euler update agrees with the raw pointwise formula. These representative equalities also permit Gaussian coordinate laws and path independence to be transferred to the exact random variables used by the numerical chain.

steps.title: The product numerical output law
steps.body:
Push \(\mu\otimes Q\) through the pointwise noise-driven chain starting at \(x\) with source path \(W(s)\). This definition omits the reference coupling entirely, making explicit the common algorithm output law for all coupling realizations.

The output on the independent product space depends on the initial law \(\mu\), fixed source probability \(Q\), and source innovation path \(W\). It is computed on \(\mu\otimes Q\), so no reference initialization appears in its definition. Every coupling extension will reproduce this same first-coordinate/source input law, establishing one common numerical output for the later transport infimum.

steps.title: The representative of the product chain
steps.body:
Induct through the lifted chain and use the representative identities for initial state, product noise, lifted drift, addition, and scalar multiplication. At each fixed index the result agrees almost everywhere with the ordinary recursion driven by \(x\) and \(W(s)\).

At each successor, replace the lifted gradient, state, and innovation by their pointwise representatives on a common full-measure set. The resulting equation is exactly the ordinary Euler recursion. Induction proves agreement for every fixed finite index. This permits its law to be computed from the raw coordinates \((x,s)\), which have already been identified independently of the coupling.

steps.title: The output law of the product chain
steps.body:
Replace the \(L^2\) chain by its almost-everywhere pointwise recursion. That recursion depends only on the algorithm's initial coordinate and noise sample, so the pushforward law under the independent product extension gives its coupling-independent law. The result is exactly the numerical law on the product construction.

The pointwise recursion ignores the reference coordinate \(y\). Under the extension, the law of the remaining pair \((x,s)\) is always \(\mu\otimes Q\). Pushforward composition therefore gives the same product-input output law for every finite initial coupling. Almost-sure replacement transfers this identity to the analytic chain whose errors are estimated in \(L^2\).

steps.title: The product probability measure
steps.body:
A coupling of the initial probability with the reference measure is itself a probability, and its product with the fixed probability noise source is a probability. The total mass is therefore one on every extension.

Every initial coupling has mass one by either marginal identity, and the source probability has mass one. Their product is consequently normalized. This fact is established separately on each extension and allows the same probability-space estimates to be reused uniformly over all couplings. It does not presume finite coupling cost or any invariant law of the numerical update.

steps.title: A reference on the independent product space
steps.body:
For every finite-cost initial coupling, the hypothesis supplies an integral reference on that coupling's product extension, with its initial state matching the second coordinate. Algorithm output laws and initial costs are consequences of the product construction; convergence is not an additional assumption.

The required data are the following: on each finite-cost extension, provide continuous joined segments with the integral equation, matching Euler noise and target-law moment bounds. The numerical law and initial cost are already consequences of the product construction. Thus the reference hypothesis specifies these analytic data, while the convergence estimate is proved from those data rather than included among them.

steps.title: Finite output transport distance
steps.body:
Finite initial Wasserstein distance supplies at least one finite-cost initial coupling. On its product extension, the numerical and reference variables belong to \(L^2\), giving a finite-cost output coupling. Their established laws identify its marginals with the common output law and \(\pi\), hence the output Wasserstein distance is finite.
