Finite initial transport guarantees the existence of at least one finite-cost initial coupling. Its analytic numerical and reference variables are in \(L^2\), so their difference has finite norm and their joint law has finite quadratic cost. Its first marginal is the common numerical output and its second is \(\pi\). Therefore output transport is finite before the real-valued numerical inequality is stated.

steps.title: The small-step bound from a product reference
steps.body:
For each finite-cost initial coupling \(c\), apply the analytic \(L^2\) Dalalyan theorem on \(c\otimes Q\). The initial class-distance theorem identifies its initial error exactly with the real coupling cost, and the common output-law theorem identifies its numerical law.

The resulting bound holds for every finite \(c\), with coefficient \((1-mh)^n\ge0\). Taking the infimum of their costs gives \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\), without selecting an optimal coupling. Output finiteness is proved first so the final real-valued inequality cannot conceal infinity.

For each initial coupling cost \(C\), synchronous analysis gives output distance at most \((1-mh)^nC+(33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{hd}\). The multiplicative coefficient is nonnegative and the other quantities do not depend on the chosen coupling. Taking the cost infimum therefore replaces \(C\) by initial \(W_2\). Finiteness was established separately, so this operation is an inequality between finite real distances.

steps.title: The large-step bound from a product reference
steps.body:
Repeat the couplingwise analytic argument for the stable large-step branch, whose contraction factor is \(Lh-1\in[0,1)\). The geometric error sum has denominator \(2-Lh>0\). The finite-coupling infimum theorem replaces the initial class distance by the initial Wasserstein distance and yields the displayed large-step bias term.

In the second stable branch, the deterministic gradient-step factor is \(q=Lh-1\). Its geometric denominator is \(1-q=2-Lh>0\), giving the additive bound \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\). The same product-law identity and coupling infimum apply because the constructed reference and common numerical output are unchanged. Only the scalar contraction branch and its denominator differ.

UnadjustedLangevin/ProductBrownian.lean.title: Brownian coordinates on an independent product extension
UnadjustedLangevin/ProductBrownian.lean.summary:
Let \(c\) be a finite-cost coupling of the numerical initial law and the Gibbs law, and let \(Q\) carry independent Brownian coordinate processes. On \(c\otimes Q\), pull the Brownian coordinates back by the noise projection. A measure-preserving pullback preserves their finite-dimensional Gaussian laws. The two initial coordinates depend on the other factor and are therefore independent of the entire Brownian family.

The normalized mesh increments are independent standard Gaussian vectors. As \(L^2\) classes they agree with the endpoint innovations of the integral reference segments, so those innovations cancel in the coupled difference. Continuity, the integral equation, and the initial second moment follow from the constructions above. The reference properties involving the Gibbs marginal and its score moment are proved under the explicit assumption that the segment laws are Gibbs; stationarity is still a hypothesis in this result.

steps.title: Pulling Brownian coordinates back by a measure-preserving map
steps.body:
A measure-preserving map leaves the law of every measurable random variable unchanged after pullback. Apply this to every finite-dimensional Brownian vector. Their Gaussian laws and covariance data are therefore preserved, giving a pre-Brownian process on the new sample space.

If a map preserves the source probability, the law of any measurable finite collection of source evaluations is unchanged after composition. Apply this to the Brownian values at arbitrary finitely many times. Their centered Gaussian joint distribution and covariance \(\min(s,t)\) are preserved. Thus pulling the paths to the coupling extension retains the required Brownian finite-dimensional laws.

steps.title: Pulling back the square-integrable Brownian vector
steps.body:
Both sides represent the vector \((B_i(t,f(\omega)))_i\). Pulling back a full-measure representative equality along a measure-preserving map again gives a full-measure equality. The two constructions therefore determine the same square-integrable class.

Both constructions evaluate the same finite vector of scalar Brownian coordinates after the measure-preserving map. Their representatives agree almost surely because the source representative equality pulls back to a full-measure event. Equality almost surely identifies the two \(L^2\) vectors. This makes coordinate assembly compatible with moving between source and extended probability spaces.

steps.title: Pulling back the endpoint innovation
steps.body:
The \(L^2\) pullback is linear, hence commutes with subtraction and scalar multiplication. Apply the preceding Brownian-vector pullback identity to the two endpoints in the normalized increment. This identifies the pulled-back Euler noise with the noise constructed after pullback.

The normalized Euler noise is a fixed scalar multiple of a difference of two Brownian \(L^2\) vectors. A measure-preserving pullback is linear, so it commutes with that subtraction and scalar multiplication. Applying the coordinate-vector pullback identity at both endpoints yields equality of the two noise constructions. Therefore extending first or normalizing first produces the same innovation.

steps.title: The source Euler innovation
steps.body:
Take a measurable representative of the previously constructed \(L^2\) Brownian Euler noise on the source space. This is the random function supplied to the generic product algorithm before choosing any initial coupling.

Choose a measurable random-function version of each source Euler innovation. These functions supply the input path for the generic product-law construction. Their finite-time laws and independence will be proved from the Brownian formulas below. Fixing the functions on the source before choosing an initial coupling ensures that the numerical output can be represented by one common source law.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the source innovation
steps.body:
A representative of an \(L^2\) class has finite second moment. Apply that fact to the Brownian Euler noise class. This avoids assuming an extra noise-moment condition in the product construction.

An \(L^2\) random variable has finite second moment for every representative agreeing with it almost surely. Therefore the selected source innovation functions inherit the finite norm already established for the Brownian-normalized class. No additional moment condition is required merely because a pointwise version is chosen for the product recursion.

steps.title: Its vector representative
steps.body:
Unfold the nested class-valued noise definition and apply representative equalities for scalar multiplication, subtraction, and the Brownian vector classes. Almost everywhere the result is \((\sqrt{2h})^{-1}\sqrt2(B_{nh+h}-B_{nh})\), with real-time clipping as in the original definition.

Expand the innovation into its two Brownian endpoint values and fixed normalization factors. Almost-sure identities for sums, differences and scalar multiples show that its pointwise version equals the normalized vector increment. The time extension only specifies how Brownian evaluation is interpreted outside nonnegative times; in the positive mesh regime every grid endpoint already lies in the ordinary Brownian domain.

steps.title: Its scalar coordinate representative
steps.body:
Evaluate the vector representative formula in coordinate \(i\). For \(h>0\), use \(\sqrt{2h}=\sqrt2\sqrt h\) and cancel the nonzero \(\sqrt2\), obtaining \((B_i((n+1)h)-B_i(nh))/\sqrt h\).

For \(h>0\), factor \(\sqrt{2h}=\sqrt2\sqrt h\) and cancel the positive \(\sqrt2\). In coordinate \(i\), the result is \([B_i((n+1)h)-B_i(nh)]/\sqrt h\). This explicit formula connects the exact innovation representative to the standard Gaussian increment law and fixes the variance normalization without an inequality.

steps.title: The coordinate at nonnegative mesh times
steps.body:
For nonnegative mesh times, restriction to nonnegative time leaves their real values unchanged. Rewrite both clipped grid endpoints into the corresponding nonnegative-real products. The coordinate formula becomes the ordinary Brownian grid increment divided by \(\sqrt h\).

All grid times \(nh\) and \((n+1)h\) are nonnegative when \(h>0\). Hence the real-time extension agrees there with the original nonnegative-time Brownian process. The coordinate identity is consequently the usual Brownian grid-increment formula. The Gaussian increment and independence results therefore apply at these endpoints.

steps.title: The normalized Brownian coordinate increment
steps.body:
The nonnegative-grid formula is the normalized Brownian mesh increment. After converting the positive real step to its nonnegative-real form, the two random functions agree almost everywhere. Equality almost surely transfers the increment laws to these representatives.

The innovation coordinate equals the established normalized Brownian increment almost surely at each fixed step and coordinate. Thus every distributional statement proved for the normalized increment applies to the source coordinate. The selected \(L^2\) representatives and the scalar increment functions have equal pushforward measures because they agree almost surely.

steps.title: The scalar innovation law
steps.body:
A normalized Brownian increment has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Transfer this law across the equality between a scalar mesh innovation and its normalized Brownian increment using almost-everywhere invariance of laws. Hence the source noise representative has the required Gaussian coordinate law.

A length-\(h\) Brownian increment is centered Gaussian with variance \(h\). Scaling by \(h^{-1/2}\) multiplies its variance by \(h^{-1}\), giving variance one. Equality almost surely of the two coordinate versions preserves their pushforward distributions. This proves the standard Gaussian law of the precise source innovation used in the algorithm.

steps.title: Independence of the source innovation array
steps.body:
The Brownian grid-path theorem gives independence of all normalized coordinates indexed by \((i,n)\). Reindex by the injective coordinate swap to \((n,i)\), then transfer across the almost-everywhere coordinate identities. This matches the index order expected by the vector innovation theorem.

Independent Brownian coordinates and independent disjoint increments give one jointly independent family indexed by coordinate and time interval. Swapping the order of these two indices is a bijection and preserves every finite factorization. Almost-sure coordinate replacement then transfers that full independence to the selected source innovations. Correct marginal laws alone would not establish this joint conclusion.

steps.title: Brownian coordinates on the product space
steps.body:
Projection from an initial-coupling product extension to the noise source is measure preserving. Pull each scalar Brownian coordinate back along it using preservation of Brownian finite-dimensional laws under a measure-preserving pullback. The coordinate processes on the extension retain their Brownian finite-dimensional laws.

On \(c\otimes Q\), the second-factor projection is measure preserving because \(c\) has mass one. Pulling every scalar Brownian path through it leaves its finite-dimensional distributions unchanged. This constructs Brownian coordinate processes on the same space as the coupled initial states, with no dependence of their source laws on the particular initial coupling.

steps.title: Identification of product and reference noise
steps.body:
The lifted source noise and the extension's constructed Brownian noise are both the measure-preserving pullback of the source \(L^2\) Brownian Euler noise. Use representative extensionality to identify the former with this pullback, then apply the equality of mesh increments before and after pullback to identify the latter.

The product innovation is the pullback of the fixed source innovation, whereas the reference noise is normalized after pulling back the Brownian coordinates. Linearity and the preceding pullback identities show that these are the same \(L^2\) vector. Consequently the numerical and reference constructions share the same endpoint noise as \(L^2\) classes, permitting exact cancellation in their coupled difference.

steps.title: The product coordinate innovation law
steps.body:
Pull the source standard-Gaussian coordinate law through the extension's noise projection. The lifted product-noise representative agrees almost everywhere with the raw pulled-back source noise. Transfer the law across that equality to obtain the coordinate law for the exact classes used by the numerical chain.

The source projection preserves the standard Gaussian coordinate law, so its raw pullback remains standard Gaussian. The product innovation representative agrees almost surely with that pullback. Changing representatives therefore gives the same Gaussian marginal for the exact variables used by the numerical chain. This verifies the distributional premise without replacing the coupled construction by a separate Gaussian source.

steps.title: Independence of product innovations
steps.body:
Identify the source coordinate-time path law as the product of standard Gaussians. Pull that law to the extension; its coordinate family is independent by the product-law independence criterion. Finally replace raw source pullbacks by the almost-everywhere equal product-noise representatives.

Pulling the complete source innovation path through a measure-preserving map preserves its whole joint product Gaussian law. Every finite subfamily of product innovation coordinates therefore remains independent. Countably many almost-sure coordinate equalities can be imposed simultaneously on a full-measure event, allowing the raw path law to be transferred to the chosen representative path.

steps.title: Independence from numerical initialization
steps.body:
The raw first initial coordinate depends only on the coupling factor, while the whole source noise sequence depends only on the noise factor. Product independence therefore applies. Countability of the sequence lets representative equalities hold simultaneously at all indices; transport independence to the selected \(L^2\) initialization and noise representatives.

The first initial coordinate is measurable from the coupling factor, while the complete innovation path is measurable from the independent source factor. Product independence gives their factorized joint law. Simultaneous almost-sure representative identities preserve this independence for the \(L^2\) initialization and innovation path. Independence therefore applies to all future innovations together, as required by the recursion law theorem.

steps.title: Independence from reference initialization
steps.body:
Use the same product independence argument with the second initial coordinate. Both initialization and whole noise-path representative equalities are transferred almost everywhere, proving the reference class is independent of all fresh Euler noise.

The reference initialization uses the second coordinate of the same coupling factor and is likewise independent of the entire source. Replacing it and the innovation path by almost-surely equal representatives leaves the joint law unchanged. This independence is used when constructing a Langevin process started at Gibbs law with fresh Brownian forcing, rather than only in the numerical algorithm-law argument.

steps.title: The Brownian product probability
steps.body:
The coupling is a probability by its marginal identity and the Brownian source measure is a probability. Their product extension is normalized. This normalization supplies the probability-space hypotheses of the Brownian pullback and \(L^2\) reference constructions.

The Brownian extension's normalization follows from \(c(E\times E)=1\) and \(Q(S)=1\). Thus all pulled-back Brownian and square-integrable constructions occur on a probability space. Unit mass also ensures that adding the source does not change initial second moments, noise norms or the cost of the chosen initial coupling.

steps.title: The Gibbs reference as a square-integrable class
steps.body:
The strongly convex Gibbs law has finite second moment. Thus the identity map belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U)\), and the second marginal identity supplies a square-integrable reference initialization on each coupling extension.

Positive strong convexity gives a Gaussian upper bound on the target density and its quadratic moment weight. The normalized Gibbs law consequently has finite second moment. This proved target fact supplies the reference-coordinate integrability on every finite-coupling extension, and finite coupling cost then supplies the algorithm-coordinate integrability as well.

steps.title: The square-integrable Brownian product reference
steps.body:
The pulled-back Brownian segments have continuous square-mean paths and satisfy the gradient integral equation. Their endpoint Brownian increments equal the common product innovations. Given the supplied stationary laws, the Gibbs score bound supplies the remaining drift-moment requirement. Thus every stated reference property is available, with stationarity retained as a premise of this intermediate result.

The constructed local segments supply continuity, joining and the gradient integral equation. Their Brownian endpoint noise equals the common product innovation by the preceding identity. Given their target laws, the Gibbs score moment supplies the uniform drift bound. The resulting analytic reference therefore has each required property, while segment stationarity remains an explicit premise at this intermediate stage.

steps.title: The product reference supplied by the Brownian construction
steps.body:
For each finite initial coupling, construct the square-integrable Brownian reference on its independent source product. The initial reference is the second-coordinate \(L^2\) class, and its endpoint noise is the product innovation. Under the stated segment-stationarity assumption, these facts give the reference hypotheses required for the comparison on every extension.

For every finite initial coupling, form the same source product and construct its Brownian reference. Its first segment starts at the second-coordinate reference state, preserving the initial cost. These references together satisfy the coupling-family requirement. The Gibbs law at each segment time remains the stated assumption; the subsequent stationarity proof establishes it for all these constructions.

steps.title: The convergence bound from the constructed product Brownian source
steps.body:
Derive \(m\le L\) from strong convexity and smoothness, construct the product reference from the stated stationary segment laws, and apply the small-step product-reference theorem. The estimate contains the initial \(W_2\) distance. Its stationarity hypothesis is proved by the subsequent independent Brownian construction.

Strong convexity and smoothness imply \(m\le L\) on a nontrivial space, placing the parameters in the deterministic contraction regime. Apply the product-reference theorem with the constructed Brownian family and supplied segment target laws. Taking the initial coupling infimum gives the initial Wasserstein term. This estimate assumes segment stationarity, which is proved subsequently.

UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalULA.lean.title: Wasserstein convergence of the Gaussian ULA transition
UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalULA.lean.summary:
Let \(U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Suppose the initial probability has finite \(W_2\) distance from Gibbs. Independent normalized Brownian increments give the Gaussian transition \(P_h\); the numerical marginal at index \(k\) is \(P_h^k\mu\).

For every finite-cost initial coupling, the product Brownian construction gives a stationary integral reference with the same innovations. Applying the mean-square comparison and taking the infimum of the initial coupling costs yields the Wasserstein estimate. In the small-step range its factor is \(1-mh\) and its additive bound is \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{hd}\). In the other stated stable range the factor is \(Lh-1\) and the additive bound is \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\). The reference existence and stationarity used in these estimates are proved from the stated potential assumptions.

steps.title: The output law of the product construction
steps.body:
The Brownian source provides jointly independent standard Gaussian innovations; the product extension makes initialization independent of the entire sequence. The realization/Markov-law theorem identifies its output with \(P_h^k\mu\). The product output-law identity removes the chosen finite coupling from this law equality.

The Brownian-generated innovations have the full iid standard vector Gaussian law. Their product construction makes the initial coordinate independent of the complete path. Thus the measurable recursion has law \(P_h^k\mu\). The product output definition removes the auxiliary reference coordinate, showing this identity is common to every finite initial coupling and depends only on the prescribed initial marginal.

steps.title: A product reference from independent Brownian coordinates
steps.body:
On each finite-coupling extension, pull back the independent Brownian coordinates and use the product independence theorems for the reference initialization. Construct a global \(L^2\) integral solution over the required finite horizon.

The proved MALA/Euler stationarity theorem gives Gibbs law for that global solution at every needed absolute time. Segment/global uniqueness identifies each recursively constructed reference segment with that solution. Consequently the reference segments on the independent initial-coupling and Brownian product space have Gibbs law, and all reference hypotheses follow from the stated source and potential assumptions.

For each finite coupling, solve the global Langevin integral equation from the target-distributed reference coordinate with independent Brownian forcing. The invariant-approximation argument proves its Gibbs law at every fixed time. Uniqueness then identifies the recursively chosen local segments with this global solution on their intervals. Hence all segment target-law premises are proved for the references used in the coupling family.

steps.title: The innovations of the fixed Brownian construction
steps.body:
Specialize the source Euler noise to the explicitly constructed independent coordinate Brownian source. This fixes the same standard Gaussian innovation sequence for every initial coupling in the law theorem.

Fix the explicitly constructed independent Brownian coordinate source once and normalize its grid increments. For any \(h>0\), the resulting coordinates are standard Gaussian and independent over step and coordinate. The innovation sequence is thus fixed independently of the input law and initial coupling.

steps.title: The reference on the independent product space
steps.body:
The independent Brownian construction supplies the coordinate Brownian laws and independence of their grid paths for every positive step. Apply the product reference with Brownian noise independent of the initial pair. The reference existence and stationary law are therefore consequences of the hypotheses.

The independent Brownian source supplies its Brownian finite-dimensional laws and full-path coordinate independence. Product extension supplies independence from the initial coupling. The stationary integral solution and segment uniqueness then provide all reference target laws. Thus the analytic reference family is obtained entirely from the potential and initial transport assumptions, because existence and invariance have been proved.

steps.title: The output law equals the Gaussian transition iterate
steps.body:
Finite initial transport provides a finite-cost coupling, and Gibbs has a finite second moment. Apply the general Brownian output-law identity on that extension with the independent Brownian source. It proves that the product construction has ULA law \(P_h^k\mu\).

Finite initial transport supplies a finite-cost coupling, and target Gaussian tails supply the reference second moment needed on its extension. The innovation law theorem identifies the numerical output with \(P_h^k\mu\). Since the output is common to all such coupling extensions, this identity does not retain any chosen coupling or auxiliary sample-space information.

steps.title: Finiteness of the output transport distance
steps.body:
The constructed product reference supplies a finite-cost output coupling for every iteration whenever initial transport is finite. Its output law is \(P_h^k\mu\). Substituting this law proves \(W_2(P_h^k\mu,\pi_U)<\infty\), so the Wasserstein distances in the estimates are finite real numbers.

The constructed numerical and stationary reference states lie in \(L^2\) on any one finite-cost extension. Their joint law is therefore a finite-cost coupling at every iteration. The numerical marginal is \(P_h^k\mu\) and the reference marginal is \(\pi_U\). This proves output transport finiteness before passing to real-valued distances in the quantitative convergence bounds.

steps.title: The small-step Wasserstein bound
steps.body:
Construct the product reference from differentiability, \(m\)-strong convexity, and \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Nontriviality of the finite coordinate space proves \(m\le L\); the finite-coupling product theorem gives the small-step bound with bias \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{hd}\).

Replace the product output by \(P_h^k\mu\) using the identification of the product-space chain law with the iterated Gaussian transition. The resulting inequality applies to the Gaussian ULA laws. Their transport finiteness and the existence of the stationary reference have already been proved.

Apply the synchronous finite-coupling estimate to the fully constructed reference family, then take the initial cost infimum. The small-step factor is \(q=1-mh\), with gap \(mh>0\). The local forcing \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}\) divided by that gap gives \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{hd}\). Rewriting the common output as the Gaussian transition iterate proves the stated bound for these probability laws.

steps.title: The large-step Wasserstein bound
steps.body:
Use the same constructed reference in the large-step product theorem. The step assumptions give \(0\le Lh-1<1\) and \(2-Lh>0\), so the bias is \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\). Rewrite its output law as the iterated Gaussian ULA law.

The same stationary reference and local defect estimate also apply in the second stable step regime. Here the deterministic factor is \(q=Lh-1\), so the positive gap is \(2-Lh\). Geometric summation gives bias \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\). The output-law identity transfers this inequality to the Gaussian transition iterates without changing either the target or initial Wasserstein distance.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianULA.lean.title: Wasserstein bounds for a square-integrable Gaussian recursion
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianULA.lean.summary:
Consider a square-integrable initial variable and scalar standard Gaussian innovations that are jointly independent over time and coordinate. Assume that the initial variable is independent of the entire innovation sequence. Assembling the scalar coordinates gives independent standard Gaussian vectors, so the stochastic recursion has marginal law \(P_h^k\mathcal L(X_0)\) at index \(k\).

The initial law has finite second moment. Positive strong convexity gives the same property for the Gibbs law, so their product coupling has finite quadratic cost. The transition convergence bounds therefore apply to this recursion. The small-step and large-step estimates retain their respective factors \(1-mh\) and \(Lh-1\), their initial Wasserstein term, and the stated additive constants. Joint independence over time and coordinate, rather than only the scalar marginal laws, is used to identify the transition recursion.

steps.title: Normalization of the initial law
steps.body:
The representative of the \(L^2\) initialization is measurable. Its pushforward of a probability measure therefore has total mass one, giving the probability hypothesis required by the ULA transition theorem.

Replacing the representative on a null set does not change this distribution. Thus it is well defined for the square-integrable equivalence class. Gaussian assumptions on the subsequent innovations are used to identify the transition kernel, whereas probability normalization here follows only from the initial probability space.

steps.title: Finiteness of the initial transport distance
steps.body:
The initialization is in \(L^2\), so its law has a finite second moment. Strong convexity proves the same for Gibbs and proves its normalization. The independent product coupling of these two laws has finite quadratic cost, hence their Wasserstein distance is finite.

Changing variables shows that the initial law has the same finite second moment as its random-variable realization. The Gibbs target has a finite second moment by positive strong convexity. Their independent product coupling has finite mean squared separation, bounded by twice the sum of those moments. Thus the initial Wasserstein distance is finite and need not be supplied as an additional assumption.

steps.title: The small-step bound for independent Gaussian innovations
steps.body:
Assemble the jointly independent standard scalar Gaussian coordinates into iid multivariate standard innovations. Initialization independence and the \(L^2\) representative theorem identify the construction's law with \(P_h^k(P_{X_0})\). Derive finite initial transport from its moments, then apply the small-step transition theorem and rewrite the law back to the construction.

Coordinate Gaussian laws together with full time-coordinate independence determine iid standard vector innovations. Initialization independence then identifies the supplied chain law with the Gaussian transition iterate. Its initial transport is finite by the moment argument. Substituting this law equality into the constructed small-step theorem gives the realization's finite-time bound, with normalization and output finiteness already justified.

steps.title: The large-step bound for independent Gaussian innovations
steps.body:
Use the same construction/Markov-law identification and derived finite initial transport, then apply the large-step transition theorem. The numerical construction therefore inherits contraction factor \(Lh-1\) and bias \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\) throughout the stated stable large-step regime.

The law-identification argument is unchanged in the large-step regime; only the deterministic contraction factor and geometric gap change. Apply the transition bound with \(q=Lh-1\) and \(1-q=2-Lh>0\), then replace the transition iterate by the supplied realization law. The result retains the exact initial Wasserstein term and the explicit bias throughout the stated stable interval.

UnadjustedLangevin/PotentialAssumptions..title: Strong convexity forces m ≤ L
UnadjustedLangevin/PotentialAssumptions..summary:
Let a differentiable potential on a nontrivial Hilbert space be \(m\)-strongly convex and have \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. For distinct \(x,y\), strong monotonicity and Cauchy–Schwarz give \(m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle\nabla U(x)-\nabla U(y),x-y\rangle\le L\|x-y\|^2\). Dividing by the positive squared distance proves \(m\le L\). No positivity assumption on \(m\) is needed for this comparison.

Nontriviality is used to choose distinct points. In a singleton space every distance vanishes, and this argument cannot establish a relation between the two constants. The transport estimates on that space follow separately from zero coupling cost.

steps.title: Compare monotonicity with Cauchy–Schwarz
steps.body:
Choose \(x e0\), possible because the Hilbert space is nontrivial. Strong monotonicity gives \(m\|x\|^2\le\langle abla U(x)- abla U(0),x angle\), while Cauchy–Schwarz and Lipschitzness bound the same quantity by \(L\|x\|^2\). Cancel the strictly positive \(\|x\|^2\) to prove \(m\le L\). No positivity premise on \(m\) is needed here.

The nontriviality assumption supplies a direction with positive squared norm. Dividing the two bounds for the same pairing by that norm gives the curvature comparison. On a singleton space no such direction exists, so the inequality need not follow; all transport errors there are instead treated directly as zero.

UnadjustedLangevin/TransportMoments.lean.title: Finite quadratic transport transfers second moments
UnadjustedLangevin/TransportMoments.lean.summary:
Suppose \(\pi\) has finite second moment and \(W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\). A finite-cost coupling and \(\|x\|^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2\) prove that \(\mu\) also has finite second moment. A finite infimum supplies a finite-cost coupling; an optimal coupling is not required.

Conversely, the independent product of two probabilities with finite second moments has finite quadratic cost, so their Wasserstein distance is finite. Changing variables under a pushforward law transfers these conclusions between a probability measure and a random vector with that law.

steps.title: A finite transport distance supplies a second moment
steps.body:
Finite Wasserstein distance supplies a finite-cost coupling. On that coupling space the second coordinate is in \(L^2\) by the reference moment, and the coordinate difference is in \(L^2\) by finite coupling cost. Their sum is the first coordinate, so its law \(\mu\) has a finite second moment. No optimal coupling is selected.

Explicitly, \(\|x\|^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2\). Integrating on a finite-cost coupling bounds the first marginal's second moment by two finite quantities. Thus finiteness of transport to one finite-moment reference determines the ordinary second-moment class of the other marginal.

steps.title: Second moments give a finite transport distance
steps.body:
Use the explicit independent coupling \(\mu\otimes\pi\). Each coordinate is in \(L^2\), hence their difference is in \(L^2\) and has finite cost. Wasserstein distance is at most this coupling cost, proving finiteness.

For independent \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Y\sim\pi\), the same squared triangle inequality gives \(\mathbb E\|X-Y\|^2\le2\mathbb E\|X\|^2+2\mathbb E\|Y\|^2\). Taking a square root supplies an explicit finite admissible cost, hence an upper bound for the transport infimum.

steps.title: Transferring the moment statement through a law
steps.body:
The finite-transport theorem first proves \(\mathrm{id}\in L^2(\mu)\). Replace \(\mu\) by the supplied pushforward law of \(X\), then use the change-of-law \(L^2\) criterion to pull this moment back to \(X\) on its original sample space.

The law change is the identity \(\int\|x\|^2d\mu(x)=\mathbb E\|X\|^2\). It transfers the moment conclusion to the original random variable without constructing a new realization or asserting any independence of that realization from other variables on its space.

steps.title: The moment implication for pushforward laws
steps.body:
Specialize the preceding theorem to \(\mu=P\circ X^{-1}\), whose law identity is reflexive. Finite transport of the pushforward to a finite-moment reference therefore gives \(X\in L^2(P)\).

The statement applies to the specified random vector on its original probability space. Measurability supplies the pushforward change of variables, while finite transport and the reference moment supply finiteness of the resulting squared-norm integral.

UnadjustedLangevin/Projection.lean.title: Projected root-mean-square error from quadratic transport
UnadjustedLangevin/Projection.lean.summary:
Let \(T:H\to K\) be continuous and linear with \(\|T\|\le1\), and let \(b\in K\). Write \(R_{T,b}(\mu)=(\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\), allowing infinity initially. On any coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), the identity \(Tx-b=T(x-y)+(Ty-b)\), Minkowski's inequality, and the contraction property of \(T\) bound this radius by the coupling cost plus \(R_{T,b}(\pi)\).

Taking the infimum gives \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\le W_2(\mu,\pi)+R_{T,b}(\pi)\). In particular, finite transport and a finite reference radius imply that the first projected second moment is finite. A reference bound \(R_{T,b}(\pi)\le c\), with \(c\ge0\), then gives the finite numerical inequality \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\le W_2(\mu,\pi)+c\).

steps.title: The projected root mean square error
steps.body:
Define the extended projected error \(R_{T,b}(\mu)=\|x\mapsto Tx-b\|_{L^2(\mu)}\). Using an extended norm retains infinity for a divergent second moment and allows the following transport comparison before any finiteness assumption.

This quantity is an error about the specified deterministic center \(b\), rather than a variance about the mean. It can therefore represent a parameter estimation error about a marginal mode. Keeping the extended integral initially allows the comparison to prove, rather than assume, its finiteness.

steps.title: Its finite ordinary value
steps.body:
Whenever the projected displacement has finite second moment, its projected root mean square radius is the ordinary finite number \(R_{T,b}(\mu)=(\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\). The transport and reference-radius bounds below establish this finiteness before the radius is used in a numerical inequality.

Once \(\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu<\infty\) is proved, its nonnegative square root is an ordinary real number. All later real-valued estimates use this finite case; a divergent second moment is never assigned a finite statistical-error interpretation.

steps.title: The pointwise projected difference bound
steps.body:
If \(\|T\|\le1\), then \(\|T(x-y)\|\le\|x-y\|\) pointwise. Monotonicity of the extended \(L^2\) norm bounds the projected difference norm by the original coupling cost.

Squaring the pointwise contraction, integrating under an arbitrary coupling, and taking nonnegative square roots gives \(\|T(X-Y)\|_{L^2}\le\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\). No relation between the projected coordinates and the unobserved coordinates is required.

steps.title: Projected error bounded by a coupling
steps.body:
On a coupling write \(Tx-b=T(x-y)+(Ty-b)\). Minkowski bounds its \(L^2\) norm by the sum of the two norms; the contraction estimate controls the first by coupling cost. Marginal identities rewrite the outer norms as \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\) and \(R_{T,b}(\pi)\).

The decomposition is valid because \(T\) is linear. The second term depends only on the reference marginal, so its value is the same for every coupling. This uniformity is precisely what lets the next step minimize only the full-state coupling cost.

steps.title: Projected error bounded by Wasserstein distance
steps.body:
The preceding bound holds for every coupling, with the same equilibrium radius. Take the infimum of coupling costs to obtain \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\le W_2(\mu,\pi)+R_{T,b}(\pi)\). The family of couplings is nonempty under the stated hypotheses; no minimizing coupling is assumed.

For any \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a coupling whose cost is within \(\varepsilon\) of the finite transport infimum. The couplingwise inequality then bounds the projected error by \(W_2+\varepsilon\) plus the reference radius. Sending \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives the claimed estimate without an optimizer.

steps.title: Finiteness of projected error
steps.body:
Finite transport guarantees a coupling exists and makes \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\) finite. The assumed equilibrium radius has a finite real upper bound. The transport-radius inequality therefore bounds the current projected norm by a sum of two finite extended values, proving its finiteness.

The argument supplies the projected moment even if no full second-moment bound for the first law has been stated separately. It needs only finite quadratic transport and a finite reference projected radius. This is useful when the statistical quantity is lower-dimensional than the full sampling state.

steps.title: The ordinary squared-moment formula
steps.body:
The finite projected square norm and measurability give \(x\mapsto Tx-b\in L^2(\mu)\). Its norm is therefore exactly \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu}\), a finite nonnegative number. Thus the projected radius estimate concerns a finite second moment.

Absolute integrability of the squared norm is established before using the ordinary integral. The identity then follows from \(\|F\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|F\|^2\), with the nonnegative square root selecting the norm rather than its negative.

steps.title: Inserting a target second-moment bound
steps.body:
The supplied \(L^2\) membership makes the squared-norm integral finite. Its bound by \(c^2\), together with \(c\ge0\), implies the root-mean-square norm is at most \(c\). The same inequality holds when the radius is viewed as an extended nonnegative value.

If the reference second moment is bounded by a radius squared, the radius must be nonnegative to conclude the desired norm bound after taking roots. The degenerate choice \(c=0\) forces the projection to equal the center almost everywhere.

steps.title: The finite projected error estimate
steps.body:
First prove current-radius finiteness using finite transport and the finite equilibrium bound. All quantities in the transport-radius inequality are now finite, so it gives \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\le W_2(\mu,\pi)+c\) as an inequality of real numbers.

The final bound separates two sources of error: transport measures how far the numerical full-state law is from the target, while \(c\) measures target fluctuations around the chosen center. Only the first term can decay through additional sampling iterations at a fixed target.

UnadjustedLangevin/ReferenceFamily.lean.title: A common-noise reference for every finite-cost initial coupling
UnadjustedLangevin/ReferenceFamily.lean.summary:
For every finite-cost coupling of the initial and target probabilities, suppose there is a square-integrable common-noise reference satisfying the stated integral equation and target marginal laws. Require that the numerical output law and the constants in the estimate are independent of the chosen coupling. The initial class distance is bounded by that coupling's cost.

The mean-square estimate then applies to every such coupling with the same output law. Taking the infimum of their initial costs gives the initial Wasserstein distance. One finite-cost initial coupling first proves that the output transport distance is finite. Requiring a reference for every finite-cost coupling is used in the infimum argument; a reference for only one coupling would give only its individual cost bound.

steps.title: Couplings with finite quadratic cost
steps.body:
Restrict the family of couplings to those with \(c\ne\infty\). This family retains the integrability needed to realize initial class distances and convert them to real values while taking the Wasserstein infimum.

Finite cost means \(\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)<\infty\). It controls the difference between initial states even before separate moment estimates for each coordinate are used. Restricting to these couplings does not alter a finite transport infimum, since infinite costs cannot improve it.

steps.title: A reference for every finite-cost initial coupling
steps.body:
On one probability space \(P\), for each finite-cost coupling, suppose there are square-integrable initial and noise variables and an integral reference. Their laws must be the prescribed initial laws, their initial class distance must be bounded by the coupling cost, and the numerical output must have one common law across the family. These are the hypotheses on the reference family; the convergence estimate is their consequence.

Index the realizations by the initial coupling \(c\). At each iteration \(n\), the required identity is \(\operatorname{Law}(X_n^c)=\nu_n\) for every \(c\), while the reference distribution is the fixed target. This common numerical distribution permits taking the infimum of the initial coupling costs without changing the distribution whose transport error is bounded. The hypothesis is the common-law identity itself.

steps.title: Finiteness of the output transport distance
steps.body:
Choose one finite initial coupling using the finite initial Wasserstein premise. Its supplied numerical/reference \(L^2\) variables yield a finite-cost output coupling. The output-law and stationary-reference hypotheses identify its marginals, proving \(W_2(\nu_n,\pi)<\infty\).

One finite initial coupling is enough to exhibit a finite output coupling, since both endpoint random vectors then have a square-integrable difference. This preliminary finiteness result permits the later convergence inequality to be stated with ordinary real Wasserstein distances.

steps.title: Passing the analytic bound through the initial infimum
steps.body:
Apply the analytic \(L^2\) estimate to every finite coupling realization in the family. Replace its initial error by the coupling cost and its numerical law by the common \(\nu_n\). Because \((1-mh)^n\ge0\), the affine finite-coupling infimum theorem gives the displayed bound with the initial Wasserstein distance.

The coefficient of the initial cost is nonnegative, so taking its infimum preserves the affine bound. A negative coefficient would reverse the minimization and invalidate this step. The small-step restrictions guarantee the required sign as well as strict contraction.

UnadjustedLangevin/ULAFromBrownian.lean.title: Convergence under stationary Brownian reference laws
UnadjustedLangevin/ULAFromBrownian.lean.summary:
Construct square-mean continuous Langevin reference segments from the supplied Brownian coordinates and potential assumptions. Assume explicitly that every segment has Gibbs law at the stated times. Brownian covariance bounds their noise increments, and the Gibbs score moment bounds their drifts.

The resulting local defect is of order \(h^{3/2}\). Combining its explicit constant with deterministic contraction gives the affine mean-square recurrence and the stated convergence bound. The initial error in this result is the supplied joint initialization's \(L^2\) distance. Segment stationarity remains a hypothesis here; the later construction proves stationarity and identifies the Gaussian transition laws.

steps.title: Apply the reference estimate to the constructed segments
steps.body:
Build the reference from Brownian segments using the displayed all-time Gibbs-law premise. Strong convexity proves finite partition and \(m\le L\), while Brownian laws prove the noise radius and the Gibbs score theorem proves its drift bound. Apply the analytic \(L^2\) theorem with the supplied joint initialization, yielding its initial class distance. This intermediate theorem retains its explicit stationarity premise.

Stationarity is an explicit hypothesis of the supplied segments. Once that property holds, Brownian covariance and the Gibbs score moment give all local-error constants automatically. A later construction proves stationarity and identifies the independent Gaussian chain, producing the unconditional sampling theorem.

UnadjustedLangevin/Degenerate.lean.title: Zero-dimensional state spaces have zero transport cost
UnadjustedLangevin/Degenerate.lean.summary:
On a subsingleton state space every two states coincide, so every coupling has zero quadratic difference cost. Probability laws on such a space therefore have zero Wasserstein distance.

In a singleton state space, any two states agree and every displacement is zero. A joint law therefore has zero quadratic cost, and the product of the two probability measures is an admissible zero-cost coupling. The transport infimum is both nonnegative and at most zero, hence zero. This resolves dimension-zero or other degenerate cases directly, before invoking arguments that cancel a nonzero distance or select a unit direction.

steps.title: Zero coupling cost in a singleton space
steps.body:
In a subsingleton state space every pair satisfies \(x=y\), so the displacement function is identically zero. Its extended \(L^2\) norm is zero under every pair measure, hence every coupling cost vanishes.

The conclusion uses only that the metric distance between any two states is zero. It therefore holds for every coupling, with no moment or regularity assumption on a potential. The quadratic cost integral is the integral of the identically zero function.

steps.title: Zero transport distance in a singleton space
steps.body:
The independent product of two probabilities is a coupling, so the family of couplings is nonempty. Every coupling has zero cost by the preceding result; taking their infimum gives \(W_2(\mu,\pi)=0\).

The product coupling demonstrates that the infimum is taken over a nonempty family. Every member of that family has value zero, so the infimum is zero as well. This avoids relying on any convention for an infimum over an empty set.

steps.title: The ordinary zero-distance conclusion
steps.body:
The Wasserstein distance is zero by the singleton-space result. In particular it is finite, and the same equality holds with the distance regarded as a real number. This covers dimension-zero spaces without invoking the nontrivial-space comparison \(m\le L\).

A zero-dimensional Euclidean space consists of the empty coordinate vector. Both the numerical update and every reference law are supported at that single state. Hence the transport conclusion is immediate and no smoothness-versus-curvature cancellation is necessary.

UnadjustedLangevin/Check.lean.title: Assumptions and verification of the ULA convergence results
UnadjustedLangevin/Check.lean.summary:
The convergence statements assume the specified potential regularity, step range, and initial integrability. Deterministic contraction and local-defect estimates give the mean-square bound. The construction of independent Gaussian innovations identifies the numerical marginal laws, and taking the initial coupling infimum gives the Wasserstein bound.

Results stated with a supplied reference or a weak-equation uniqueness hypothesis retain those assumptions. An application must either provide them or use the subsequent theorems that prove the required reference properties. The convergence statements are therefore read together with their complete hypotheses.

steps.title: Verification and mathematical hypotheses
steps.body:
The source audit lists the logical dependencies and complete hypotheses of the convergence theorems after compilation. It covers the potential estimates, Brownian reference, Gibbs stationarity, and Wasserstein conclusions. The dependency check does not remove theorem hypotheses, including the stated uniqueness assumptions of conditional weak-equation results.

This module imports the assembled strong-convexity theory and checks the logical dependencies of its public convergence theorems. A successful run verifies the compiled proofs using the imported lemmas. The mathematical arguments are given on the linked theorem modules; this audit file introduces no additional mathematical hypothesis or theorem.

The convergence result separates deterministic geometry, probabilistic construction, and the final transport comparison. Each application must verify the hypotheses at the appropriate level: gradient regularity for contraction, target moments and stationarity for local error, and independent innovations for identifying the numerical laws. Conditional weak-equation statements retain their uniqueness hypotheses.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Check.lean.title: Assumptions of the ULA entropy results
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Check.lean.summary: The final Gaussian ULA entropy theorem assumes a differentiable potential with a globally Lipschitz gradient, LSI for its Gibbs probability measure, the positive step restriction, and finite initial relative entropy. It proves the needed gradient moment, Gaussian density regularity, finite Fisher information, entropy absolute continuity, and the estimate near elapsed time zero. The conditional interpolation results retain their additional density and weak-equation assumptions.

steps.title: Verification of the hypotheses and proof dependencies
steps.body:
The mathematical implication is

\[H'\le-\tfrac34I+E\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hdL^2/\alpha.\]

The first implication also uses LSI and the specified gradient and discrepancy bounds. The second uses the step restriction and geometric summation. The final theorem proves the required analytic estimates for the Gaussian interpolation. Conditional variants require those estimates as explicit hypotheses.

The audit displays the theorem types and the logical axioms used by their proofs. The types distinguish the conditional interpolation results from the final Gaussian ULA theorem.

UnadjustedLangevin.lean.title: Wasserstein and relative-entropy convergence of ULA
UnadjustedLangevin.lean.summary:
There are two convergence results for the unadjusted Langevin recursion. Positive strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient give an explicit quadratic-Wasserstein estimate by common-noise coupling with a stationary continuous reference. A target log-Sobolev inequality and a Lipschitz gradient give a relative-entropy recurrence from finite initial relative entropy by positive-time Gaussian interpolation.

In each proof, a local estimate is integrated or summed and then used in a scalar recurrence. The supporting results establish the probability laws, second moments or entropy integrability, density regularity, and limiting identities required at the interpolation endpoints. Strong convexity supplies distance contraction and target tail bounds in the Wasserstein proof. The log-Sobolev inequality converts Fisher dissipation into entropy contraction in the entropy proof, which does not require convexity of the potential.

steps.title: Wasserstein convergence under strong convexity
steps.body:
The imported modules prove Gibbs normalization and score moments, construct independent Brownian coordinates and \(L^2\) Langevin solutions, establish Gibbs stationarity by invariant Metropolis approximation, and assemble a stationary coupling reference for every finite initial coupling. Taking the infimum of the resulting costs gives

\[W_2(P_h^k\mu,\pi)\le(1-mh)^kW_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}\]

under differentiability, \(m>0\) strong convexity, \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(0<h\le2/(m+L)\), and finite initial \(W_2\). The alternative stable branch and the theorem for an square-integrable iid-Gaussian \(L^2\) recursion are imported as well.

The strongly convex convergence theorem controls \(W_2(\mu_k,\pi)\) by a geometric initialization term and a step-dependent additive bound. Its proof first constructs the stationary diffusion, then couples the Gaussian chain to that diffusion. Strong convexity is used both for contraction and for the target's Gaussian tails.

steps.title: Relative-entropy convergence and its hypotheses
steps.body:
The imported entropy results prove the recurrence under their stated interpolation and analytic hypotheses, giving the bound \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hdL^2/\alpha\). Their hypotheses are not removed by this import. The compiled library and the two source audits verify the proofs and list their logical dependencies. The module pages also display the source statements with their mathematical explanations.

The entropy proof assumes a log-Sobolev inequality and finite initial relative entropy. It derives a discrete affine recurrence from a positive-time interpolation, with endpoint limits supplying the initial value. Convexity of the potential is not required for that argument; the two convergence results therefore have distinct hypotheses and conclusions.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ConditionalDrift..title: Conditional expectation of the gradient discrepancy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ConditionalDrift..summary: Let \(Y\) be an observed random variable and let \(D\) be a square-integrable random vector. Under the stated measurability assumptions, the conditional expectation given \(\sigma(Y)\) has a measurable representation \(e(Y)\). Conditional Jensen gives \(\int\|e\|^2d(Y_\#P)\le\mathbb E\|D\|^2\). Applied to \(D_t=\nabla U(Y_t)-\nabla U(X)\), this produces the state-dependent discrepancy in the relative-density weak equation and preserves the Gaussian energy bound.

steps.title: A measurable representation of a conditional mean
steps.body:
Assume \(D\in L^2(P)\) and \(Y\) is measurable. The conditional expectation \(\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) is strongly measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\). Doob–Dynkin factorization, under the stated assumptions on the spaces, gives a strongly measurable field \(e\) such that \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) almost surely. Conditional Jensen and integration give

\[\int\|e(y)\|^2d(Y_\#P)(y)=\mathbb E\|\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\|^2\le\mathbb E\|D\|^2.\]

The conditional expectation is square-integrable, so the integral on the left is finite. The field is determined only up to a null set under the law of \(Y\), which does not affect these integrals.

steps.title: The conditional mean on measurable sets
steps.body:
Suppose \(D\) is integrable and \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) almost surely. For every measurable observation set \(A\), the pushforward integral formula and the defining property of conditional expectation give

\[\int_A e(y)d(Y_\#P)(y)=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}e(Y)\,dP=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}D\,dP.\]

The inverse image \(Y^{-1}(A)\) belongs to \(\sigma(Y)\), so the last equality is a valid conditional-expectation identity. All terms are vector-valued integrals under the stated integrability assumptions.

steps.title: Pairing the conditional mean with an observed test
steps.body:
Let \(\varphi\) be strongly measurable, and assume \(\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\) is integrable. The function \(\varphi(Y)\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\). The conditional expectation rule for a continuous bilinear pairing therefore gives

\[\mathbb E[\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\mid\sigma(Y)]=\langle\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)],\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

Integrate this equality, replace the conditional mean by \(e(Y)\), and change variables by the law of \(Y\). The result is

\[\int\langle e(y),\varphi(y)\rangle d(Y_\#P)(y)=\mathbb E\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

The integrability hypothesis is required for this test; it is not inferred for arbitrary unbounded functions.

steps.title: The gradient discrepancy before conditioning
steps.body:
On the product space of the initial state and independent Gaussian variable, put \(Y_t(x,z)=x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\) and define

\[D_t(x,z)= abla U\!\left(x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z ight)- abla U(x).\]

Thus \(D_t= abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\). The order of subtraction fixes its sign in the weak equation: the conditional field is \(e_t(y)= abla U(y)-\mathbb E[ abla U(X)\mid Y_t=y]\). The definition alone asserts no integrability or energy bound.

steps.title: The sigma-algebra of the interpolated state
steps.body: The observation at elapsed time \(t\) is \(Y_t\), and its sigma-algebra is \(\sigma(Y_t)=\{Y_t^{-1}(A):A\text{ measurable}\}\), interpreted as the generated sigma-algebra. A random variable measurable for this sigma-algebra depends only on the value of \(Y_t\). Conditioning the gradient discrepancy on \(\sigma(Y_t)\) therefore yields a field on the state space. If the gradient is Lipschitz, the observation map is measurable and this sigma-algebra is contained in the ambient one.

steps.title: The conditional discrepancy and its second moment
steps.body:
Assume \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu<\infty\). The Gaussian displacement estimate proves that \(D_t\) is square-integrable and \(\mathbb E\|D_t\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2tn)\), where \(n=\dim E\). Apply the measurable conditional-mean result to obtain a strongly measurable field \(e_t\) satisfying

\[e_t(Y_t)=\mathbb E[D_t\mid\sigma(Y_t)],\qquad \int\|e_t(y)\|^2d\rho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2,\]\[\rho_t=(Y_t)_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)).\]

The equality identifies the field for the same Gaussian interpolation used in the algorithm. Its square-integrability and energy bound follow from conditional Jensen and the preceding joint Gaussian estimate.

steps.title: The discrepancy energy relative to the Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Suppose a measurable nonnegative density identifies the interpolation law as \( ho_t=r_t u\). The conditional-mean construction gives a square-integrable field under \( ho_t\). Changing measure proves integrability of the weighted square under \( u\), and

\[\int r_t(y)\|e_t(y)\|^2d u(y)=\int\|e_t(y)\|^2d ho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2.\]

The conditional-mean identity is unchanged. This is the form of the energy estimate that appears in entropy production.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InteriorEntropy.l.title: Entropy comparison using positive-time derivatives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InteriorEntropy.l.summary: A continuous function on \([0,T]\) can satisfy an affine comparison using derivative bounds only on \((0,T)\). This applies to Gaussian entropy calculations where derivatives are first proved at positive times. The second result identifies the relative-entropy derivative with the differentiated density integral at an interior time, under the stated local domination assumptions. Control near zero is required separately when passing to the initial law.

steps.title: An affine comparison without endpoint derivatives
steps.body:
Let \(a>0\), assume \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), and suppose \(H'(t)\le-aH(t)+b\) on \((0,T)\). Set \(F(t)=e^{at}(H(t)-b/a)\). Then

\[F'(t)=e^{at}\bigl(a(H(t)-b/a)+H'(t)\bigr)\le0.\]

The mean-value theorem implies that \(F\) is nonincreasing on the closed interval, using continuity at its endpoints and differentiability in its interior. Thus \(F(t)\le F(0)\). Multiplication by \(e^{-at}>0\) and rearrangement give

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at}).\]

The cancellation \(a(b/a)=b\) uses \(a\ne0\). No derivative is required at zero or at \(T\).

steps.title: The entropy derivative at an interior time
steps.body:
Fix \(0\[ rac d{dt}\operatorname{KL}(r_t u\mid u)=\int\dot r_t(x)(\log r_t(x)+1)\,d u(x).\]

The assumptions concern interior times only. Continuity or a one-sided bound at zero must still be proved before applying an estimate that involves the initial entropy.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GradientMoment.le.title: A gradient moment bound from a coupling
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GradientMoment.le.summary: Let \((X,Y)\) couple \(\mu\) and \( u\), with finite squared distance, and suppose the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz. The inequality \(\| abla U(X)\|\le L\|X-Y\|+\| abla U(Y)\|\) gives a second-moment bound under \(\mu\) when that moment is finite under \( u\). For a normalized Gibbs target, the latter is at most \(nL\). An explicitly assumed entropy bound on the coupling cost then gives the stated entropy-dependent gradient estimate. The final ULA entropy theorem instead obtains its gradient moment directly from exponential integrability of the Gibbs score.

steps.title: Integrability and the coupling estimate
steps.body:
Let \(c\) have marginals \(\mu, u\), and assume \(\int\|x-y\|^2dc<\infty\) and \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u<\infty\). Lipschitzness and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give the pointwise inequality

\[\| abla U(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-y\|^2+2\| abla U(y)\|^2.\]

The right-hand side is integrable under \(c\). Measurability and domination imply integrability of the first-coordinate gradient square, hence of \(\| abla U\|^2\) under \(\mu\). Integration and the marginal identities give

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)+2\int\| abla U\|^2d u.\]

steps.title: The estimate for a Gibbs target
steps.body:
Let \( u=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dx\) be a Gibbs probability measure, with differentiable \(U\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Probability normalization supplies a finite positive partition function. The Gibbs score estimate proves square-integrability and \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u\le nL\), without strong convexity. Substituting these facts in the coupling estimate gives

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc+2nL.\]

The same argument proves gradient square-integrability under \(\mu\); it is not assumed before this conclusion.

steps.title: Substitution of an entropy bound on the coupling cost
steps.body:
Suppose the given finite-cost coupling also satisfies

\[\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)\le rac2\alpha\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u),\qquad \alpha>0,\quad \operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u)<\infty.\]

Multiply this inequality by \(2L^2\ge0\) and substitute it in the preceding gradient estimate. Since \(2L^2(2/\alpha)=4L^2/\alpha\),

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le rac{4L^2}{\alpha}\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u)+2nL.\]

The cost-to-entropy estimate is an explicit hypothesis for the supplied coupling. This result does not prove a transport inequality from LSI.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationDens.title: Construct the positive Gaussian mixture and Gibbs-relative density
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationDens.summary:
Let \(\mu\) be the initial probability, \(t>0\), and \(c_t(x)=x-t abla U(x)\). The update \(c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\), with \(Z\) an independent standard Gaussian vector, has density \(q_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\), where \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). This follows by conditioning on \(X\) and applying Tonelli. No initial Lebesgue density is needed.

Each Gaussian component is positive and bounded by \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). The mixture is consequently positive and finite at every observation. Dominated convergence gives spatial continuity, and parameter integration gives measurability. If the Gibbs probability has density \(J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\), the positive continuous function \(r_t=q_t/J=Ze^Uq_t\) satisfies \(r_t u=q_tdy\) and \(\int r_td u=1\). Its differentiability, entropy, and Fisher information require the subsequent estimates.

steps.title: The nonnegative Gaussian mixture integral
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), put \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\) and \(C_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Define

\[K_t(x,y)=C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right),\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x).\]

For fixed \(x\), this is the Gaussian density with mean \(c_t(x)\) and covariance \(2tI_d\). The mixture is initially defined by a nonnegative integral, which may take the value infinity. Tonelli is therefore available before a pointwise finiteness assertion has been proved.

The subsequent peak bound will show that this same integral is finite at every \(y\), even for an initial law with no density or moments. The positive-time assumption is used in the Gaussian normalization and denominator.

steps.title: Apply measurable parameter integration to the mixture
steps.body:
A Lipschitz gradient is continuous and measurable, so \(c_t\) is measurable in the starting point. The map \((x,y)\mapsto y-c_t(x)\) is jointly measurable. Squared norm, multiplication by the fixed scalar, and exponential preserve measurability, so \(K_t\) is a jointly measurable nonnegative kernel.

Integration in \(x\) against \(\mu\) yields a measurable function of \(y\). The mixing measure is finite and hence sigma-finite, as required for measurable parameter integration. This measurability assertion concerns the defining formula and does not use a positive-time finiteness estimate.

steps.title: The update law has the Gaussian mixture density
steps.body:
Let \(X\sim\mu\), let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) be independent, and write \(Y_t=c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). For a measurable set \(A\), independence and the pushforward formula give

\[\mathbb P(Y_t\in A)=\int\mathbb P\bigl(c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}Z\in A\bigr)d\mu(x).\]

The inner probability is \(\int_AK_t(x,y)dy\), by the fixed-state affine Gaussian density. Joint measurability permits Tonelli under \(\mu\) and Lebesgue measure restricted to \(A\). Consequently

\[\mathbb P(Y_t\in A)=\int_A\left(\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\right)dy=\int_Aq_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)dy.\]

Thus the mixture is the density of the update law. Equivalently, the same computation applies to every nonnegative measurable test function. It does not assume that \(\mu\) itself has a density.

steps.title: Use positivity of every Gaussian component
steps.body:
At positive time the normalizer \(C_t\) is strictly positive, and the exponential is strictly positive at every finite argument. Hence \(K_t(x,y)>0\) for every pair \(x,y\).

Fix \(y\). The nonnegative measurable function \(x\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is positive on the whole state space, which has \(\mu\)-mass one. A nonnegative integral can vanish only when its integrand is zero almost everywhere. Therefore \(q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)>0\). This proves positivity at every observation, before any assertion about its finiteness.

steps.title: Bound every mixture value by the common Gaussian peak
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the Gaussian exponent is nonpositive, hence

\[0\le K_t(x,y)\le C_t,\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\le C_t.\]

The proof establishes the exponential bound with the fact that an exponential with nonpositive exponent is at most one: the numerator \(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonpositive and the denominator \(4t\) is positive. Multiplication by the nonnegative normalizer preserves the inequality, and the same inequality holds for nonnegative extended values.

Monotonicity of the nonnegative integral integrates this pointwise bound. The integral of the constant \(C_t\) equals \(C_t\mu(E)=C_t\) because \(\mu\) is a probability measure. This theorem requires no regularity of the gradient: its bound concerns the nonnegative integrand at every point, and the upper nonnegative integral remains monotone even before measurability is established.

The exponential factor is at most one, independently of the Gaussian center. Hence averaging over any starting probability retains the same peak bound, without requiring an initial moment.

steps.title: Pointwise finiteness of the mixture
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and let \(C_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}<\infty\). Every Gaussian component satisfies \(0\le K_t(x,y)\le C_t\), independently of its center. Because \(\mu\) is a probability, integration in the starting point gives

\[0\le\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\le\int C_t d\mu=C_t<\infty.\]

Thus the initially nonnegative-integral definition of the mixture is finite at every observation \(y\). It has an ordinary real value pointwise, with the same peak bound, even if \(\mu\) has no density or position moments. The positive-time condition is essential: at zero the Gaussian peak need not have a finite limiting bound.

steps.title: The finite real-valued mixture density
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the preceding peak bound makes the mixture finite at every observation. We therefore use its ordinary real-valued representative

\[p_t(y)=\int (4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-x+t\nabla U(x)\|^2}{4t}\right)d\mu(x).\]

This nonnegative integral is at most \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\) and is strictly positive because every Gaussian component is positive and \(\mu\) is a probability. Its ordinary value and nonnegative extended value agree everywhere. The positive-time law identity, regularity statements, and logarithmic derivatives below all use this same finite representative.

steps.title: The update law has the finite density
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), write \(q_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\), which is finite everywhere by the preceding peak bound. For every measurable set \(A\), the proposal law satisfies

\[\begin{aligned} \rho_t(A)&=\int\left(\int_AK_t(x,y)dy\right)d\mu(x)\\ &=\int_A\left(\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\right)dy =\int_Aq_t(y)dy. \end{aligned}\]

The first identity conditions on the initial point and uses the affine Gaussian proposal density. The second is Tonelli for the nonnegative kernel. Its finite pointwise mixture is precisely the ordinary density defined above, so no change of law accompanies passage to real-valued density notation. This identification remains valid for singular initial laws.

steps.title: Deduce absolute continuity for every positive time
steps.body:
The law identity \(\rho_t=q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}dy\) immediately implies \(\rho_t\ll dy\): every Lebesgue-null set has zero integral against the density and thus zero proposal probability.

The interpolation law has density \(q_t\) with respect to Lebesgue measure. Hence a Lebesgue-null set has zero interpolation probability, proving absolute continuity at positive time. This holds even for singular initial laws. Finite KL with respect to Gibbs and entropy behavior at zero require the separate score and endpoint arguments.

The proposed law has a Lebesgue density, so every Lebesgue-null set has proposed mass zero. This absolute continuity holds for arbitrary initial laws once the elapsed Gaussian time is positive.

steps.title: The ordinary integral formula for the mixture
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and an observation \(y\). The real Gaussian kernel is measurable in \(x\), nonnegative, and bounded by \(C_t\). Since \(\mu\) is a probability, this constant is integrable, so the kernel has an ordinary finite integral.

For a nonnegative integrable function, its ordinary integral equals its nonnegative integral viewed as a real value. The finite mixture therefore satisfies

\[q_t(y)=\int C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right)d\mu(x).\]

The equality identifies two forms of the same integral. It does not change the probability law or choose a different density.

steps.title: Pass spatial continuity through the probability mixture
steps.body:
At a fixed positive time, \(q_t:E\to\mathbb R\) is continuous. For every fixed initial state \(x\), the Gaussian kernel \(y\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is continuous, and its absolute value is bounded by the same constant \(C_t\), independent of \(x\) and \(y\).

The proof first replaces the explicit Gaussian-mixture Lebesgue density by the ordinary integral formula from the previous theorem. It applies continuity under an integral with the common integrable majorant \(x\mapsto C_t\). Measurability in \(x\) follows from gradient continuity. The nonpositive Gaussian exponent proves \(\|K_t(x,y)\|=K_t(x,y)\le C_t\); probability normalization makes this majorant integrable. Pointwise continuity in \(y\) is then assembled from subtraction, norm, square and exponential.

Dominated convergence therefore passes the pointwise kernel continuity through the mixture integral. The conclusion is spatial continuity; spatial and time differentiation require separate domination estimates.

At a fixed positive time the component kernel is continuous in the observation and bounded by one common peak. Dominated convergence passes that continuity through the mixture integral.

steps.title: Derive finite partition from target normalization
steps.body:
Write the normalized Gibbs measure as \( u=Z^{-1}(e^{-U}dy)\), where initially \(Z=\int e^{-U}dy\) is a nonnegative extended integral. Assume this normalized measure is a probability. If \(Z=\infty\), its reciprocal is zero, so \( u\) would be the zero measure, contradicting \( u(E)=1\). Thus \(Z<\infty\).

The separate positivity argument for the partition gives \(Z>0\) under the displayed assumptions. Together these facts make \(Z\) an ordinary positive finite denominator. This deduction uses target normalization and the partition's positivity, without a strong-convexity assumption. In particular it applies when probability normalization is part of the log-Sobolev hypothesis.

steps.title: Write the explicit density relative to Gibbs
steps.body:
The normalized Gibbs target has Lebesgue density \(Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\). Therefore the relative density corresponding to the mixture \(q_t(y)dy\) is

\[r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}q_t(y).\]

The relative density is the ordinary product \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\). The positive finite partition and mixture peak bounds make all factors finite at positive time. Multiplication by the Gibbs density cancels \(Ze^{U(y)}\), producing the Lebesgue density \(q_t\).

The definition makes the coordinate conversion explicit: the ratio to the target is obtained by multiplying the Lebesgue density by the reciprocal target density. Entropy differentiation, convergence, and weak differential equations are separate conclusions requiring their own hypotheses.

The Gibbs Lebesgue density is \(J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\), so the relative density is \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). Multiplying by \(J\) recovers \(p_t\) pointwise.

steps.title: Multiply measurable factors to obtain relative-density measurability
steps.body: Write the relative density as \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). The mixture \(p_t\) is measurable by parameter integration; differentiability of \(U\) gives measurability of \(e^U\); and the partition \(Z\) is a fixed finite scalar. Products of these measurable factors are measurable. Thus the explicit relative density is measurable, as required to define its weighted target measure. This statement is a measurability conclusion; spatial differentiation and finite entropy are established separately.

steps.title: Obtain relative-density continuity at positive time
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the mixture \(q_t\) is spatially continuous by the Gaussian peak domination argument. Differentiability of the potential implies continuity of \(U\), so \(y\mapsto e^{U(y)}\) is continuous. The partition \(Z\) is a fixed finite scalar.

Multiplying these continuous factors proves continuity of \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\). Equivalently, the Gibbs density \(J\) is continuous and everywhere positive, so \(r_t=q_t/J\) has no singular denominator. This proves continuity only; the differentiability required for the log-Sobolev application follows from the subsequent Gaussian derivative estimates.

steps.title: Strict positivity of the relative density
steps.body:
Assume the Gibbs target is a probability and \(t>0\). The partition positivity result and target normalization give \(0<Z<\infty\). The Gaussian peak and positivity results give \(0<q_t(y)<\infty\) at every observation. The ordinary exponential \(e^{U(y)}\) is also finite and strictly positive.

Every factor in \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\) is therefore a positive finite real number, proving \(r_t(y)>0\). Both positivity and finiteness are needed: neither an infinite mixture value nor a zero partition could be used as an ordinary positive relative density.

steps.title: The relative density represents the update law
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and assume the Gibbs partition satisfies \(0<Z<\infty\), as proved under the target normalization hypotheses. Let

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)},\qquad r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y).\]

The mixture \(q_t\) is finite and measurable, and the Gibbs density is strictly positive. Pointwise multiplication therefore gives the ordinary identity

\[r_t(y)J(y)=\bigl(Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\bigr)\bigl(Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\bigr)=q_t(y).\]

Integrating over any measurable set identifies the measures:

\[r_t\nu=q_tdy=\rho_t.\]

The last equality is the Gaussian-mixture law identity already proved. Hence this relative density represents the specified interpolation law. Positivity, spatial regularity, time differentiation, and finite entropy remain separate properties established in the subsequent analysis.

steps.title: Normalization of the relative density
steps.body:
The measure induced by the constructed relative density is a probability measure:

\[\int r_t\,d u=1\qquad(t>0).\]
