Integrating the identity \(r_t u= ho_t\) over the entire state space gives \(\int r_t\,d u=1\), because the Gaussian update is a probability law. Thus the explicitly constructed density is normalized; no separate assumption about its mass is required.

Positivity, continuity, and normalization all concern this same density. Normalization alone does not imply finite entropy or Fisher information; these properties will follow from the positive-time moment and derivative bounds.

Integrating the law identity on the whole space gives \(\int r_t\,d u=1\). Normalization is therefore inherited from the Gaussian transition rather than proved by a separate algebraic manipulation of a possibly infinite density.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/BoundedLog.lean.title: Bounded logarithmic tests and their entropy primitives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/BoundedLog.lean.summary:
For \(M=m+1\), define \(\chi_m(z)=M\arctan(z/M)\) and \(w_m(z)=(1+(z/M)^2)^{-1}\). Then \(\chi_m\) is smooth and bounded, \(\chi_m^{\prime}=w_m\), \(0\le w_m\le1\), and \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). For each fixed \(z\), the test and its derivative converge to \(z\) and 1 respectively.

For a positive density value \(r\), the primitive \(\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du\) has derivative \(\chi_m(\log r)\), is nonnegative, and is bounded by \(r\log r-r+1\). Its pointwise limit is this entropy integrand. These estimates justify bounded tests in the weak equation, their time chain rules, and dominated convergence to the entropy identity under finite relative entropy.

steps.title: Choose the bounded test and its weight
steps.body:
For a natural number \(m\), write \(c=m+1>0\). Define

\[\chi_m(z)=c\arctan(z/c),\qquad w_m(z)=\frac1{1+(z/c)^2},\qquad\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du.\]

The positive offset in \(c\) prevents division by zero even for \(m=0\). The interval integral is oriented: when \(r<1\), its sign reverses. The formulas define these expressions for every real argument; the entropy claims below explicitly require \(r>0\).

The scale \(M=m+1\) is strictly positive for every allowed index, avoiding a zero denominator. The arctangent bounds the test uniformly in its argument, while the derivative weight remains between zero and one.

steps.title: Differentiate and bound the test
steps.body:
The arctangent chain rule gives \(\chi_m(0)=0\) and \(\chi_m^{\prime}(z)=w_m(z)\). The denominator is at least one, so \(0\le w_m\le1\). The derivative bound implies that \(\chi_m\) is 1-Lipschitz, hence \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). Independently, \(|\arctan u|<\pi/2\) gives \(|\chi_m(z)|\le c\pi/2\). This last bound controls the time derivative integrand without any log-integrability requirement. Since arctangent has the sign of its argument, \(\chi_m\) does too.

The test is smooth of all orders because arctangent is smooth and \(c>0\). In its first derivative, the factor \(1/c\) from the inner argument cancels the outer factor \(c\), leaving exactly the stated weight.

Differentiating arctangent gives the rational weight \(1/(1+(z/M)^2)\). Its denominator is at least one, proving nonnegativity and the upper bound used to dominate every truncated score energy.

steps.title: Recover the logarithm and its primitive
steps.body:
As \(m\to\infty\), \(z/(m+1)\to0\). The derivative of arctangent at zero is one; its difference quotient therefore gives \(\chi_m(z)\to z\). At \(z=0\) the claim is exact at every index. Continuity of inversion at the positive denominator one gives \(w_m(z)\to1\).

The function \(u\mapsto\chi_m(\log u)\) is measurable and bounded, hence integrable on every finite interval, including intervals containing zero. When \(r>0\), continuity in a neighborhood of \(r\) and the fundamental theorem of calculus imply \(\Phi_m^{\prime}(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\).

For fixed \(z\), the ratio \(z/M\) tends to zero, and \(\arctan u/u\to1\). This gives recovery of the logarithmic test and, after integration in the density variable, its entropy primitive.

steps.title: Dominate the entropy endpoints
steps.body:
We have \(\Phi_m(1)=0\). For \(r\ge1\), both \(\log u\) and its test are nonnegative on \([1,r]\), giving \(\Phi_m(r)\ge0\). For \(0<r\le1\), the test is nonpositive on \([r,1]\), and reversing the interval again gives nonnegativity.

On the positive side, \(0\le\chi_m(\log u)\le\log u\). On the negative side, \(\log u\le\chi_m(\log u)\le0\); reversing the interval preserves the corresponding upper bound for the primitive. In both cases,

\[0\le\Phi_m(r)\le\int_1^r\log u\,du=r\log r-r+1.\]

Pointwise convergence of the test and domination by \(|\log u|\), integrable on the finite interval between 1 and \(r\), prove \(\Phi_m(r)\to r\log r-r+1\). These are exactly the hypotheses for dominated convergence against the finite-KL relative density later.

The entropy integrand \(r\log r-r+1\) is nonnegative and dominates the bounded primitives. For a probability density its integral equals KL, so finite relative entropy supplies the endpoint majorant for dominated convergence.

steps.title: Identify the spatial gradient of the test
steps.body:
For a differentiable scalar field \(f\), the Fréchet chain rule gives \(D(\chi_m\circ f)=w_m(f)Df\). Applying the Hilbert-space identification of linear derivatives with gradients yields

\[ abla(\chi_m\circ f)(x)=w_m(f(x)) abla f(x),\qquad\| abla(\chi_m\circ f)(x)\|\le\| abla f(x)\|.\]

The inequality uses \(0\le w_m\le1\). With \(f=\log r_t\), it supplies square-integrability of the bounded log test gradient from the Fisher information bound.

Applying the spatial chain rule multiplies the relative score by \(w_m(\log r)\). Since this weight is at most one, the gradient's squared energy is bounded by Fisher information, proving admissibility of every bounded test.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianMeasurabi.title: Jointly measurable density and relative score
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianMeasurabi.summary:
The Gaussian kernel and its explicit spatial derivative are jointly measurable in positive time, starting point, and observation. Parameter integration gives jointly measurable mixture densities and derivative fields. This is the measurability needed for the subsequent space-time integrals.

At positive time the density is everywhere positive. Dividing its gradient by the density and adding \(\nabla U\) yields one jointly measurable relative score field, equal pointwise to \(\nabla\log r_t\). A separately assigned value at time zero or negative times changes none of the integrals over positive time.

steps.title: Integrate a jointly measurable Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The density is a nonnegative parameter integral \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). The normalizer, affine center, norm, and exponential are measurable in \((t,y,x)\). The parameterized nonnegative integral is therefore measurable. Passing from the extended integral to its real value preserves measurability. Multiplication by \(Z e^{U(y)}\) gives the joint measurability of \(r_t(y)\).

The explicit positive-time formulas give one jointly measurable family on the domain \((0,\infty)\times E\). If a value at zero is needed to define an ambient spacetime field, it may be assigned separately on that measurable time slice. No choice at zero affects any positive-time density identity or spacetime integral.

The Gaussian kernel is a composition of measurable algebraic operations with the continuous exponential. Parameter integration preserves joint measurability in the remaining time and observation variables.

steps.title: Measurability of the spatial derivative
steps.body:
The derivative kernel is a continuous linear functional proportional to the inner product with the Gaussian residual:

\[D_yK_t(x,y)[v]=-\frac{K_t(x,y)}{2t}\langle y-x+t\nabla U(x),v\rangle.\]

The inner-product-to-dual map is continuous, so this is jointly strongly measurable as a continuous-linear-map-valued function. Its Bochner integral in \(x\), denoted \(A_t(y)\), remains strongly measurable. At positive times the earlier differentiation theorem identifies \(A_t=D p_t\).

The explicit spatial derivative is the kernel times a linear displacement functional. Its joint measurability and finite-dimensional coordinate integration yield a measurable mixture derivative field.

steps.title: One relative-score field for all spacetime integrals
steps.body:
Define

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+p_t(y)^{-1}\mathcal R^{-1}(A_t(y)),\]

where \(\mathcal R^{-1}\) is the inverse Riesz identification of the continuous dual with the Hilbert space. Continuous scalar multiplication, inversion as a measurable real function, and the previous measurability results make \(\mathcal S\) jointly strongly measurable.

For \(t>0\), \(p_t>0\), so the log chain rule and \(r_t=Z e^U p_t\) give

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+ abla\log p_t(y)= abla\log r_t(y).\]

Thus the measurable field is the relative score wherever it is used. Its auxiliary extension at nonpositive time introduces no analytic premise into the proof.

Dividing the mixture gradient by its strictly positive density defines one jointly measurable Lebesgue score. Adding the continuous potential gradient gives the relative score field used uniformly throughout positive-time spacetime integrals.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GibbsInterpolatio.title: A Gaussian density comparison at the initial endpoint
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GibbsInterpolatio.summary:
Assume the differentiable potential has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. For \(0<t<1/(4L)\), put \(\delta=1-4tL>0\) and \(s=t/\delta\). The smoothness inequalities compare the transition exponent weighted by Gibbs with a Gaussian exponent in the starting variable, centered at \(y-s abla U(y)\).

Completing the square leaves the term \(s\| abla U(y)\|^2/4\). Integration of the remaining Gaussian gives the normalizer ratio \((s/t)^{d/2}=\delta^{-d/2}\). Therefore the density of \( u P_t\) relative to \( u\) is at most \(\delta^{-d/2}\exp(s\| abla U(y)\|^2/4)\). This comparison supplies the reference-density correction in the initial entropy estimate, using only the stated differentiability and Lipschitz gradient assumptions.

steps.title: The Gaussian normalizer ratio
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), integration of the radial Gaussian gives \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Therefore for positive \(s,t\),

\[N_t/N_s=(s/t)^{d/2}.\]

The proof obtains the individual integrals from the finite-dimensional Gaussian integral, uses positivity to invert them, and applies the multiplication and division identities for real powers.

The normalizer scales as \(t^{-d/2}\), so replacing \(t\) by \(s=t/\delta\) contributes \((s/t)^{d/2}=\delta^{-d/2}\) when the reversed Gaussian is integrated. The direction of this ratio matters for the entropy correction's sign.

steps.title: Complete the square using only first derivatives
steps.body:
Write \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(g_y=\nabla U(y)\), and choose positive \(s,t\) with \(s(1-4tL)=t\). The smooth upper model at \(y\) bounds \(U(y)-U(x)\) by \(\langle g_y,y-x\rangle+(L/2)\|y-x\|^2\). Lipschitzness gives \(\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|\). Expanding squares and bounding their cross term yields

\[U(y)-U(x)-\frac{\|y-x+tg_x\|^2}{4t}\le-\frac{\|x-y+sg_y\|^2}{4s}+\frac s4\|g_y\|^2.\]

The relation between \(s\) and \(t\) absorbs the Lipschitz error in the negative quadratic. Exponentiation preserves order. Multiplying by the positive Gaussian normalizer rewrites this as an upper bound on the Gibbs-weighted transition kernel.

Only the first-order smooth upper model and Lipschitz gradient comparison are used. Their quadratic terms are collected into the reversed Gaussian square, leaving the explicit positive correction in the observation-gradient norm.

steps.title: Integrate the comparison against the Gibbs start
steps.body:
The relative density of the updated Gibbs law is

\[r_{ u,t}(y)=\int N_t\exp\!\left(U(y)-U(x)- rac{\|y-x+t abla U(x)\|^2}{4t} ight)dx.\]

Insert the pointwise comparison. The remaining \(x\)-dependent expression is a normalized Gaussian with time \(s\) centered at \(y-s abla U(y)\), so its integral is one. The factors independent of \(x\) give

\[r_{ u,t}(y)\le(s/t)^{d/2}\exp\!\left( rac s4\| abla U(y)\|^2 ight).\]

Normalization of the original Gibbs probability cancels its partition function. Taking \(s=t/(1-4tL)\) later supplies an explicit reference-density bound whose logarithmic cost tends to zero.

After pointwise comparison, integrate the reversed Gaussian in the starting variable. Its total mass is one after its own normalizer is inserted, yielding the density-ratio upper bound needed at the initial entropy endpoint.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/IntegratedEntropy.title: Integrating entropy dissipation with almost-everywhere derivatives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/IntegratedEntropy.summary:
Suppose the entropy is locally absolutely continuous on positive-time compact intervals and satisfies an affine differential inequality almost everywhere. Multiplication by the exponential integrating factor and the fundamental theorem of calculus give the corresponding affine comparison on each such interval.

At the lower endpoint use an explicit upper bound \(H(s)\le M(s)\), where \(M\) is continuous at zero. Sending \(s\downarrow0\) gives the comparison with \(M(0)\), without requiring continuity or differentiability of \(H\) at zero. Applying this argument to the Fisher dissipation and gradient-moment estimates, then using the stated step restriction, proves the one-step bound with forcing \(6h^2dL^2\).

steps.title: Integrate the affine differential inequality
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on \([s,t]\) and \(H^{\prime}\le-aH+b\) almost everywhere, with \(a>0\). Set \(F(u)=e^{au}(H(u)-b/a)\). Products of absolutely continuous functions on a compact interval are absolutely continuous. The product rule holds almost everywhere and gives \(F^{\prime}(u)=e^{au}(a(H(u)-b/a)+H^{\prime}(u))\le0\).

The fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions gives \(F(t)-F(s)=\int_s^tF^{\prime}\le0\). Multiply by \(e^{-at}>0\), cancel the exponentials, and rearrange:

\[H(t)\le e^{-a(t-s)}H(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(t-s)}).\]

The proof removes no exceptional set by assuming a derivative there; both differentiability and the inequality are used only almost everywhere.

Local absolute continuity gives an integrable derivative and the fundamental theorem on each positive compact interval. Multiplying by the smooth integrating factor preserves absolute continuity, so integrating its almost-everywhere derivative bound is legitimate.

steps.title: Send the positive initial time to zero
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on every \([s,T]\), \(0<s<T\), and \(H(s)\le M(s)\) for all sufficiently small positive \(s\). If \(M\) is continuous at zero, the preceding estimate gives

\[H(T)\le e^{-a(T-s)}M(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(T-s)}).\]

The right side tends to \(e^{-aT}M(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-aT})\). Order is preserved under limits, giving the desired initial-endpoint bound. Single endpoints have zero Lebesgue measure, so an inequality on the open interval suffices. Continuity or differentiability of \(H\) at zero is not needed.

The upper initial majorant converges to the finite initial entropy. Applying it at the lower positive endpoint and sending that endpoint to zero therefore bounds the limiting comparison term from above, which is all the scalar inequality requires.

steps.title: Absorb the ULA forcing with its exact constants
steps.body:
Assume \(2\alpha H\le I\), \(H^{\prime}\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\), and \(G_0\le4L^2M(0)/\alpha+2dL\). Let \(0<h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\), \(0<\alpha\le L\), and \(M(0)\ge0\). Then \(hL\le1/4\), \(\alpha h\le1/4\),

\[h^2L^2(4L^2/\alpha)\le\alpha/4,\qquad h^2L^2(2dL)\le hdL^2/2.\]

The derivative is therefore at most \(-3\alpha H/2+B\), where \(B=\alpha M(0)/4+(5/2)hdL^2\). The affine comparison and \(1-e^{-ah}\le ah\) imply \(H(h)\le e^{-3\alpha h/2}M(0)+Bh\). Finally \(e^{-x}\ge e^{-3x/2}+x/4\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\) absorbs the entropy part of \(Bh\). Bounding \(5/2\) by 6 gives

\[H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}M(0)+6h^2dL^2.\]

The probability-law convergence theorem supplies each of these analytic hypotheses before applying this scalar estimate.

The time-dependent forcing is first bounded uniformly using \(t\le h\). The initial-entropy contribution is absorbed by the exponential gap, while the dimensional forcing integrates to a multiple of \(h^2dL^2\), giving the stated one-step coefficient.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Compatibility.lea.title: Why the LSI constant cannot exceed smoothness
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Compatibility.lea.summary:
Let \( u(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) on a nontrivial finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Suppose \(U\) is differentiable, \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and the target satisfies the stated positive \(C^1\)-density log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\). Then \(\alpha\le L\). No position moment, Hessian, or strong convexity is assumed.

For bounded \(C^1\) tests with \(\| abla f\|\le D\), apply the inequality to normalized exponential tilts. The small-tilt limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\le D^2\). For a unit vector \(v\), Gibbs integration by parts applied to \(\sin(t\langle v,x angle)\), together with the directional score second-moment bound \(L\), gives \(\alpha(\int\cos(t\langle v,x angle)d u)^2\le L\). Bounded convergence as \(t\downarrow0\) proves the conclusion without integrability of \(x\).

steps.title: Integrability of bounded exponential tests
steps.body:
If \(|f|\le B\), then \(tf\le |t|B\), so \(0<e^{tf}\le e^{|t|B}\). The right side is an integrable constant under every finite measure. Measurability follows from that of \(f\); integrable domination then proves integrability of the exponential. This establishes the whole real line as the domain of the moment generating function used below.

Boundedness of the test gives \(e^{sf}\le e^{|s|\|f\|_\infty}\). This constant is integrable under the target probability, uniformly for \(s\) in a compact interval, allowing derivatives of its moment generating function.

steps.title: Testing LSI with a normalized exponential tilt
steps.body:
Let \(f\) be bounded and \(C^1\), with \(\| abla f\|\le D\). Put \(M(t)=\int e^{tf}d u\), \(\psi(t)=\log M(t)\), and \(r_t=e^{tf}/M(t)\). Boundedness of \(f\) gives \(0<M(t)<\infty\). Thus \(r_t\) is a positive \(C^1\) probability density relative to \( u\).

Its logarithm is \(tf-\psi(t)\). Differentiation under the bounded exponential integral gives \(\int fr_td u=\psi'(t)\), so

\[H(r_t u\mid u)=t\psi'(t)-\psi(t).\]

This entropy is finite because its integrand is bounded under the tilted probability. The logarithmic gradient is \(t abla f\); its squared norm is at most \(t^2D^2\), so Fisher information is also finite. Applying the log-Sobolev inequality to this density gives

\[2\alpha igl(t\psi'(t)-\psi(t) igr)\le t^2D^2.\]

The finite entropy and Fisher bounds justify this ordinary real-valued inequality for every scalar tilt.

steps.title: The small-tilt entropy quotient
steps.body:
For a \(C^3\) scalar function \(\psi\) with \(\psi(0)=0\), both numerator and denominator of \((t\psi'(t)-\psi(t))/t^2\) tend to zero as \(t\downarrow0\). The product rule cancels the two copies of \(\psi'(t)\), leaving numerator derivative \(t\psi''(t)\); the denominator derivative is \(2t\). On the punctured right neighborhood, their quotient equals \(\psi''(t)/2\). Continuity of the second derivative and one application of l'Hopital's rule prove the limit \(\psi''(0)/2\). The proof explicitly supplies the nonzero denominator derivative and both zero limits.

The constant and first-order terms cancel in \(s\Lambda'(s)-\Lambda(s)\). Its leading term is \(s^2\Lambda''(0)/2\), where \(\Lambda''(0)\) is the variance of the bounded test.

steps.title: A variance bound for bounded differentiable tests
steps.body:
For bounded \(f\), its moment and cumulant generating functions are analytic on all real parameters. The standard second derivative formula at zero is \(\psi''(0)=\int f^2\,d u-(\int f\,d u)^2\), since \(M(0)=1\). This computes the variance limit directly from the bounded exponential tests.

Divide the exponential-test inequality by \(t^2>0\), for \(t>0\), and use the second-order small-tilt entropy expansion. The left side tends to \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\), while the right side remains \(D^2\). Passing to the limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\le D^2\). The boundedness and gradient-bound hypotheses here describe this test function; they are not additional assumptions on the target.

Dividing the tilted LSI by \(s^2\) and taking the small-tilt limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}(f)\le D^2\). The bounded test class makes this step independent of unknown position moments.

steps.title: Weighted Gibbs integration
steps.body:
Unfold \(\nu=Z^{-1}(e^{-U}dx)\). Scalar multiplication of a measure multiplies its real Bochner integral by \((Z^{-1})\). The weighted-density integral formula then gives \(\int g\,d\nu=(Z^{-1})\int e^{-U}g\,dx\). Continuity of \(U\) makes the weight measurable, and its pointwise value is finite. This equality concerns total integrals; integrability for its later uses is established separately.

The Gibbs change of measure inserts its ordinary positive density into the Lebesgue integral. This is the form in which the weighted derivative identity can be integrated by parts.

steps.title: Weighted Gibbs integrability
steps.body:
Strict positivity of the Gibbs partition follows from differentiability of \(U\); the hypothesis here also excludes an infinite partition. Consequently multiplication of the weighted Lebesgue measure by \(Z^{-1}\) preserves integrability in both directions. The weighted-density integrability equivalence then gives \(g\in L^1(\nu)\) exactly when \(e^{-U}g\in L^1(dx)\). This is the justification for moving the bounded-test integration-by-parts calculation to Lebesgue measure.

The bounded test and gradient bounds, together with finite score energy, control the weighted test-score products. These integrability checks justify the Gibbs integration-by-parts identity on the noncompact state space.

steps.title: The Gibbs integration-by-parts identity for bounded tests
steps.body:
Let \(\psi\) be bounded and \(C^1\) with bounded gradient, and fix a vector \(v\). The directional score \(\langle abla U,v angle\) is integrable by the previously established exponential-moment bound. Therefore the test-score product is integrable. Boundedness of the directional derivative of \(\psi\) also gives its integrability under \( u\).

The Gibbs change of measure makes the three functions \(\psi e^{-U}\), \((D_v\psi)e^{-U}\), and \(\psi D_v(e^{-U})\) integrable under Lebesgue measure. Since

\[D_v(e^{-U})=-e^{-U}\langle abla U,v angle,\]

the global integration-by-parts identity gives \(\int(D_v\psi)e^{-U}dx=\int\psi e^{-U}\langle abla U,v angle dx\). Multiplication by the positive Gibbs normalizer yields

\[\mathbb E_ u\langle abla\psi,v angle=\mathbb E_ u igl[\psi\langle abla U,v angle igr].\]

The weighted integrability conditions justify this identity on the whole state space. No position moment or separately imposed boundary value is used.

steps.title: The sine-score covariance bound
steps.body:
For real \(L^2\) functions \(f,g\), Holder's inequality proves \(fg\in L^1\); their squares are integrable as well. For every real \(c\), integrate \((cf+g)^2\ge0\) to obtain the quadratic \((\int f^2)c^2+2(\int fg)c+\int g^2\ge0\). Its discriminant is nonpositive. Dividing the resulting algebraic inequality by four gives \((\int fg)^2\le(\int f^2)(\int g^2)\). This elementary squared Cauchy-Schwarz form avoids square roots in the compatibility argument.

Center the bounded sine test before applying Cauchy–Schwarz against the centered directional score. The score variance bound and the bounded-test variance estimate then control the square of their covariance.

steps.title: Compatibility of LSI and smoothness constants
steps.body:
Choose \(\|v\|=1\), possible because the space is nontrivial. Put \(s(x)=\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\). The score MGF gives \(\mathbb E s^2\le L\); the bounded Stein identity with \(\psi=1\) gives \(\mathbb E s=0\).

For \(t>0\), use the bounded test \(f_t(x)=\sin(t\langle v,x\rangle)\). Its gradient is \(t\cos(t\langle v,x\rangle)v\), so its norm is at most \(|t|\). The bounded-test variance theorem gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\le t^2\). Stein's identity and score centering give \(\mathbb E[s(f_t-\mathbb Ef_t)]=t\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle)\). Squared Cauchy-Schwarz now yields \(t^2(\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle))^2\le L\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\).

Multiply by \(\alpha\ge0\), insert the variance bound, and cancel \(t^2>0\). This proves \(\alpha(\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle))^2\le L\). Dominated convergence applies because cosine is bounded by one and tends pointwise to one as \(t\downarrow0\). Its expectation tends to one, proving \(\alpha\le L\). No integrability of \(X\) itself is needed.

For the unit direction, the derivative of the sine test is \(t\cos(t\langle v,x\rangle)\). Cancelling the positive factor \(t^2\) gives the cosine inequality, and bounded convergence sends its expectation to one.

steps.title: The positive-dimensional compatibility conclusion
steps.body:
This result removes two temporary restrictions from the previous proof. If \(\alpha<0\), then \(\alpha\le0\le L\) immediately. Otherwise, LSI includes the assertion that the Gibbs law is a probability measure. An infinite partition would make its normalizing scalar zero and hence make the Gibbs measure zero, contradicting mass one. Thus the partition is finite, and the nonnegative-constant compatibility theorem applies. The final hypotheses are precisely LSI, differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, finite dimension, and a nontrivial state space.

In positive dimension a unit vector exists, so the preceding directional argument proves \(\alpha\le L\). In the singleton case no unit direction is available; the final entropy theorem handles that case directly with zero KL.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianTimeDeriv.title: Time differentiation and local space-time integrability of the Gaussian mixture
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianTimeDeriv.summary:
Let \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(c_t(x)=x-tg_x\), and \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). At \(t>0\), differentiation of the normalizer and exponent gives \(\partial_tK_t=K_t[-d/(2t)+\|y-x\|^2/(4t^2)-\|g_x\|^2/4]\). No derivative of \(g_x\) is taken.

Assume \(G_0=\int\|g_x\|^2d\mu<\infty\). On a neighborhood of each positive time, a bound by a constant multiple of \(1+\|g_x\|^2\) justifies differentiation under the initial-law integral and proves \(\partial_tp_t(y)=\int\partial_tK_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). Retaining the Gaussian factor instead gives a bound integrable in both starting point and observation. Its explicit integral proves local space-time integrability of \(\partial_tp_t\) on intervals bounded away from zero. The entropy chain rule uses these estimates after initial gradient energy has been deduced from finite initial relative entropy.

steps.title: The Gaussian normalizer as an explicit time power
steps.body:
The proposal normalizer is defined as the reciprocal of the Gaussian integral. Gaussian Fourier integration evaluates \(\int e^{-a\|z\|^2}dz=(\pi/a)^{d/2}\) for \(a>0\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\), simplify \(\pi/a=4\pi t\), and invert the real power to obtain \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Positivity of \(t\) justifies the Gaussian formula and the real-power inversion.

The Gaussian normalizer has time dependence \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Expressing it as a real power separates the positive constant from the time power and permits ordinary scalar differentiation.

steps.title: The time derivative of the Gaussian normalizer
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\). On a neighborhood of \(t\), every time \(s\) remains positive, and the Gaussian integral formula gives \(N_s=(4\pi s)^{-d/2}\). The real-power chain rule therefore gives

\[N_t'=(-d/2)(4\pi t)^{-d/2-1}(4\pi).\]

Because \(4\pi t>0\), the identity \((4\pi t)^{p-1}=(4\pi t)^p/(4\pi t)\) is valid. Substituting \(p=-d/2\) simplifies the derivative to

\[N_t'=-\frac d{2t}N_t.\]

The local equality with the explicit power transfers this derivative to the normalizer defined by the Gaussian integral. Thus the density normalization contributes logarithmic derivative \(-d/(2t)\).

steps.title: The frozen-drift Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The real component kernel is \(K_t(x,y)=N_t\exp(-\|y-x+tg_x\|^2/(4t))\). The gradient \(g_x\) is evaluated at the initial state \(x\), and is constant when differentiating in \(t\) or \(y\). Its integral over \(y\) is one at positive time by the previously proved Gaussian proposal normalization.

The frozen kernel is the Gaussian density conditional on the initial state. Its center moves linearly with time through the fixed vector \(\nabla U(x)\), while its covariance grows as \(2tI_d\).

steps.title: Its explicit candidate time derivative
steps.body:
Define the explicit candidate derivative \(\dot K_t=K_t[-d/(2t)+\|y-x\|^2/(4t^2)-\|g_x\|^2/4]\). The dimension term comes from the normalizer; the remaining terms come from differentiating the exponent. In the expanded exponent, the mixed inner-product term is independent of time, which explains its absence from this expression. The following theorem verifies that this formula is the derivative.

The derivative field is defined by the explicit normalizer and exponent formula. Naming this function before differentiation makes later measurability and integrability statements refer to one fixed spacetime integrand.

steps.title: Expanding the frozen Gaussian exponent
steps.body:
Set \(z=y-x\). The squared-norm identity gives \(\|z+sg_x\|^2=\|z\|^2+2s\langle z,g_x\rangle+s^2\|g_x\|^2\). For \(s\ne0\), division by \(-4s\) yields \(-\|z+sg_x\|^2/(4s)=-\|z\|^2/(4s)-\langle z,g_x\rangle/2-s\|g_x\|^2/4\). The vector identity and scalar denominator cancellation are proved separately in the proof calculation.

Expanding \(\|y-x+t g\|^2\) and dividing by \(4t\) yields \(\|y-x\|^2/(4t)+\langle y-x,g\rangle/2+t\|g\|^2/4\). The middle term has zero time derivative, simplifying the formula.

steps.title: Differentiating the frozen Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
Write the expanded exponent as \(-A/s-B-sC\), where \(A=\|y-x\|^2/4\), \(B=\langle y-x,g_x\rangle/2\), and \(C=\|g_x\|^2/4\). Its derivative at positive \(t\) is \(A/t^2-C\). The expansion agrees with the original exponent on a neighborhood avoiding zero, so this is also the derivative of the original expression.

Apply the exponential chain rule and multiply by the normalizer. Its derivative contributes \(-dK_t/(2t)\); the exponential derivative contributes \(K_t(A/t^2-C)\). Collecting terms gives exactly its explicit time derivative. No derivative of \(g_x\), and therefore no Hessian, is taken.

Combine the normalizer derivative with the derivative of the expanded exponent. The cross term contributes no time derivative, leaving exactly the stated squared-position and squared-gradient terms.

steps.title: An absolute bound on the kernel time derivative
steps.body:
Put \(r=y-x+tg_x\) and \(e=e^{-\|r\|^2/(4t)}\). The triangle inequality and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\). The Gaussian exponential bound gives \(\|r\|^2e\le4t\), while \(e\le1\). Consequently \(\|y-x\|^2e\le8t+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\).

Bound the absolute value of each derivative-coefficient term by their nonnegative sum, multiply by \(e\), and insert these bounds. The resulting upper bound is \(|\dot K_t(x,y)|\le N_t[(d+4)/t+\|g_x\|^2]\). It is uniform in \(y\), and is integrable in the initial variable whenever \(G_0<\infty\). Its purpose is time differentiation under the initial-state integral, and will be replaced by a Gaussian-weighted bound for output-space integration.

Take absolute values term by term in the explicit derivative. Nonnegativity of the kernel allows its factor to be retained, producing a sum of Gaussian-weighted nonnegative energy terms.

steps.title: Measurability of the normalizer
steps.body:
At positive time the Gaussian normalizer has the continuous explicit form \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\), hence is measurable. Assigning an arbitrary value at zero gives a measurable extension if a whole-time parameter field is desired. Only the positive-time values are used in the Gaussian density and derivative identities.

At positive time the normalizer is continuous, hence measurable. Its reciprocal-power expression also permits a measurable extension when the proof organizes all times in one ambient domain.

steps.title: Joint measurability of the kernel time derivative
steps.body:
Lipschitzness makes \(x\mapsto g_x\) continuous and measurable. Combine this with the measurable normalizer and the explicit algebraic formula for \(\dot K_t\). Products, norms, scalar inverses, and exponentials preserve measurability, giving joint measurability in \((t,y,x)\). This is the input needed to integrate out the initial variable while retaining measurable time-space dependence.

The explicit derivative uses only measurable gradient, norms, scalar operations, and the Gaussian exponential. Their composition is jointly measurable in time, initial state, and observation.

steps.title: The candidate time derivative of the mixture
steps.body:
Define \(\dot p_t(y)=\int\dot K_t(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\). At this point it is an ordinary parameter integral. The subsequent differentiation theorem proves it is the derivative of \(p_t(y)\), and the energy estimates prove its integrability, so differentiation and integrability remain conclusions to prove.

Integrating the explicit kernel derivative over the initial probability defines the candidate mixture time derivative. Its later identification as a derivative requires the uniform integrable bound proved separately.

steps.title: Joint measurability of the mixture derivative
steps.body:
The component derivative is jointly measurable in \((t,y,x)\). Its strongly measurable parameter integral over the probability measure \(\mu\) is therefore measurable in \((t,y)\). This gives a single measurable version of \(\dot p\) for spacetime Fubini and the entropy chain rule.

Parameter integration of the jointly measurable derivative field gives a measurable candidate in time and observation. Absolute integrability, when invoked later, ensures it is also the ordinary integral required by the chain rule.

steps.title: The time derivative of the mixture
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\). Continuity of \(N_s\) gives a neighborhood \(S\) of \(t\) on which \(s>t/2\) and \(N_s<N_t+1\). The derivative bound implies, for every \(s\in S\) and fixed observation \(y\),

\[|\dot K_s(x,y)|\le(N_t+1)\left[\frac{2(d+4)}t+\|g_x\|^2\right].\]

The right side is integrable in \(x\) because \(G_0<\infty\) and \(\mu\) is a probability. The component kernel at \(t\) is also integrable, since it is bounded by \(N_t\). Each component has the time derivative already computed.

Differentiation under an integral with this common integrable derivative bound gives both integrability of \(\dot K_t(\cdot,y)\) and

\[\frac{d}{dt}\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)=\int\dot K_t(x,y)d\mu(x).\]

The integral on the left agrees with the mixture density on the positive-time neighborhood. Hence \(\partial_tp_t(y)=\dot p_t(y)\) at every observation. This argument does not require invertibility of the Euler map or a step-size restriction.

steps.title: Equality of the two Gaussian kernel formulas
steps.body:
The spatial Fisher calculation uses precision notation \(q_a(c,y)=Z_a^{-1}e^{-a\|y-c\|^2}\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\) and \(c=x-tg_x\). The normalizers agree by definition, and \(-a\|y-c\|^2=-\|y-c\|^2/(4t)\). This pointwise identity makes the time and spatial calculations use precisely the same normalized Gaussian kernel.

Both kernels have the same Gaussian center and covariance. Substituting their normalizers and exponents proves equality pointwise, allowing spatial and time results developed in the two notations to be combined.

steps.title: A weighted derivative bound
steps.body:
Retain the Gaussian factor instead of replacing it by its supremum. With \(r=y-x+tg_x\), the bound \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\) implies that the absolute derivative coefficient is at most \(d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2\). Multiplication by \(K_t\ge0\) yields \(|\dot K_t|\le K_t[d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2]\). Unlike the initial-variable envelope, this bound remains integrable in the output variable.

The weighted bound retains the kernel's Gaussian decay and separates the initial-gradient square from displacement-dependent terms. This is the form suitable for integrating first in the observation.

steps.title: A Gaussian weight controlling the time derivative
steps.body:
Define the nonnegative weight \(\mathcal E_t(x,y)=K_t(x,y)(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2)\). Its three terms correspond to Gaussian mass, initial gradient energy, and Gaussian displacement energy. This weight dominates the derivative with a time-dependent scalar coefficient and can also be reused in spatial integration by parts.

The energy combines one, displacement square, and initial-gradient square under the Gaussian kernel. These are chosen to dominate every polynomial term appearing in the explicit time derivative.

steps.title: Nonnegativity of the Gaussian weight
steps.body:
At positive time the normalizer and the Gaussian exponential are positive, so \(K_t\ge0\). Every term in \(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonnegative. Their product is nonnegative; this identifies its norm with itself in the Fubini integrability proof.

Every component is a nonnegative square or constant multiplied by a nonnegative kernel. Their sum is therefore nonnegative, permitting nonnegative Fubini before finiteness is established.

steps.title: The component energy integral
steps.body:
For fixed \(x\), Gaussian normalization gives \(\int K_t(x,y)dy=1\), and the centered Gaussian covariance gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\|y-c_t(x)\|^2dy=2td\). Both integrands are integrable. The initial gradient factor is constant in \(y\), so its integral is \(\|g_x\|^2\). Expand the common energy into these three integrable terms to obtain \(\int\mathcal E_t(x,y)dy=1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\).

For each fixed initial state, integrate the kernel to one and its displacement square using the Gaussian moment formula. The resulting expression depends only on time, dimension, and the initial-gradient norm.

steps.title: Integrability of the Gaussian weight in both variables
steps.body:
The common energy is jointly measurable. For every initial \(x\), its output section is integrable by the component energy theorem. Since the energy is nonnegative, the integral of its norm is exactly \(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\), an integrable function of \(x\) under the probability law \(\mu\). The product integrability criterion therefore proves \(\mathcal E_t\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\).

The initial-gradient square is integrable by the score-energy hypothesis, and all remaining terms are finite constants. The component integral calculation therefore proves integrability of the full pair energy.

steps.title: The integral of the Gaussian weight
steps.body:
Joint integrability allows Fubini, giving \(\int\mathcal E_t\,d(\mu\otimes dy)=\int(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td)d\mu(x)\). Probability normalization and the definition of \(G_0\) reduce this to \(1+G_0+2td\). The displayed equality supplies a finite quantitative bound, in addition to proving integrability.

Integrating the component formula over the starting law replaces the squared gradient by \(G_0\). This gives an explicit finite energy expression, retaining its time dependence for uniform compact-interval estimates.

steps.title: A uniform coefficient on a positive time interval
steps.body:
Set \(C_t=d/(2t)+1/(2t^2)+1\). It is positive for \(t>0\), and is bounded above on any interval \([a,b]\) with \(a>0\) by \(C_a\). This finite coefficient suffices for the local space-time integrability required by the entropy chain rule.

On a positive compact interval, \(t\) is bounded above and \(1/t\) is bounded above by the reciprocal of the lower endpoint. One coefficient can therefore dominate all scalar time factors uniformly.

steps.title: Derivative domination by the Gaussian weight
steps.body:
In the weighted derivative bound, denote the three nonnegative coefficients by \(A=d/(2t)\), \(B=1/(2t^2)\), and \(1\). Each is at most \(C_t=A+B+1\). Therefore \(A+B\|r\|^2+\|g_x\|^2\le C_t(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|r\|^2)\). Multiply by \(K_t\ge0\) to prove \(|\dot K_t|\le C_t\mathcal E_t\).

Multiply that coefficient by the nonnegative Gaussian weight. The pointwise derivative bound then holds throughout the interval with one common integrable function, which is the domination hypothesis for the space-time integral.

steps.title: Integrability of the kernel time derivative
steps.body:
The component time derivative is jointly measurable, and its norm is bounded by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The common energy is integrable on \(\mu\otimes dy\), and \(C_t\) is a finite scalar at positive time. Domination therefore proves joint integrability of \(\dot K_t\), which licenses the changes of integration order used in the time weak equation.

The energy envelope has finite pair integral and the derivative is measurable. Absolute-value domination consequently proves integrability of the kernel time derivative under the Gaussian pair measure.

steps.title: Spatial integrability of the mixture derivative
steps.body:
Fubini applied to the jointly integrable component derivative first gives \(\dot p_t\in L^1(dy)\). The norm inequality for Bochner integration gives \(|\dot p_t(y)|\le\int|\dot K_t(x,y)|d\mu(x)\). Integrate in \(y\), exchange the two integrals, and dominate by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The exact envelope integral yields \(\int|\dot p_t(y)|dy\le C_t(1+G_0+2td)\).

The norm of the mixture derivative is at most the mixture of the kernel derivative norms. Fubini and the finite pair bound therefore give spatial integrability after the initial state is averaged out.

steps.title: Spacetime integrability of the mixture derivative
steps.body:
Joint measurability of \(\dot p\) permits the product integrability criterion on \([a,b]\times E\), where \(a>0\). Every time section is in \(L^1(dy)\). For times in the interval, \(C_t\le C_a\) and \(1+G_0+2td\le1+G_0+2bd\), giving the common finite scalar bound \(\int|\dot p_t|dy\le C_a(1+G_0+2bd)\). The time interval has finite measure, so the section norms are integrable. Hence \(\dot p\in L^1(dt\,dy)\) locally away from zero. If \(a>b\), the restricted time measure is zero and the same argument remains valid.

The uniform compact-time coefficient and the energy integral provide an integrable time majorant. Integrating that majorant over the finite interval proves the full spacetime \(L^1\) estimate used by bounded entropy calculus.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEnergyInt.title: Relative Fisher information and the frozen-gradient error
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEnergyInt.summary:
Let \( ho_t\) be the frozen Gaussian interpolation, \(r_t=d ho_t/d u\), \(s_t= abla\log r_t\), and \(G_0=\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu<\infty\). The decomposition \(s_t= abla\log p_t+ abla U\), the Gaussian score estimate, and the propagated gradient moment give

\[I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t.\]

This estimate is uniformly finite on positive compact time intervals and proves local space-time integrability of \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\) under \(dt\,d u\). The same intervals have integrable frozen-gradient discrepancy, with the bound \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). Changing variables to the initial/output pair law gives the identical bound with Gaussian kernel weight. These two energies justify the score pairings and removal of bounded-log tests.

steps.title: A square bound for the sum of two vectors
steps.body:
The triangle inequality gives \(\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|\). Square both nonnegative sides and use \(2\|x\|\|y\|\le\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2\), which follows from \((\|x\|-\|y\|)^2\ge0\). This proves \(\|x+y\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2\), the pointwise estimate used to split relative Fisher energy.

Expand \(\|a+b\|^2\), bound the mixed term by \(2\|a\|\|b\|\), and use \(2uv\le u^2+v^2\). This gives the factor two without requiring any relation between the vectors.

steps.title: Splitting the relative-score energy
steps.body:
The jointly measurable score field agrees at positive time with the relative score. Its decomposition is \(s_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t\). The propagated gradient is square integrable, and Gaussian smoothing gives \(\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le d/(2t)\). These facts also prove integrability of the relative-score square.

Apply the squared sum bound pointwise and integrate: \(I_t\le2G_t+2\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le2G_t+d/t\). The proof keeps the integrability witnesses for all terms before using integral monotonicity.

Split the relative score into the Lebesgue score and potential gradient. The preceding square inequality bounds its energy by twice each component energy, which are estimated by Gaussian smoothing and propagated score moments.

steps.title: An explicit finite relative-score energy bound
steps.body:
The interpolation gradient-moment estimate is \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\). Substitute it into \(I_t\le2G_t+d/t\) and distribute the factor two. This gives \(I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t\). Every quantity on the right is determined by the initial gradient energy and the original potential; no entropy-production assumption is used.

Insert the Gaussian Fisher bound \(d/(2t)\) and the propagated gradient estimate. The result is finite at each positive time and uniformly integrable on intervals bounded away from zero.

steps.title: The weighted density representation of score energy
steps.body:
The explicitly constructed relative density satisfies \(r_t u= ho_t\). The weighted-density integrability equivalence therefore transports integrability of \(\|s_t\|^2\) under \( ho_t\) to integrability of \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\) under the fixed target \( u\). The corresponding integral identity is \(\int r_t\|s_t\|^2d u=\int\|s_t\|^2d ho_t\). Strict positivity and measurability of the constructed density justify the ordinary weighted-integral formulas.

Changing from the proposed law to its density multiplies the score square by \(p_t\), or by \(r_t\) under Gibbs. These are equivalent representations of the same finite energy.

steps.title: Spacetime integrability of relative-score energy
steps.body:
The relative density and the chosen relative-score field are jointly measurable in time and space. Their weighted energy is nonnegative. On a positive interval \([a,b]\), the section at every time is integrable by the density-change theorem.

Since \(0<a\le t\le b\), the quantitative estimate is bounded uniformly by \(4(1+L^2b^2)G_0+8bdL^2+d/a\). The integral of the section norm is exactly its nonnegative energy, so this finite scalar bound makes it integrable in time. The product criterion yields \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\in L^1(dt\,d\nu)\) on the interval. This is the spacetime dominating function required to pass from bounded entropy tests to the full relative Fisher term.

The explicit time bound is a sum of powers of time and \(1/t\). On a positive compact interval each is integrable, proving spacetime square integrability of the measurable relative-score field.

steps.title: The frozen-gradient discrepancy on the independent-noise space
steps.body:
For the fixed independent pair \((X,Z)\sim\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\), define \(e_t(X,Z)= abla U(X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z)- abla U(X)\). The underlying probability space is independent of time. This avoids assuming a jointly measurable choice of a state-space conditional expectation when integrating the error energy over time.

The discrepancy is evaluated at the independent-noise proposal and its initial state. Its measurability follows from the continuous gradient and update map, fixing one field for subsequent pair integrals.

steps.title: Spacetime integrability of discrepancy energy
steps.body:
The proposal and Lipschitz gradient make \((t,X,Z)\mapsto\|e_t(X,Z)\|^2\) jointly measurable. For \(t\ge0\), the exact Gaussian calculation already gives integrability and \(\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). On a compact nonnegative time interval this is at most \(L^2(b^2G_0+2bd)\). The time measure is finite, so Fubini's integrability criterion proves the squared error is integrable on the time/initial-state/noise product.

The pointwise gradient Lipschitz estimate bounds its square by \(L^2\) times displacement square. The exact displacement formula is polynomial in time with finite coefficients, giving an integrable spacetime energy.

steps.title: The gradient-error energy under the Gaussian pair law
steps.body:
Map the independent initial/noise pair by \(T_t(x,z)=(x,x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z)\). The squared error as a function of the output pair is \(F(x,y)=\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2\). Its composition with \(T_t\) is exactly the frozen-gradient discrepancy from the Gaussian energy calculation. Measurability of \(T_t\) and continuity of \(F\) let the map-measure integrability and integral theorems transport both the integrability witness and the bound \(L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\) to the initial/output pair law.

The pair-law change of variables transports the discrepancy energy from independent noise to the Gaussian starting-observation pair. Because the integrand is nonnegative, the identity can be established before signed Fubini is needed.

steps.title: The kernel representation of gradient-error energy
steps.body:
The pair law is identified with \(K_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)dy\) by the previously proved Gaussian proposal pair-density theorem. The proof specializes its measurable center to \(x-t abla U(x)\); the precision and step-size versions of the kernel agree pointwise.

Rewrite the pair-law energy theorem using this exact density identity. The weighted-density integrability equivalence gives \(K_t\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\), and its integral formula gives the sharp bound \(\int K_t\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2d\mu\,dy\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The change of measure preserves the constants in this error-energy bound, which are used in the entropy recurrence.

Rewriting the pair measure using its conditional Gaussian density gives the kernel-weighted energy. Thus the same sharp bound is available in the weak PDE's Lebesgue integral representation.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianScorePair.title: Averaging the Gaussian component score
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianScorePair.summary:
At positive time the Gaussian component score is \(S_{t,x}(y)=-(y-x+t abla U(x))/(2t)\). Differentiation of the mixture and positivity of \(p_t\) give \(p_t abla\log p_t=\int K_tS_{t,x}d\mu\). For a continuous field \(V\in L^2( ho_t)\), this identity may be paired with \(V\) and integrated.

Under the initial/output pair law, the component score has energy \(d/(2t)\), and \(V(y)\) has the same energy as under \( ho_t\). Cauchy–Schwarz therefore proves absolute integrability before Fubini is used. The resulting identity equates the kernel-weighted component-score pairing with the mixture-score pairing. Changing variables to \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\) expresses the same pairing on the fixed independent initial/noise space used for entropy production.

steps.title: The score of one Gaussian component
steps.body:
For a fixed initial state \(x\), the Gaussian proposal has center \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\). Its score in the proposed state is \(S_{t,x}(y)=\nabla_y\log K_t(x,y)=-(y-c_t(x))/(2t)\). This definition is an explicit affine vector field. It is different from the mixture score, which averages this field over the posterior initial-state distribution.

Differentiate the logarithm of one Gaussian component in the observation variable. The normalizer is constant in that variable, leaving the negative centered displacement divided by \(2t\).

steps.title: Square-integrability of the component score
steps.body:
Represent the initial/output pair as \((X,Y_t)\), with \(Y_t=c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\) and independent standard Gaussian \(Z\). Substituting into the component score cancels the center: \(S_{t,X}(Y_t)=-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z\). The Gaussian identity random variable is square integrable; scalar multiplication and pullback to the product preserve this property. The map-measure theorem transfers it to the pair law. No initial position or gradient moment is needed for this component score.

Under the independent-noise representation the centered component displacement is \(\sqrt{2t}Z\). Its score energy is therefore \(d/(2t)\), finite for every positive time.

steps.title: Pulling a finite-energy state field to the pair space
steps.body:
If \(V\in L^2(\rho_t)\), then \(V(Y_t)\in L^2(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I))\), because \(\rho_t\) is the pushforward by the proposal. Map the independent pair to \((X,Y_t)\); a second application of the map-measure equivalence gives \((x,y)\mapsto V(y)\in L^2\) under the pair law. Continuity of \(V\) supplies the measurability required in both transfers.

A state-space field with finite square energy under \(\rho_t\) has the same square energy when composed with the proposed coordinate on the joint pair. This is pushforward change of variables.

steps.title: Integrability of the score-test pairing
steps.body:
The component score and the state field \(V(y)\) are both square integrable under the pair law. Holder's inequality makes the product of their norms integrable, and \(|\langle S,V\rangle|\le\|S\|\|V\|\) proves integrability of their inner product. The exact pair-density identity then rewrites this law as \(K_t(x,y)\mu(dx)dy\). The weighted-density equivalence gives joint integrability of \(K_t\langle S_{t,x},V(y)\rangle\) under \(\mu\otimes dy\), which is the hypothesis needed for Fubini in the averaging calculation.

Cauchy–Schwarz on the pair probability bounds the absolute pairing integral by the product of component-score and state-field \(L^2\) norms. Hence the signed pairing is integrable before its order is exchanged.

steps.title: The weighted mixture-score identity
steps.body:
The already constructed spatial derivative of the Gaussian mixture identifies its score as the posterior mean of the component score. The posterior density in \(x\) is \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\), where \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)>0\). Substitute this explicit weighted-density formula into the posterior integral and multiply by \(p_t(y)\). The common denominator cancels pointwise, giving \(p_t(y) abla\log p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)S_{t,x}(y)d\mu(x)\). The precision and step-size forms have equal Gaussian normalizers, so this identity follows from the previously proved mixture derivative formula.

Integrating the component gradient over the starting law gives \( abla p_t\). Dividing by the positive mixture identifies its averaged score with \( abla\log p_t\), the posterior-score identity in weighted form.

steps.title: Integrability of the kernel-weighted score pairing
steps.body:
The component score is \(L^2\) under the pair probability law, hence is also \(L^1\). Identify that law with its explicit density \(K_t\) under \(\mu\otimes dy\). The vector-valued weighted-density integrability theorem gives \((x,y)\mapsto K_t(x,y)S_{t,x}(y)\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\). In particular, Fubini supplies integrability of the vector section in \(x\) for almost every output \(y\); this is needed before moving an inner product through its integral.

The Gaussian score has finite square norm and the tested state field has finite square norm. Their product is therefore integrable, supplying the precise Fubini hypothesis for the following averaging identity.

steps.title: Averaging the Gaussian component score
steps.body:
For almost every \(y\), vector-section integrability permits the linear functional \(w\mapsto\langle w,V(y)\rangle\) to commute with integration. The pointwise weighted-score identity then gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\langle S_{t,x}(y),V(y)\rangle d\mu(x)=p_t(y)\langle\nabla\log p_t(y),V(y)\rangle\).

The scalar pairing is jointly integrable by the preceding Holder argument, so Fubini exchanges the initial-state and output integrals. Integrate the displayed identity in \(y\). Finally \(p_t(y)dy=\rho_t(dy)\), with its explicit measurable finite density, changes the weighted Lebesgue integral into the integral under the interpolation law. Thus \(\int K_t\langle S_{t,x},V\rangle d\mu\,dy=\int\langle\nabla\log p_t,V\rangle d\rho_t\).

Average the component score at a fixed observation, then integrate its pairing with the state test. The mixture-gradient identity converts the result into the pairing with the Lebesgue score under \(\rho_t\).

steps.title: The score identity on the independent-noise space
steps.body:
Apply the measurable pair map \(T_t(x,z)=(x,Y_t(x,z))\) to the continuous pairing \(\langle S_{t,x}(y),V(y)\rangle\). The map-integral theorem expresses its pair-law integral as an integral over the fixed independent initial/noise space. The exact pair-density theorem expresses the same integral as the Gaussian-weighted Lebesgue pairing just evaluated.

Substitute \(Y_t=c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\) in the component score. The residual becomes \(\sqrt{2t}z\), so the result is \(\mathbb E\langle-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z,V(Y_t)\rangle=\mathbb E_{\rho_t}\langle\nabla\log p_t,V\rangle\). With \(V=\nabla\log r_t\), this identity turns the Gaussian-noise part of the raw entropy flux into the Lebesgue-score pairing needed for the full Fisher term.

Use the joint-law identity to rewrite the same integral on the original independent state-noise space. This lets the entropy flux be combined with the exact displacement and gradient-error estimates already proved there.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyMoment.lea.title: The gradient second moment from finite relative entropy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyMoment.lea.summary:
Assume the Gibbs potential is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(L>0\), and the Gibbs law is normalized. Its directional score exponential-moment estimate implies \(\int e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}d u\le2^{d/2}\le e^{d/2}\). To prove this, average the directional inequality against an auxiliary radial Gaussian and evaluate the inner Gaussian integral by completing the square. Tonelli applies before the desired exponential integrability has been established.

The pointwise entropy/exponential Young inequality proves integrability of a nonnegative observable under a finite-relative-entropy law when its exponential is integrable under the reference. Applying its integrated form to \(\| abla U\|^2/(4L)\) yields \(G_\mu\le4L H(\mu\mid u)+2dL\). If \(0<\alpha\le L\), nonnegativity of entropy permits the coefficient \(4L\) to be enlarged to \(4L^2/\alpha\). No initial position moment or transport inequality is assumed.

steps.title: Convex duality for the entropy integrand
steps.body:
Let \(\Phi(a)=a\log a-a+1\), with its continuous value \(\Phi(0)=1\). For \(a>0\), the elementary inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\), applied to \(u=b-\log a\), gives \(e^b\ge a+ab-a\log a\). Rearranging proves \(ab\le\Phi(a)+e^b-1\). The zero-density case is handled separately: its left side is zero, and its right side is \(e^b\ge0\). Thus this entropy/exponential Young inequality remains valid at zero Radon-Nikodym density.

For \(a\ge0\), convex duality for \(a\log a-a+1\) gives \(ab\le a\log a-a+e^b\). The nonnegative entropy correction controls the negative part at \(a=0\) and supports integrability before optimization.

steps.title: Integrability from finite KL and an exponential moment
steps.body:
Write \(a=d\mu/d u\). Finite KL supplies absolute continuity \(\mu\ll u\) and integrability of the log likelihood; equivalently \(\Phi(a)\) is integrable under \( u\). For a measurable nonnegative observable \(f\), the Young inequality gives \(0\le af\le\Phi(a)+e^f\). Both terms on the right are integrable by the finite-KL and exponential-moment hypotheses.

Domination proves \(af\in L^1( u)\). The Radon-Nikodym weighted-integrability equivalence then gives \(f\in L^1(\mu)\). In particular, the moment conclusion is derived before any ordinary expectation is manipulated; it is a consequence of the two integrability hypotheses.

Apply the pointwise inequality with the Radon–Nikodym density and the nonnegative observable. Finite KL and an integrable exponential dominate their product, proving the observable is integrable under the changed law.

steps.title: The entropy variational inequality
steps.body:
Assume \(\int e^f d u\le e^c\). First derive \(f\in L^1(\mu)\) with the preceding theorem. Apply the Young inequality to \(a=d\mu/d u\) and \(f-c\), and integrate: \(\int(f-c)d\mu\le\int\Phi(a)d u+\int e^{f-c}d u-1\).

Probability normalization identifies \(\int\Phi(a)d u\) with the finite relative entropy and \(\int(f-c)d\mu=\int f d\mu-c\). The MGF hypothesis makes \(\int e^{f-c}d u\le1\), canceling the final two terms. Thus \(\int f d\mu\le H(\mu\mid u)+c\), together with the integrability witness used in its derivation. The proof explicitly justifies each weighted integral and subtraction.

Subtract a scalar normalization from the observable before applying the inequality. Choosing that normalization as the logarithm of its exponential moment produces the variational entropy bound with the sharp log-moment term.

steps.title: Integrability of the auxiliary radial Gaussian
steps.body:
For \(b>0\), the real radial Gaussian \(e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is integrable on every finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. This also follows from the complex Gaussian integrability formula at real positive precision: taking its norm gives exactly the displayed real exponential. This supplies the finite integral needed in the Gaussian linearization argument.

A positive Gaussian precision gives integrable radial decay in finite dimension. This supplies the auxiliary Gaussian averaging measure used to turn directional score estimates into a squared-score estimate.

steps.title: The nonnegative radial Gaussian integral
steps.body:
Let \(b>0\) and let \(d\) be finite. The radial Gaussian \(v\mapsto e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is nonnegative and integrable. Its nonnegative extended integral therefore equals its ordinary integral, and Gaussian integration gives

\[\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-b\|v\|^2}dv =\left(\frac\pi b\right)^{d/2}<\infty.\]

The expression on the right is strictly positive because \(b>0\). It supplies the finite nonzero normalizing constant for the auxiliary Gaussian average. In dimension zero the empty product is one, so the same formula remains valid. Nonnegativity also permits Tonelli to exchange this Gaussian averaging with the target integral before their final numerical bound is evaluated.

steps.title: Completing the square in an exponentially tilted Gaussian
steps.body:
Complete the square in \(-b\|v\|^2+\langle g,v\rangle\): it equals \(\|g\|^2/(4b)-b\|v-g/(2b)\|^2\). Exponentiating separates the constant factor \(e^{\|g\|^2/(4b)}\) from a translated radial Gaussian. Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure and the radial normalization give \(\int e^{-b\|v\|^2}e^{\langle g,v\rangle}dv=e^{\|g\|^2/(4b)}(\pi/b)^{d/2}\). The identity is proved for nonnegative integrals before any integrability of a random score is assumed.

Completing the square in the auxiliary variable evaluates its exponentially tilted Gaussian integral. The remaining factor is an exponential of the squared norm of the vector paired with it.

steps.title: From directional moment bounds to a squared-norm moment
steps.body:
Suppose \(\mathbb E e^{\langle g,v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\) for every direction \(v\). Multiply by \(e^{-L\|v\|^2}\) and integrate in \(v\). Tonelli applies to the nonnegative jointly measurable integrand, so the order of integration can be exchanged without assuming the desired exponential moment in advance.

Gaussian linearization identifies the left side with \((\pi/L)^{d/2}\mathbb E e^{\|g\|^2/(4L)}\). The directional MGF bound controls the right side by \(\int e^{-(L/2)\|v\|^2}dv=(2\pi/L)^{d/2}\). Cancel the positive finite factor \((\pi/L)^{d/2}\) in the nonnegative integral inequality to obtain \(\mathbb E e^{\|g\|^2/(4L)}\le2^{d/2}\).

Average the directional exponential bound against the auxiliary Gaussian. Tonelli applies to the positive integrand, and square completion converts its left side into an exponential squared-norm moment.

steps.title: The exponential Gibbs score moment
steps.body:
The smooth Gibbs score has the previously proved directional MGF bound \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\langle abla U,v angle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\), obtained from translation invariance and first-order smoothness. Apply Gaussian averaging with \(g= abla U\). This gives a finite nonnegative exponential integral bounded by \(2^{d/2}\); measurability and this finiteness prove ordinary integrability.

Convert the nonnegative integral back to its real expectation. Since \(\log2\le1\), \(2^{d/2}\le e^{d/2}\), giving the convenient bound \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}\le e^{d/2}\). Only differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, positive \(L\), and finite Gibbs normalization are used; neither convexity nor LSI enters this exponential-moment theorem.

Choosing the auxiliary variance to match \(4L\) gives the factor \(2^{d/2}\). Bounding \(\log2\le1\) turns its logarithm into at most \(d/2\), which is the dimensional constant needed in the score bound.

steps.title: The gradient moment supplied by finite entropy
steps.body:
Apply the entropy inequality with \(f(x)=\| abla U(x)\|^2/(4L)\) and \(c=d/2\). The Gibbs exponential-moment theorem provides both exponential integrability and the MGF bound; finite initial KL provides the absolute-continuity and entropy inputs. Therefore \(\mathbb E_\mu[\| abla U\|^2/(4L)]\le H(\mu\mid u)+d/2\), with this observable integrable under \(\mu\).

Multiply by \(4L>0\), proving \(G_\mu\le4L H(\mu\mid u)+2dL\) and square integrability of the score. The proof also derives finite Gibbs partition from its assumed probability normalization. The estimate is obtained directly from entropy and Gibbs score exponential moments, without a transport comparison.

Use the observable \(\| abla U\|^2/(4L)\) in the entropy variational inequality, then multiply by \(4L>0\). This yields integrability and \(G_0\le4LH_ u(\mu)+2dL\) simultaneously.

steps.title: The gradient moment in the compatible LSI normalization
steps.body:
If \(0<\alpha\le L\), then \(4L\le4L^2/\alpha\). Finite KL is nonnegative, so replacing the direct estimate's coefficient \(4L\) by \(4L^2/\alpha\) preserves the inequality. Thus \(G_\mu\le(4L^2/\alpha)H(\mu\mid\nu)+2dL\), the coefficient used in the ULA one-step calculation. Integrability is inherited from the stronger direct theorem. The preceding compatibility proof derives \(\alpha\le L\) from the log-Sobolev and smoothness hypotheses in positive dimension.

Because KL is nonnegative and \(\alpha\le L\), the coefficient \(4L\) may be enlarged to \(4L^2/\alpha\). The dimensional term stays \(2dL\), giving exactly the form used in one-step forcing absorption.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyEndpoint.l.title: Data processing and a finite-entropy change of reference
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyEndpoint.l.summary:
Apply the same Gaussian transition to the initial law \(\mu\) and the Gibbs law \( u\). Relative-entropy data processing gives \(H(\mu P_t\mid u P_t)\le H(\mu\mid u)\). To compare \(\mu P_t\) with \( u\), use the density bound for \( u P_t\) relative to \( u\).

The logarithmic likelihood through an intermediate reference is the sum of the two logarithmic likelihoods wherever their positive finite density ratios are defined. An integrable upper bound controls its positive part, and the exponential of the negative likelihood controls its negative part. This proves finite entropy against the new reference before the integrated comparison is used. The Gaussian reference-density bound is a constant plus a multiple of \(\| abla U\|^2\), and propagation of the gradient moment makes that correction integrable without an initial position moment.

steps.title: KL is unchanged by adjoining the same independent law
steps.body:
Adjoin the same independent probability innovation \(\eta\) to two finite measures. The log likelihood of \(\mu\otimes\eta\) relative to \(\nu\otimes\eta\) depends only on the first coordinate, so KL is unchanged. The proof uses the standard conditional-product KL identity with the constant Markov kernel \(x\mapsto\eta\); its conditional products are exactly the ordinary product measures. This equality supplies the independent-noise step in data processing.

Taking a product with the same independent probability does not change the likelihood ratio: it depends only on the first coordinate. Integrating out the extra factor therefore preserves the relative entropy.

steps.title: Adding log likelihoods through an intermediate law
steps.body:
For \(\mu\ll ho\ll u\), the Radon-Nikodym chain rule gives \(d\mu/d u=(d\mu/d ho)(d ho/d u)\) almost everywhere under the integrated law \(\mu\). Each factor is positive and finite there: positivity is transported along absolute continuity, and finiteness uses the probability measures' finite Radon-Nikodym derivatives.

On this full-measure set the density ratios are ordinary positive finite values, so the logarithm product rule applies. This proves \(\log(d\mu/d u)=\log(d\mu/d ho)+\log(d ho/d u)\), as an almost-everywhere identity under \(\mu\). The positivity and finiteness checks prevent using logarithm algebra at a zero or infinite density.

For three mutually compatible absolutely continuous laws, their density ratios multiply. Taking logarithms gives the sum of the two log likelihoods on the common full-measure set, before any integration is attempted.

steps.title: An exponential bound on the negative log likelihood
steps.body:
For \(\mu\ll u\), the reciprocal likelihood \(e^{-\log(d\mu/d u)}\) agrees \(\mu\)-almost everywhere with the real reverse Radon-Nikodym derivative \((d u/d\mu)\). This derivative is integrable under \(\mu\), even when \( u\) has a singular component relative to \(\mu\). Thus the negative exponential of the log likelihood is always integrable; finite KL has not been assumed at this stage.

The exponential of the negative log likelihood is a reciprocal density ratio. Its integral under the first law is bounded by the reference mass, giving control of the negative log-likelihood tail.

steps.title: Log-likelihood integrability from an upper bound
steps.body:
Suppose the log likelihood \(\ell=\log(d\mu/d\nu)\) has an integrable upper bound \(b\). Where \(\ell\ge0\), \(|\ell|\le b\le|b|\). Where \(\ell<0\), the elementary exponential bound gives \(|\ell|=-\ell\le e^{-\ell}\). Hence globally \(|\ell|\le|b|+e^{-\ell}\). The first term is integrable by hypothesis, and the second by reciprocal-likelihood integrability. Measurable domination proves \(\ell\in L^1(\mu)\), controlling its negative tail without a lower density bound.

An integrable upper bound controls the positive part, while the exponential estimate controls the negative part. Together they establish absolute integrability of the log likelihood needed for the entropy chain rule.

steps.title: Entropy comparison through a reference density bound
steps.body:
Assume finite \(H(\mu\mid ho)\), \( ho\ll u\), and \(d ho/d u\le e^b\), with \(b\in L^1(\mu)\). Finite KL gives \(\mu\ll ho\), hence \(\mu\ll u\). The density bound transfers to \(\mu\)-almost every point, where positivity of the intermediate density permits logarithms. Thus \(\log(d ho/d u)\le b\).

The log-likelihood chain rule gives \(\log(d\mu/d u)\le\log(d\mu/d ho)+b\). Its right side is integrable. The preceding one-sided integrability theorem therefore proves the new log likelihood integrable and hence \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Only after proving finiteness do we integrate the inequality, yielding \(H(\mu\mid u)\le H(\mu\mid ho)+\mathbb E_\mu b\). Finite entropy against the new reference is a conclusion, rather than an additional premise.

Decompose the log likelihood through the intermediate reference law. Its first entropy is controlled by data processing, and the density-ratio upper bound controls the added term by an integrable observable.

steps.title: Data processing for the Gaussian transition
steps.body:
The interpolation is the measurable image of the initial law times standard Gaussian noise under \((x,z)\mapsto x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). Apply KL data processing to this same map for both initial laws. The independent-noise product identity removes the common Gaussian factor, giving \(H( ho_t^\mu\mid ho_t^ u)\le H(\mu\mid u)\). This argument compares two evolved laws and does not assert that either law is invariant under the discrete step.

Both inputs are passed through the same measurable Gaussian update with the same independent noise law. Relative-entropy data processing therefore bounds the two output laws by the divergence of their inputs.

steps.title: Propagation of the gradient moment
steps.body:
Write \( abla U(Y_t)=[ abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)]+ abla U(X)\). The initial gradient is \(L^2\), and the frozen-error energy theorem makes the bracketed discrepancy \(L^2\) on the independent initial/noise space. Their sum is \(L^2\); the map-measure equivalence transfers this to the interpolation law.

Pointwise, the squared norm of the sum is at most twice each squared norm. Integrate and insert \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The initial-coordinate marginal gives the remaining \(G_0\), so \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\). This proves both integrability and the quantitative estimate without a position moment.

Lipschitzness bounds \(\| abla U(Y_t)\|^2\) by \(2\| abla U(X)\|^2+2L^2\|Y_t-X\|^2\). The exact displacement moment then yields the displayed propagated energy.

steps.title: The interpolation entropy upper bound
steps.body:
Let \( ho_t\) be the evolved input and \(\sigma_t\) the evolved Gibbs target. Data processing gives \(H( ho_t\mid\sigma_t)\le H_0<\infty\). Suppose the reference law satisfies \(d\sigma_t/d u\le\exp(b+c\| abla U\|^2)\), with its absolute continuity retained explicitly.

Finite initial KL first supplies finite \(G_0\) through the direct entropy/score estimate. The propagated gradient-moment theorem then proves \(G_t<\infty\). Consequently the logarithmic reference correction \(b+c\| abla U\|^2\) is integrable under \( ho_t\). Apply the finite-entropy change-of-reference theorem to obtain \(H( ho_t\mid u)<\infty\) and \(H( ho_t\mid u)\le H_0+b+cG_t\). The preceding Gibbs comparison establishes the pointwise reference-density bound.

Insert the explicit log density-ratio bound and the propagated gradient moment into the entropy decomposition. This gives a finite upper bound on interpolation entropy, suitable for sending elapsed time to zero.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InitialEntropy.le.title: An entropy upper bound at the initial time
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InitialEntropy.le.summary:
Let \(H_0<\infty\) be the initial relative entropy and \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu\), finite by the preceding entropy-moment estimate. With \(\delta(t)=1-4tL\), define

\[B(t)=H_0-\frac d2\log\delta(t)+\frac{t}{4\delta(t)}\left[2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\right].\]

The updated Gibbs density comparison, data processing, and propagated gradient bound give finite interpolation entropy \(H_t\le B(t)\) for sufficiently small positive \(t\). The denominator tends to one, so \(B\) is continuous at zero and \(B(0)=H_0\). This upper bound supplies the initial value in the scalar comparison. No initial Fisher information, position second moment, or continuity assumption on the entropy path at zero is needed.

steps.title: The explicit initial-endpoint majorant
steps.body:
Put \(\delta(t)=1-4tL\) and \(G_0=\mathbb E_\mu\|\nabla U\|^2\). Define the explicit upper bound \(B(t)=H_0-\frac d2\log\delta(t)+\frac{t}{4\delta(t)}[2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2]\). The logarithmic term is the normalizer correction from the updated Gibbs density; the final term uses the propagated gradient moment. The definition is a scalar function at all times, while its entropy interpretation below requires \(t>0\) and \(\delta(t)>0\).

The majorant combines the data-processing entropy with the Gaussian normalizer correction and a gradient-energy correction. Its explicit denominator is positive for all sufficiently small positive times, so the expression is an ordinary finite scalar there.

steps.title: The majorant at zero
steps.body:
At \(t=0\), the logarithm has argument \(\delta(0)=1\), hence is zero. The coefficient \(t/(4\delta(t))\) is zero as well. Both correction terms vanish exactly, proving \(B(0)=H_0\). This is a direct algebraic evaluation of the constructed scalar function. No limit of the entropy path is assumed.

At zero the logarithmic term is \(\log1=0\), and the entire energy correction has a factor \(t\). Hence the value is precisely the initial entropy, even when the initial law has no smooth density.

steps.title: Continuity of the majorant at zero
steps.body:
The denominator \(\delta(t)\) has value one at zero, so it stays nonzero locally. The logarithm is continuous at that same positive value. All other terms in \(B\) are polynomial or constant scalar operations. Their continuity proves \(B(t)\to B(0)=H_0\) as \(t\to0\). The initial gradient integral is an already defined scalar; its finiteness in the entropy application is established by the finite-KL moment theorem.

The denominator tends to one and is nonzero near zero. Continuity of the logarithm at one, polynomial factors, and reciprocal then proves continuity of the full majorant at the endpoint.

steps.title: The interpolation entropy lies below the upper bound
steps.body:
For positive \(t\) with \(\delta=1-4tL>0\), choose the comparison Gaussian time \(s=t/\delta\). The updated Gibbs law has an explicit relative density bounded by \((s/t)^{d/2}\exp(s\|\nabla U(y)\|^2/4)\). Since \(s/t=\delta^{-1}\), this is \(\exp[-(d/2)\log\delta+(s/4)\|\nabla U(y)\|^2]\).

The relative density identifies the Radon-Nikodym derivative and proves absolute continuity of the updated Gibbs reference law. The change-of-reference entropy estimate then gives finite \(H_t\) and \(H_t\le H_0-(d/2)\log\delta+(s/4)G_t\). The coefficient \(s/4\) is nonnegative, so inserting \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\) proves \(H_t\le B(t)\).

The density-ratio comparison bounds output entropy by the majorant whenever \(1-4tL>0\). The finite score moment supplies all integrability required for the likelihood decomposition.

steps.title: The entropy majorant on a positive neighborhood
steps.body:
For all sufficiently small positive \(t\), specifically \(t<1/(8L)\), one has \(1-4tL>0\). The previous positive-time entropy bound therefore applies eventually in the right neighborhood of zero, giving \(H_t\le B(t)\). Combined with continuity of \(B\) and \(B(0)=H_0\), this supplies the upper initial boundary used in scalar comparison. It does not insert an assumption that \(H_t\) is differentiable or continuous at zero.

A sufficiently small positive neighborhood satisfies the denominator condition. Thus the entropy upper bound is available along every approach to zero through positive times, exactly the endpoint control used in scalar comparison.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyChainRule..title: An integrated chain rule from spacetime integrability
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyChainRule..summary:
Consider a time-dependent integrand with an integrable initial section, the stated pointwise time derivative, and a jointly integrable derivative on a compact time interval times the spatial measure.
